The Olin McIntosh plant currently monitors and reports on numerous facilities within the plant that are permitted through the EPA and the Alabama Department of Environmental Management (ADEM). The Olin Corp.  (McIntosh Plant) Site (hereinafter, "the Site") is located approximately 1 mile east-southeast of the town of McIntosh, in Washington County, Alabama.  The property is bounded on the east by the Tombigbee River, on the west by land not owned by Olin west of U.S. Highway 43, on the north by the Ciba-Geigy Corporation plant site and on the south by River Road.  The Olin McIntosh plant is an active chemical production facility.  The main plant and associated Olin properties cover approximately 1,500 acres, with active plant production areas occupying approximately 60 acres.

The McIntosh plant today produces chlorine, caustic soda, sodium hypochlorite and sodium chloride and blends and stores hydrazine compounds.  Current active facilities at the plant include: a diaphragm cell chlorine and caustic production process area; a caustic concentration process area; a caustic plant salt process area; a hydrazine blending process area; shipping and transport facilities; process water storage, transport and treatment facilities; and support and office areas.  Olin mines a salt dome through a series of brine production wells located to the west of the active plant facility.  The salt dome cap is at a depth of approximately 500 feet below the surface.  The dome is approximately 4,500 feet in diameter and greater than two miles deep.  Nine brine wells have been completed in the salt dome for the production of brine.  The first six wells were associated with the mercury cell chlor-alkali plant and are no longer in service.  The other three brine production wells were developed in a different portion of the salt dome, have been used exclusively for the diaphragm cell plant, and are still in use.  A tenth cavity was developed in the dome by Olin for use by the Alabama Electri c Cooperative to store high-pressure (1200 psi) air for off-peak power production. These include water and air permits as well as a Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) post-closure permit.  The RCRA post-closure permit requires ground water monitoring for closed RCRA units, including the weak brine pond, the stormwater pond and the brine filter backwash pond.  The post-closure permit also requires corrective action for releases of 40 CFR 261 Appendix VIII constituents from any solid waste management units (SWMUs) at the facility.  There are no active RCRA units at the facility.  Olin also  has permits for three injection wells for mining salt and a neutralization/percolation field.

Investigations have indicated contamination in a 65-acre natural basin, located on the Olin property east of the active plant facilities.  The plant wastewater ditch currently carries the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) discharge and storm water runoff from the manufacturing areas, as well as from some of the west, east and southeast manufacturing areas of Olin property to the Tombigbee River.  From 1952 to 1974, plant waste water discharge was routed through the basin and then to the Tombigbee River.  In 1974, a discharge ditch was constructed to reroute the wastewater directly to the Tombigbee River.

There are two aquifers of concern at the Olin McIntosh site: the Alluvial Aquifer and the Miocene Aquifer.  Based on investigations of the Alluvial Aquifer Olin implemented a ground water corrective action program in 1987.  The ongoing RCRA monitoring includes quarterly sampling of compliance and corrective action wells screened in the Alluvial Aquifer.  The ground water flow direction over the horizontal extent of Operable Unit (OU1) is towards the corrective action wells.

In OU1 there are four (4) general areas which have been evaluated for remediation.  Those areas are:

(1) ground water: the ground water at the site.

(2)  Old Plant (CPC) L andfill (includes Old Plant Landfill Drainage Ditch).  The landfill was used from 1954 to 1972 to neutralize acidic wastewater from the CPC plant operations.

The former CPC plant was constructed in 1952 and initially manufactured monochlorobenzene, adding pentachloronitrobenzene (PCNB) in 1956.  In 1973, the plant was expanded to produce trichloroacetonitrile (TCAN) and 5-ethoxy-3-trichloromethyl-1,2,4-thiadiazole (Terrazole).  The PCNB, TCAN, and Terrazole manufacturing areas were collectively referred to as the crop protection chemicals (CPC) plant.  The CPC plant was shut down in 1982.  In 1984 the plant area was dismantled and covered with an approximately 2-foot-thick recompacted clay cap and topsoil.  The capped area was then vegetated.  The old plant landfill drainage ditch formerly drained from the old plant (CPC) landfill to the wastewater ditch.  Due to extensive earth work in the area associated with the closure of the old plant (CPC) landfill, there is no longer any surface remnant of the ditch.

(3)  Area West of the Former CPC Plant

(4) (Collectively)  The Sanitary Landfills, Lime Ponds, Strong Brine Pond, Mercury Cell Plant and the Well Sand Residue Area.

The Mowbray Engineering Company (MEC) Superfund site consists of an approximate three-acre swamp located on Beeland Street in Greenville, Butler County, Alabama. The actual study area investigated in the Remedial Investigation (RI) and Feasibility Study (FS) includes this swamp area and the MEC plant property located across Beeland Street from the swamp. The swamp area is bordered on the north by a parking area adjacent to the Greenville Apparel Company and on the south and southwest by First Street and Tanyard Branch. The company property is bordered on the west by Beeland Street and by Second Street on the south. The Alabama Power Company (APC) is located across Beeland Street from the swamp and across Second Street from the plant. The study area, which is less than half a mile from downtown Greenville, lies in the 100 year floodplain of Tanyard Branch. The swamp and Tanyard Branch represent a topographic low for the area, which receives surface drainage from the surrounding watershed. The population of Greenville is approximately 8,069 (Census Bureau, 1964 estimate).

The upland area in the northeast corner of the swamp is covered by a stand of loblolly pine with a thick growth of under story shrubs. The northwest corner of the swamp, adjacent to Tanyard Branch, is saturated a majority of the time and is covered with a dense growth of wetland grasses and swamp oak. The central portion of the swamp, comprising the affected area, is essentially denuded of surface vegetation and is stained with a black oily substance, while the southern portion is covered with a diverse group of weeds and underbrush and small pines.

Since the early 1940's, MEC has been in the business of repairing electrical transformers. The company was first located in downtown Greenville, but in the mid 1950's, moved to its present location in a residential/light industrial area on the outskirts of the Greenville business district. From that time, MEC disposed of waste transformer oil by dum ping it onto the ground behind the plant. The oil was allowed to flow into a city storm sewer drain at the property and ultimately into the swampy area across Beeland Street from the MEC plant. MEC continued discharging in this manner until the mid-1970's. Between 1955 and 1974, the company drained, repaired, and refilled an annual average of approximately 1,000 used transformers, each containing approximately nine gallons of oil.

In May 1975, a major fish kill in Tanyard Branch was traced to an overflow of waste oils from a MEC holding tank. As a result, EPA and the Alabama Water Improvement Commission (AWIC) sampled and analyzed soils from the swamp for polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs). At that time, only trace amounts of PCBs were found so no further action was taken by the state. In late 1975, MEC installed two underground storage tanks to collect the waste oil for resale and to prevent future spills.

In 1980, following a second spill and fish kill, the state sampled and found soil PCB levels of approximately 500 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg). During February 1981, EPA responded to the situation on an emergency (spill) basis (under Section 311 of the Clean Water Act [CWA]) and conducted an extensive sampling investigation to determine the extent of contamination in the swamp and to delineate an area for possible removal of contaminated soil to an acceptable level (maximum 50 mg/kg PCBs). Following completion of this investigation, EPA officials proceeded to remove the top six inches of contaminated soil from the swamp. The contaminated soils were sent to an approved, off site hazardous waste facility. In August 1981, after removal of the soil, EPA collected three surface samples from around the study area to verify that PCB levels were below 50 mg/kg. Analytical results from the three samples revealed a maximum concentration of 19 mg/kg.

Also in February 1981, personnel from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) collected catfish, which are bott om feeders, from Tanyard Branch downstream of the site and concluded that PCB concentrations in edible tissue were below the FDA level (2.0 mg/kg). In addition, EPA collected samples of root systems of bullrush (Scirpus sp.) growing in the northwest corner of the swamp to determine if the plants were concentrating PCBs. The analyses of the root systems from two separate plants growing in the water saturated soils indicated levels of PCBs above background in the short, thick rhizomes of the plants. Concurrently with the extent of contamination survey of the swamp, EPA's Environmental Services Division, Ecology Branch, conducted an ecological survey of Tanyard Branch and Persimmon Creek, which joins with Tanyard Branch approximately one mile downstream of the site. The results of this investigation showed that the Tanyard Branch was almost completely devoid of biota from below the swamp to its confluence with Persimmon Creek. Two miles below the confluence, Persimmon Creek biota appeared to be normal.

In February 1981, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) requested assistance from National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) to evaluate occupational exposures to PCBs by employees at MEC. Based on the data collected in this study, NIOSH concluded that workers did not appear to be exposed to excessive levels of PCBs; however, NIOSH recommended that workers reduce skin exposure to transformer oil as much as possible.

In 1982, the MEC site was listed on the National Priorities List (NPL) with a ranking score of 53.67.

No further investigations occurred at the site until November 1983, when grab soil samples were collected from the swamp by the Alabama Department of Environmental Management (ADEM) during a routine inspection at MEC. One of the soil samples collected from the storm water drainage pathway through the site was reported to have a PCB concentration of 1,737 mg/kg. This triggered renewed interest in the site at the federal level.

In  February 1984, the EPA Field Investigation Team (FIT) conducted a site inspection of the swamp to characterize existing conditions and to prepare a detailed sampling study plan to determine the possibility and extent of recontamination of the swamp. In April 1984, FIT conducted a sampling investigation of the swamp and found that soils and groundwater in the swamp were contaminated with PCBs (Aroclor 1260) at levels similar to those measured prior to EPA's 1981 cleanup of the site.

In January 1985, EPA received approval to begin remedial activities and to conduct a Remedial Investigation/ Feasibility Study (RI/FS) at the MEC site. In March 1985, a general site reconnaissance was conducted for which soil and sediment samples were collected from the Alabama Power Company (APC) property and from Tanyard Branch and Persimmon Creek. Since all samples were below the detection limit (1.0 mg/kg) for PCBs, the APC was ruled out as a potential source of PCB contamination to the swamp.

In August 1985, the RI Work Plan received approval by EPA, and a Public Meeting was held to present it to the public and to receive comments. Subsequently, the field work began and was completed in November 1985. The RI /FS Report was completed in July 1986 and was presented to the public for comment on August 12, 1986 at the FS Public Meeting.

A Record of Decision addressing Operable Unit 1 at the MEC site was completed in September of 1986.

The Interstate Lead Company (ILCO) Superfund Site is located approximately 15 miles east of Birmingham, in Leeds, Jefferson County, Alabama. The ILCO Site consists of the ILCO Main Facility and seven satellite sites located in and around the City of Leeds, where lead-contaminated wastes from the ILCO Main Facility were disposed.

The ILCO Main Facility is located at 1247 Borden Avenue on the southwestern side of the City of Leeds. The ILCO Main Facility (including the ILCO Parking Lot across the street) occupies approximately 11.5 acres of real property, most of which is owned by ILCO with a portion owned by Interstate Trucking Company, Inc., an affiliated company. The ILCO Main Facility is bordered by an abandoned foundry and a wooded area to the south, an unnamed tributary to Dry Creek to the west, Borden Avenue and the ILCO Parking Lot to the north, and another business to the east. The area is primarily industrial with a few residences within a half-mile radius.

The satellite sites include the ILCO Parking Lot, located across the street from the ILCO Main Facility; the Gulf/BP Service Station, located in the center of Leeds on U.S. Highway 78; J&L Fabricators, located east of Leeds on U.S. Highway 78; Fleming's Patio, located west of Leeds on Alaska Avenue; the Connell Property, located east of Leeds in St. Clair County; the Acmar Church of God, located off Acmar Road in Moody, Alabama; and the City of Leeds Municipal Landfill, located off Dunavant Road at the end of Peach Street.

ILCO operated a secondary lead smelting and lead battery recycling business from approximately 1970 to 1992 at the ILCO Main Facility. In March 1992, ILCO ceased operating pursuant to an order of a state court of Alabama. ILCO manufactured refined lead alloys through the smelting and refining of lead-bearing scrap materials. The primary materials reclaimed by ILCO were discarded lead-acid automobile and industrial batteries. The used batteries were cracked open and the lead pla tes and lead oxides were smelted in a blast furnace. Furnace slag was produced as a by-product and is regulated under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) as a characteristic hazardous waste due to its lead content. Wastewater treatment sludge and baghouse dust were also generated. Wastewater treatment sludge is a RCRA regulated hazardous waste and baghouse dust is a RCRA listed hazardous waste.

ILCO stored furnace slag, battery chips, and wastewater treatment sludge in piles on the ILCO Main Facility. Furnace slag generated by ILCO was used as fill material at the ILCO Main Facility and at the satellite sites. Wastewater treatment sludge and battery casings were also disposed of at the ILCO Main Facility and at some of the satellite sites.

In May 1984, the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the Alabama Department of Environmental Management (ADEM) conducted a joint inspection of the ILCO Main Facility, which was found to be in violation of the interim status standards set forth in RCRA.

In March 1985, the United States brought suit against ILCO and its principal, Diego Maffei, seeking injunctive relief, penalties, and damages for violations of the Clean Water Act and RCRA. The government also sought to recover response costs pursuant to CERCLA for a removal action taken by EPA at the Acmar Church of God satellite site. The complaint also included a count for corrective action at the ILCO Main Facility. The case was brought in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Alabama (District Court Case). The State of Alabama intervened in the litigation asserting violations of Alabama's Water Pollution Control Act and Hazardous Waste Management and Minimization Act.

There was a partial settlement of the District Court Case in August 1988. A partial consent decree was entered requiring ILCO to conduct all necessary corrective actions and remediation of contaminated sediment in the surrounding waterways.

T he outstanding issues were tried in July and August 1988. On December 10, 1990, the district court issued an Order and Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law holding that the defendants had violated the Clean Water Act and RCRA and that injunctive relief and penalties were appropriate. The court also found that the defendants were liable for all response costs incurred by the United States in connection with the removal action at the Acmar Church of God satellite site.

In its December 10, 1990 Order, the district court did not enter a judgment but ordered the parties to endeavor to reach an agreement as to the relief which should be provided. The parties were unable to come to such an agreement, and each submitted a proposed final judgment. On October 8, 1991, the court entered a judgment. The district court granted injunctive relief and assessed a penalty of two million dollars against ILCO, in favor of the United States, for violations of RCRA and the Clean Water Act. In addition, the district court entered judgment in favor of the United States against ILCO and Diego Maffei, in the amount of $845,033.40, as reimbursement for response costs for the removal action at the Acmar Church of God satellite site. The district court also awarded a penalty in the amount of $1.5 million in favor of the State of Alabama. On appeal, the Eleventh Circuit Court issued a decision in favor of the United States and the State of Alabama on every issue and affirmed the district court's award of civil penalties and response costs.

In June 1986, the ILCO Site (including the ILCO Main Facility and the seven satellite sites) was placed on the National Priorities List (NPL) of uncontrolled hazardous waste sites.

EPA conducted a Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (RI/FS) of the satellite sites (Operable Unit One) which was completed in July 1991. A proposed plan was issued shortly after completion of the RI/FS. After a public comment period, a Record of Decision (ROD) was s igned on September 30, 1991, which set forth the selected remedy for Operable Unit One.

When ILCO ceased operations in March 1992, EPA initiated a removal action to mitigate the imminent threat associated with the abandoned ILCO Main Facility. During the removal action at the ILCO Main Facility, approximately 5,368 tons of lead contaminated slag, found stored in different areas around the facility, were removed to a permitted hazardous waste landfill. Approximately 200,000 gallons of lead contaminated sludge found in the onsite waste water treatment system was removed, stabilized, and stockpiled onsite with contaminated soils excavated from the facility. Acid from several impoundments was collected and treated in the onsite wastewater treatment system, in addition to approximately 15,000,000 gallons of wastewater. The battery cracking building, the furnace building, and the small slag vault were demolished and decontaminated due to extensive lead contamination. The contents of the small slag vault were removed and stockpiled onsite with the contaminated soils. Waste encountered during the demolition of the furnace building included lead waste, baghouse dust, and a sulfur residue from the emissions system. The lead waste was stockpiled inside a building onsite. The baghouse dust was placed into two roll-off boxes, covered, labeled K069, and also stored inside a building onsite. The sulfur residue found inside the duct pipe was placed on the contaminated soil stockpile. During the demolition of the battery cracking building, process soils from the battery cracking operation were removed and stockpiled inside a building onsite. The process soils consisted of a mixture of battery chips and contaminated soils.

EPA conducted a RI/FS of the ILCO Main Facility (Operable Unit Two), which was completed in June 1994. A proposed plan was issued shortly after completion of the RI/FS. After a public comment period, a ROD was signed on October 13, 1995, which set forth the s elected remedy for Operable Unit Two. The ROD for Operable Unit One was also amended as part of the ROD for Operable Unit Two.

The third and final operable unit consists of surface water, sediment, and biota contamination attributable to the ILCO Main Facility. EPA also conducted a RI/FS for Operable Unit Three which was completed in April 1995. The proposed plan setting forth EPA's preferred cleanup alternative was issued in July 1995.

When the ROD was prepared, the ILCO site was not operational. The future land use envisioned for the purposes of a human risk assessment was residential.

A ROD addressing OU-3 was completed in September 1995.

ROD Amendment for OUs 1, 2, & 3 (2012)

Data collected since the initial remedy selection indicate that the soil, sediment, and groundwater remedies specified for the City of Leeds Landfill, Gulf/British Petroleum (BP) Service Station, and Dry Creek and unnamed tributary are no longer necessary. Also, recent data support amending the groundwater remedy for the Interstate Lead Company, Inc. (ILCO) Main Facility and Parking Lot to In Situ Precipitation. The new circumstances support the selection of these amended remedies. The previously selected remedies for the other portions of the ILCO Site remain unchanged by this document. This decision represents the final remedy selected for the ILCO Site. Following completion of this remedial action, the ILCO Site may qualify for deletion from the National Priorities List and may also meet criteria that will allow it to be ready for reuse.

An Amendment to the Record of Decision addressing Operable Units 1, 2, and 3 of the Interstate Lead Co. (ILCO) Site was completed in September, 2012.

The 220-acre Stauffer Chemical (Cold Creek Plant) Superfund Site is located in Mobile County, in Bucks, Alabama, approximately 25 miles north of the city of Mobile.  The Site is situated between Highway 43 to the west and the Mobile River to the east.  Surrounding land use in the vicinity of the Site is predominantly industrial, related to chemical processing and electrical power generation.  The Alabama Power Company Barry Steam Generating Plant is located immediately north of the Site.  The Stauffer Chemical (LeMoyne Plant) Superfund Site borders the Site to the south.  Other chemical processing facilities surround the Site to the north, west, and south.  Most land east of the Site (across the Mobile River) is undeveloped riverbottom swamp with some timber harvesting use.  Some small residential communities are located within a three mile radius.

The Cold Creek plant began operating in 1966 under the ownership of the Stauffer Chemical Company and is currently owned by ICI Americas, Inc. Until 1974, an unknown amount of sludges and solid wastes containing a variety of herbicides and pesticides were placed in two waste disposal sites, referred to as the Cold Creek North and South Landfills. Both were closed in 1974 with geomembrane caps and side-wall liners. One clay-lined lagoon was used for neutralization of wastewater until 1975. It was closed in 1978. A new membrane-lined pond was constructed to replace it and is currently in use.

The aforementioned disposal practices led to ground water contamination. This was recognized by Stauffer and the Alabama Department of Environmental Management (ADEM) in the early 1970s when contaminants were detected in both onsite and offsite wells. Several improvements and waste-handling modifications were made including the construction of lined wastewater ponds and the closure of some of the old unlined ponds. In 1973, Stauffer installed twenty-one ground water monitoring wells. By 1977, the water quality had deteriorated su bstantially. The Stauffer Site Cold Creek Plant was placed on the National Priorities List (NPL) in September 1983 and is ranked number 221.

In November 1984, EPA Region IV sent a general notice letter to Stauffer Chemical Company notifying them of potential liability for contamination at the Stauffer Chemical Site. EPA's contractor performed preliminary sampling in May 1985 to assist in preparing a work plan for the Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (RI/FS). The Stauffer Chemical Company agreed to conduct the RI/FS under a consent agreement with EPA, and the present owners, Akzo and ICI, completed the RI in May 1988. A draft FS report was submitted by the present owner/operator in July 1988. EPA required modifications to the FS report in comment letters sent in November 1988 and January 1989. A revised report was submitted in June 1989. This report was reviewed by EPA and was partially disapproved.

The Chlorine Plant Surge Pond was certified clean-closed in September 1988 according to the approved closure plan. The Old Brine Mud Pond has been delisted. An additional provision was included in this permit as a result of the 1984 Hazardous and Solid Waste Amendments to the Resource Conservation and Recover Act (RCRA). This is the requirement of 40 CFR, Section 264.101, which addresses prior or continuing releases at solid waste management units. The requirement has been satisfied by adoption of the RI/FS work plan, developed under CERCLA, into the permit. The permit will be modified once the Record of Decision (ROD) has been issued.
Surface runoff from the eastern portion of the Site drains to the Cold Creek Swamp, which borders the Site to the east.  Surface runoff on the active portions of the facility is either captured by the plant drainage system, or drains to the Cold Creek Swamp.  At the Old Neutralization Pond, rainwater tends to pond due to the locally depressed soil conditions and berming of adjacent structures.  Surface runoff at this potentia l source area is primarily to the South Rainwater Pond, which supplies dilution water to Zeneca's on-site wastewater biotreatment plant.

The Site is located on the Mobile River Valley water-table aquifer which is recharged through infiltration from the Mobile River, Cold Creek Swamp and associated wetlands, and rainfall.  This aquifer is the principal source of water for users within the Valley.  The regional horizontal direction of the ground water flow would normally (if not altered by pumping) be eastward toward the Mobile River.  Presently, the ground water flows to the south-southeast due to the local influence of pumping at Courtaulds Fibers and from interceptor wells at the southern limits of the LeMoyne Plant.  Ground water usage within the Site area is believed to be limited to the upper aquifer above a 20 foot thick clay layer which separates the shallow aquifer into two water-bearing zones and produces semi-confined conditions in certain areas.

The proposed cleanup addressed the on-site source of contamination at the Cold Creek Plant, which includes the Cold Creek North and South Landfills, the Cold Creek LeCreek Wastewater Treatment Pond (WWTP), and the Old Neutralization Pond.

The North Landfill occupies 1.8 acres at the eastern edge of the active plant area and was used from 1970 to 1974 for disposal of process and non-process waste materials.  The process materials were primarily waste products of thiocarbamate production and by-product brine filtration.  The South Landfill occupies 0.2 acres and was used for disposal of waste materials in a similar fashion to the North Landfill.  The closure of both sites, which occurred in 1974, consisted of the installation of a combination clay and geomembrane cap.  A statistical evaluation of ground water chemical data was performed using the Analysis of Variance technique.  Based on these analyses, it was concluded that no statistically significant evidence exists to suggest that contaminants are leachi ng from either landfill.

The Cold Creek LeCreek WWTP is currently used to collect stormwater runoff from the plant site, and treated sanitary wastewater.  The pond was constructed in 1975 to serve as a check point for runoff; it has a recompacted clay base, a membrane liner and a leachate collection system.  From approximately December 1975 to June 1993, discharge from the Cold Creek LeCreek WWTP was to the Mobile River under the old discharge permit.  Under the new discharge permit (effective April 1993), collected wastewater and stormwater are to be used as process water for the new onsite wastewater biotreatment plant.  The presence of thiocarbamates in ground water and soil samples were detected at concentrations below their target concentration.  The presence of molinate was detected in ground water above the target concentration in only one of four samples.  Based on these analyses, it was concluded that no statistically significant evidence exists to suggest that contaminants have leached from this unit.

The Old Neutralization Pond was constructed during 1966-1967 on the southern portion of the Cold Creek Plant, and covers one-third of an acre.  Closure of the pond occurred in 1976 by filling with native soil materials.  This pond was utilized for the equalization of neutralized wastewater.   Soil samples taken during the initial 1986 remedial investigation revealed concentrations of thiocarbamates as high as 25 mg/kg.  Four consecutive ground water sampling events exceeded the 14 ug/L target concentration ranging from 26 to 400 ug/L.  During a 1993 limited field investigation, thiocarbamates were found in all soil borings.  Maximum thiocarbamate concentrations appear to be located in the western portion of the Old Neutralization Pond.

The Remedial Investigation, conducted by the owner/operator under a consent agreement with the EPA, was divided into two major subtasks - source and area characterization. Source characterization was performed by soil  sampling around the landfills and ponds, and sampling of pond liquids. Ground water sampling of two newly installed and thirteen existing monitoring wells was also conducted. All of these wells were analyzed for location-specific compounds, and three of them were also analyzed for priority pollutants. Area characterization involved sampling 36 site area wells for location-specific compounds. Seven of the 36 wells were also analyzed for priority pollutants. In addition, two surface water samples and two soil samples were collected offsite to determine background concentration of the contaminants of concern. 

As a result of the above analysis, ten areas were identified as possibly needing remediation. These included five inactive ponds, three landfills, the Cold Creek Swamp, and the ground water. The ponds and landfills are classified as Solid Waste Management Units (SWMUs) under RCRA regulations. EPA has grouped these units into nine Solid Waste Management Unit Areas. They are as follows:

SWMU Area 1:  Cold Creek LeCreek Wastewater Treatment Pond, Cold Creek Old Neutralization Pond, Cold Creek South Landfill
SWMU Area 2:  Old Carbon Disulfide Wastewater Treatment Pond and Old Carbon Tetrachloride Plant Wastewater Treatment Pond
SWMU Area 3:  Cold Creek North Landfill
SWMU Area 4:  Old Brine Mud Pond
SWMU Area 5:  New Carbon Tetrachloride Plant Wastewater Treatment Pond
SWMU Area 6:  LeMoyne LeCreek Wastewater Treatment Pond
SWMU Area 7:  Old Chlorine Plant Wastewater Treatment Pond
SWMU Area 8:  LeMoyne Landfill
SWMU Area 9:  Halby Pond

Two previous Records of Decision (ROD) have been signed for operable units (OUs) 1 and 3.  The ROD for OU1, signed September 27, 1989, addresses ground water contamination, and the OU3 ROD, signed September 17, 1993, addressed contamination of Cold Creek Swamp.  This ROD addresses OU2, source areas at the site. 

The 1995 ROD for OU 2 addressed the following potential groundwater contamination source areas:

1. Co ld Creek North Landfill
2. Cold Creek South Landfill
3. Cold Creek LeCreek Wastewater Treatment Pond
4. Cold Creek Old Neutralization Pond

For the Cold Creek LeCreek Wastewater Treatment Pond, the selected remedy was no further action. For the Cold Creek North Landfill and Cold Creek South Landfill, the selected remedy was cap maintenance with continued groundwater monitoring.

For the contaminated soil in the Old Neutralization Pond the remedy selected in the ROD consists of bioremediation of contaminated soil, backfilling, and capping the pond. Major components are as follows:

-Perform a treatability study to determine the design and operational parameters for
the ex-situ land treatment of contaminated soils.
-Set up the treatment pad.
-Excavate contaminated soil and place it in the treatment cell.
-Periodically fertilize, irrigate, till and sample the soils until they have reached the target concentration.
-Backfill excavated areas with clean and treated soil.
-Construct a cap equivalent to a Resource Conservation and Recovery Act Subtitle C cap.
-Conduct groundwater monitoring for 30 years.
-Maintain the integrity of the cap.

The ROD established soil cleanup levels for six thiocarbamate herbicides: s-ethyl dipropylthiocarbamate, vernolate, pebulate, molinate, butylate, and cycloate.

A treatability study report was completed in January 1998 and concluded that the ROD soil cleanup levels for the six thiocarbamate chemicals of concern could be achieved by bioremediation. The report also concluded that it would take significantly longer to achieve the performance standards contained in the ROD.

An ESD for OU 2 was completed in June 1999.

Between 1953 and 1966, the Stauffer Chemical Company (Stauffer) built and started operating two chemical manufacturing plants on Highway 43 in Mobile County, Alabama. The Cold Creek Plant (CCP) and the adjacent LeMoyne Plant are located approximately 25 miles north of Mobile, Alabama, in the communitie s of Bucks and Axis respectively. Both plants are separate Superfund Sites: the CCP Site and the Stauffer Chemical Co. (LeMoyne Plant) Site (LP Site). The CCP Site encompasses approximately 200 acres situated between Highway 43 toward the west and the Cold Creek Swamp and the Mobile River toward the east. Surrounding land use in the vicinity of the CCP Site is predominately industrial, related to chemical processing and electrical power generation. The Alabama Power Company Barry Steam Generating Plant is located immediately north of the CCP Site. Other major chemical processing facilities surround the Site to the north, west, and south. The LP Site borders the CCP Site to the south. Timber production (southern pine) is the other major land use in the immediate vicinity. Most land east of the project site (across the Mobile River) is undeveloped river bottom swamp with some timber harvesting use. Some small residential communities are located within a three-mile radius.

Stauffer began agricultural chemical manufacturing operations at the CCP Site in 1966. Ownership of the CCP Site property later transferred to ICI Americas, Inc., which later became Syngenta, the Potential Responsible Party (PRP) for the CCP Site. Agricultural pesticides and herbicides including thiocarbamates were manufactured at the CCP Site. 

Operations of the chemical manufacturing facility at the CCP Site ceased in 2008, and facility decommissioning operations were completed in October 2009. Dismantling of the manufacturing process area was completed in December 2010.

During chemical manufacturing operations at the CCP Site, an unknown amount of sludge and solid wastes containing a variety of herbicides and pesticides were placed in two waste disposal areas known as the Cold Creek North and South Landfills. Both landfills were closed in 1974 with geo-membrane caps and sidewall liners. Until 1975, the Old Neutralization Pond (ONP), a clay-lined lagoon, was used for wastewater neutralizat ion. In 1978, this lagoon was closed and replaced with a membrane-lined pond that held non-process wastewater and storm water from the CCP Site process units.

In the early 1970s, groundwater contamination was detected by Alabama Department of Environmental Management (ADEM) in on-site and off-site wells at the Stauffer Sites. Disposal practices at the Sites contributed to the groundwater contamination. The primary contamination detected on the CCP Site was the thiocarbamate herbicides in the subsurface soils in the closed ONP and in the groundwater beneath the Site.

Following the discovery of groundwater contamination, Stauffer installed 21 groundwater monitoring wells at the Sites in 1973. Although by 1977, Stauffer had completed improvements to their waste handling practices, groundwater quality at the Sites had continued to deteriorate. As a result, Stauffer installed an additional seven observation wells on the southern property line of the LP Site. Based on the results of a hydrogeological investigation, Stauffer installed three intercept wells and a groundwater treatment system, utilizing an air stripper, on the LP Site in late 1980. This groundwater treatment system was approved by Alabama Water Improvement Commission (AWTC).

An assessment of the Stauffer Sites was conducted in 1982 by the Alabama Department of Public Health (ADPH) in response to submissions made by Stauffer to the House Committee on Interstate Commerce (The Eckhardt Survey). At the recommendation of ADPH, additional monitoring wells were installed around the LeMoyne Landfill. Data from these wells formed the basis for Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to place the CCP and LP Sites on the National Priorities List (NPL). EPA proposed the CCP and LP Sites for listing on the NPL in September 1983 and finalized the listing in September 1984.

In November 1984, EPA Region 4 sent a general notice letter to Stauffer notifying them of potential liability for contamination at the Stauff er Sites. Camp, Dresser & McKee, Inc, under contract with EPA, performed preliminary sampling in May 1985 to assist in preparing a work plan for the Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (RI/FS). On January 21,1986, Stauffer agreed to conduct the RI/FS under an Administrative Order on Consent.

The RI/FS divided the Sites into five areas for investigation: 1) inactive ponds; 2) the Old Carbon Disulfide Plant Wastewater Treatment Pond drainage line; 3) landfills; 4) the Cold Creek Swamp; and 5) groundwater.

The OU2 Remedial Design (RD) was approved on September 1998. The Remedial Action Work Plan (RAWP) developed to implement the design was approved in October 1998. The RAWP called for implementing the design in three phases:

Phase 1 - Civil and Site Development for Biopile Remediation including excavation of contaminated soils from the ONP and the construction of an ex-situ biological treatment cell (biopile). 

Phase 2 - Remediation Operation and Maintenance (O&M) and Monitoring involving performance of biopile O&M activities until Record of Decision (ROD) Performance Standards have been achieved or upon EPA approval to discontinue treatment. Additional requirements included implementing O&M activities (i.e., long-term ground-water monitoring and cap maintenance) at the ONP (following remediation), the North Landfill, and the South Landfill.

Phase 3 - Civil and Site Development for Cap Closure and Site Restoration including backfill of the excavated ONP area with treated soil and construction of a Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) Subtitle C cap over the area.

Phase 1 of the Remedial Action started on September 13, 1999 and was completed in late December 1999. A total of 3181 cubic yards of contaminated soils and debris were excavated from the ONP. Of this total, 528 cubic yards were shipped off-site for disposal and the remaining 2653 cubic yards were placed in the biopile for treatment. A detailed description of  the soil excavation  and the construction of the biopile can be found in the February 2000 Final Construction Report. A copy of the report can be found in the CCP Site Administrative Record.

Phase 2 of the Remedial Action started operation in March 2000 and continued until March 2004. During this period the biopile was actively operated and monitored. It has been calculated that the treatment operation reduced the mass of the contaminants in the soils by an average of 50%. The treatment did not achieve the 1995 OU2 ROD Performance Standards at all monitoring points in the biopile. From March 2004 to present, the biopile has been used to store the treated soils.

The issuance of this Explanation of Significant Differences (ESD) will start Phase 3 of the Remedial Action. The PRP will develop, for the EPA's review and approval, a RD detailing how the biopile will be dismantled, how the biopile soils will be placed back in the ONP excavation, and how a RCRA Subtitle C cap will be constructed over the ONP area.

An Explanation of Significant Differences addressing Operable Unit 02 of the Stauffer Chemical Co. (Cold Creek Plant) Site was completed in August 2012.

OU03:

Two separate areas within Cold Creek Swamp, the Upper Arm Swamp Zone (UASZ)  and the Middle Lower Swamp Transition Zone (MLSTZ), have been identified as containing the highest levels of mercury. The UASZ is a tributary to Cold Creek and joins Cold Creek upstream of the MLSTZ, which is situated near the mouth of Cold Creek at the Mobile River.

Cold Creek Swamp received effluent from the LeMoyne and Cold Creek plants as well as from a previous tenant, HCC, until approximately 1975. The effluent from the LeMoyne Plant included discharges of process waters from several production units, one of which contained mercury. Neutralized waste brine from the Cold Creek Plant was also discharged to the swamp during the late 1960s. Data from the June 1988 Remedial Investigation Report indicate that the contribution from HCC  may have included triocyanate and metal-contaminated wastewater. Processed wastewater discharge to Cold Creek Swamp ceased in 1975 when an effluent transport line was constructed to convey wastewater from treatment areas directly to the Mobile River, subject to a NPDES permit. Treated effluent discharge to the Mobile River is conducted in accordance with Syngenta and Akzo individual NPDES permits, and no wastewater is currently discharged to the swamp.

After groundwater contamination (carbon tetrachloride and other volatile organic compounds) was discovered in the early to mid-1970s, investigations of potential sources were initiated. A number of monitoring wells were installed and groundwater analysis commenced. A limited swamp sediment sampling program was also conducted. In 1982, an assessment of the plant sites was made by the Alabama Department of Public Health (ADPH) in response to submissions made by SCC to the House Committee on Interstate Commerce ("the Eckhardt Survey"). At the request of the ADPH, additional monitoring wells were installed around the three closed landfills. In 1983, EPA concluded that data from these monitoring wells justified inclusion of the former SCC chemical facilities on the NPL.

In early 1986, field activities for a Remedial Investigation (RI) were initiated, including soil borings and tissue sampling within the swamp, as well as soil borings and groundwater sampling around existing ponds and landfills on the Plant Sites. Priority pollutant volatile or semi-volatile organic compounds were not detected in any of the samples that were analyzed. Mercury was the only priority pollutant detected at concentrations exceeding trace element content ranges for natural soils. Thiocarbamates were found at concentrations ranging from below method detection levels (BMDL) to 1.8 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg). The maximum concentration of mercury was 690 mg/kg in soils sampled from the Upper Swamp.

No mercury was detected in any of the  groundwater samples taken at the Plant Sites. It was concluded that residual mercury in swamp soils existed in a relatively insoluble form and that mercury contamination was not being transmitted from the swamp to underlying ground water. Mercury concentrations in biological tissue samples ranged from below quantitation limits to 3.1 mg/kg based on whole-body analysis, with an average concentration of 1.43 mg/kg. Of the 80 fish collected, based on the low average weights and few numbers of predatory species collected, it suggests these mercury concentrations are largely representative of forage-type fish (e.g., sunfish). The largest average fish (41.7grams = 1.5 ounce) was collected in the Upper Swamp. This sample also had the fewest number of fish (6) in the composite sample and the highest mercury concentration suggesting predatory fish (e.g., largemouth bass) may be a major contributor to the sample result.

Surface water samples were collected from two locations in small unnamed tributaries to Cold Creek. No priority pollutants, organics, or polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) were detected in these samples. The only compounds detected were mercury at 0.0002 grams per liter (g/L) and zinc at 0.31 milligrams per liter (mg/L).

In a letter dated May 4, 1990, EPA requested that Akzo and ICI Americas (ICIA, now Zeneca) initiate a Supplemental Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (RI/FS) to further examine the nature and extent of contamination within the swamp. The RI Report (EA 1992) presented the findings of this staged supplemental study, which focused on the nature and extent of contamination in Cold Creek Swamp.

Assessment of the sediment data indicated that mercury was the primary COPC. Other COPCs included thiocarbamates, aluminum, cadmium, copper, silver, and zinc. Detailed examination of these compounds based on risk assessment and mineralogical analyses revealed that mercury was the only COC. One source of mercury in Cold Creek Swamp is presumably  the former chloro-alkali plant discharge. 

A Feasibility Study (FS) was conducted to analyze remedial alternatives. EPA evaluated each of the alternatives based upon cost, technical feasibility, institutional requirements, and the degree of protection. After considering the public's comments on the preferred alternative, EPA signed and issued the ROD in September 1993.

The 1993 Record of Decision for 0U3 specified the following major requirements:
- Constructing sheet pile stream barriers isolating the UASZ and MLSTZ;
- Creating wetlands in the surface water diversion channel;
- Excavating contaminated sediments from within the MLSTZ with placement of material in the UASZ prior to constructing the multi-media cap (the extent of excavation will be determined in the Remedial Design phase);
- Constructing a multi-media cap on the UASZ with surface water diversion;
- Implementing a 10-year annual monitoring program within Cold Creek Swamp;
- Performing long-term monitoring to assess UASZ cap effectiveness; and
- Developing institutional controls.

In May 1996, an Explanation of Significant Differences (ESD) for 0U3, EPA removed the 1993 ROD requirement for a levee between the Cold Creek Swamp and the Mobile River. The ESD also provided the requirement that the long-term monitoring program for the Cold Creek Swamp include monitoring a section of the Mobile River.

Implementation of the 1993 ROD has been under discussion with all stakeholders since the 1998 formation of the Cold Creek Swamp Project Alliance (Alliance). A major concern was the excavation requirement in the 1993 ROD, which would have destroyed a large area of existing wetlands and the loss of significant upland woodland habitat resulting from the construction of the surface water diversion. The Alliance requested EPA's reconsideration of the selected remedy because the permanent loss of significant habitat could not be adequately mitigated for a long period. While wetlands can be physically  constructed in a relatively short period, natural reestablishment of the complex biota, including mature wooded upland area, is a time consuming process.

Additional monitoring was conducted in Cold Creek Swamp and background locations in 2000, 2001, and 2006. The 2000/2001 data were collected to establish a baseline of mercury concentrations in Cold Creek Swamp, assess if there were any changes in mercury concentrations since previous investigations, and identify regional background mercury concentrations. The results of the sampling were presented in the EPA 2002 Report entitled "Final Report of Cold Creek Swamp Operable Unit 3 Ecological Baseline Investigations".

The data indicated that mercury was present in soil, sediment, and biota from each of the background locations. Within Cold Creek Swamp, sediment mercury concentrations were highest in the UASZ. The EPA 2002 Report also concluded that mercury concentrations in soils in the MLSTZ decreased significantly between 1994 and 2000. The data also indicated that for sediment MLSTZ mercury concentrations were comparable to background. For biota, mercury was detected in each of the samples, including those from background locations. For example, fish tissue mercury concentrations were as high as 3.5 mg/kg in fish from the Southeastern background location, which was higher than the maximum detected concentration for the UASZ fish (3.4 mg/kg). Data for other organisms (e.g., small mammals and lizards) were limited, but concentrations were much lower than other types of organisms. Subsequent biological sampling, conducted in 2006, focused on fish tissue. Collectively, the results from the 2000/2001 sampling indicated that mercury occurrence was widespread throughout the area due to non-Site related sources, primarily due to airborne transport (e.g., burning of fossil fuels for electrical power generation), and possible contribution from chemical processing activities from other chemical plants in the vicinity of  Cold Creek Swamp. Possible mercury contribution from chemical processing activities at other chemical plants in the vicinity of the swamp was also considered, but it was not investigated. Therefore, no specific conclusions were made with respect to potential contribution from other industrial activities in the vicinity. Nonetheless, data from the sampling and analysis of background locations indicate that non-site related sources likely have contributed some level of mercury to the Cold Creek Swamp, presumably principally through air transport- Average mercury concentrations in several of the background samples (i.e., sediment, fish) was comparable to many of the samples from Cold Creek Swamp.

The background locations were relied upon as a point of reference within the EPA document in order to discover trends in the data and determine if the mercury measured in the Upper and Transition zones demonstrated significant (statistically based) differences from ambient mercury conditions. A description of the background locations used within the EPA report is as follows:

- The background locations were selected to represent neighboring conditions in all four cardinal directions from the nearby steam plant and industrial facilities to account for downwind air deposition of mercury regardless of the direction of the prevailing wind.

- A fifth location (designated as near-site or central) lies between the Cold Creek drainage and the steam plant to the north.

- All background locations are outside of the Cold Creek drainage, or sufficiently upstream of the site to be above the influence of back-flooding from the Mobile River.

- Locations were selected to match the hydrogeomorphic setting of the Upper or Transition swamps and to ensure capture of animals whose home ranges do not overlap with 0U3.

In 2006, Akzo Nobel's contractor conducted an additional round of monitoring consistent with the sampling that was conducted in 2000/2001. The data were reported in  the 2007 report "Cold Creek Swamp Supplemental Investigation'' and indicated that mercury concentrations in sediment were highest in the UASZ. The data also showed that MLSTZ soil mercury concentrations continued to decrease.

A Focused Feasibility Study (FFS) was completed in July 2010 that compared the 1993 Remedy with the 1993 Remedial Alternative No. 3: Excavation of UASZ with Off-Site Disposal and natural recovery of the MLSTZ, with Enhanced Performance Monitoring; with the 1993 Remedial Alternative No. 4: Excavation of UASZ with On-Site Disposal and natural recovery of the MLSTZ, with Enhanced Performance Monitoring; and with a new In-Situ Capping Technology Alternative for the UASZ and natural recovery of the MLSTZ, with Enhanced Performance Monitoring. The FFS determined that the new alternative is superior to the 1993 Remedy and the 1993 Remedial Alternatives No. 3 and 4, when short-term effectiveness, implementability, and costs are considered.

Cleanup levels for OU3 were initially established in the FFS to address potential impacts to ecological receptors. Specifically the cleanup levels were developed based on the uptake of mercury into the biota of Cold Creek Swamp. Because of the nature of mercury in the wetland system and the fact that the potential for long-term methylation of mercury can affect the amount of methylmercury within sediment over time, the measurement of mercury body burdens was considered the most accurate method for determining if contaminates in Cold Creek Swamp are at levels which may adversely affect the ecosystem. Thus, in 1993 a target level of 0.5 ppm mercury in whole body tissue of bottom feeders, carnivorous, and omnivorous fish was established. These values were based upon the proposed levels set by EPA's Office of Science and Technology that were based on human health consumption; however, they were interpolated for consumption of upper trophic level ecological consumers. In addition, a standard of 1.1 ppm mercury in mu scle, kidney, and brain tissue of upper trophic level mammals had been established based upon a value of safety as interpolated from the literature review of Eisler.

Since 1993, information has become available that has resulted in the revision of the target level for mercury in fish tissue as well as the standard in tissue of upper trophic level mammals. The target level in fish tissue has been revised from 0.5 ppm of whole body of bottom feeders, carnivorous, and omnivorous fish to 0.3 ppm mercury in edible fish fillet and the standard for upper trophic level mammals of 1.1 ppm has been replaced by a performance measure of 0.2 ppm mercury in whole body of forage-sized fish or background if 0.2 ppm is not attainable.

The Perdido Groundwater Contamination Site is located in Perdido, Baldwin County, Alabama.  In 1965 a train derailment occurred in the town.  In 1981 the Alabama Department of Public Health reported problems in domestic water supplies.  In 1982 the Baldwin County Health Officer recommended that residents stop drinking their water.  

In 1983 the site was listed on the final National Priorities List. 

In 1983 the Railroad installed the Perdido water system.  CSX Transportation, Inc. installed the water line, conducted the Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study at the site and has expressed a desire to perform the selected remedy.

A Record of Decision addressing Operable Unit 01 at the Perdido Groundwater Contamination Site was completed in September 1988.

The Redwing Carriers, Inc. (Saraland) Site ("Redwing Site or the Site") is 5.1 acres in size and is located in the City of Saraland, Mobile County, Alabama. From 1961 to 1971, Redwing Carriers, Inc. (Redwing), a trucking company, owned and operated the site as a terminal for cleaning, repairing and parking its fleet of trucks. The firm transported a variety of substances, including asphalt, diesel fuel, chemicals and pesticides from local plants. During cleaning, untreated hazardous substances were released to the ground creating a tar-like sludge and contaminating site soils. The tar-like sludge is composed predominately of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon compounds together with lesser amounts of pesticides, herbicides and volatile organic compounds.

In 1973, Saraland Apartments Ltd. purchased the site and built a U.S. Housing and Urban Development (HUD) subsidized apartment complex on the site. During construction, the sludge and contaminated soils were covered over with up to five feet of clean soil. When completed, the complex consisted of 60 apartment units located in 12 buildings and at one time housed approximately 160 residents including eighty to ninety preschool-age or elementary school-age children.

In 1984, the Alabama Department of Environmental Management (ADEM) investigated apartment residents' complaints about the tar-like sludge seeping to the surface at numerous locations at the Site. In 1985, EPA conducted initial studies in which high concentrations of 1,2,4-trichlorobenzene and naphthalene were detected in the soil and in leachate coming from the sludge. On July 9, 1985, the Agency and Redwing entered into an Administrative Order on Consent which required Redwing to (among other things) conduct a limited sludge and contaminated soil removal.

The site was placed on the National Priorities List (NPL) in February 1990. On December 15, 1992, EPA issued a Record of Decision (ROD) for the Site. Redwing continued periodic removal of surface se eps until 1994 when they stopped doing any work at the site.

On July 12, 1996, EPA issued a Unilateral Administrative Order to Redwing and Saraland Apartments, Ltd. directing them to remove the source of the recurring tar seeps. When both parties refused to comply with the order, EPA took action to do the removal by temporarily relocating 57 families living in the complex and excavating and transporting off site for disposal approximately 20,724 tons of sludge, contaminated soil and debris.

Air monitoring conducted in the Saraland Apartments after the removal was completed detected unacceptable levels of benzene and the pesticide Aldrin in some of the Saraland Apartments. Based on this monitoring, EPA determined that the residents could not return to live in the Saraland Apartments. Working together, EPA and HUD have relocated the residents to comparable permanent housing.

In July, 1997, EPA collected soil, sediment, and water samples from twenty three properties adjacent to the Redwing Carriers Superfund Site. The purpose for this sampling was to address community concerns about possible releases from the site. Based on a risk evaluation of the analytical results of these samples, the Agency determined that there is no unacceptable health risk or hazard in the neighborhood adjacent to the Redwing site.

In April, 1999, EPA published a Proposed Plan to amend the 1992 ROD based on new data collected during the 1996-1997 Removal Action. The amended ROD was signed on June 14, 2000.

In 2002, a global settlement between the Redwing potentially responsible parties (PRPs) and the Federal government was reached on the final cleanup of the Redwing Site. A Remedial Design/Remedial Action Consent Decree was entered on February 26, 2002.

Demolition of the Saraland Apartments was completed in the summer of 2004. The 100% Remedial Design for the site has been approved.

The ROD for the Redwing Carriers, Inc. (Saraland) Superfund Site was signed on December 15,  1992. The 1992 ROD was subsequently amended on June 14, 2000.

An Explanation of Significant Differences addressing Operable Unit 1 was completed in September 2007.

The American Brass, Inc. (ABI) Site is located in Headland, Henry County, Alabama. The Site is a former secondary brass smelter/foundry facility located in Henry County just west of Headland, Alabama, near the City of Dothan. The Site is located on State Highway 134. The Site can be located by traveling south from Montgomery on U.S. Route 231 to State Highway 134 (east) and is situated on the south side of Highway 134 about 6 miles from the U.S. Route 231 exit. The Dothan airport is located approximately 3 miles to the west of the Site. The Site area is approximately 148 acres, 24 acres of which are occupied by the former foundry buildings (the developed portion of the Site). ABI industrial operations were conducted at the Site from the 1978 until December 1992.

The Site is currently owned by the Industrial Development Board of Headland who leased the property to ABI. It appears that the companies which operated at the Site leased the property from the Industrial Development Board and the previous Site owner, the Dothan Industrial Board.

Past Site Operators:
-Mississippi Chemical Company: The Site was developed from farmland in the mid to late 1960s. Aerial photographs show industrial buildings present at the Site in 1968, operated by a fertilizer packaging company named Mississippi Chemical, although little is known about this company and its operations. File information indicates Mississippi Chemical received bulk shipments of ammonium nitrate and possibly other types of fertilizer materials (according to local citizens) by rail for blending and repackaging the materials on-site for resale.

-Sitkin Smelting and Refining: In 1976, Lewis Sitkin began brass smelting operations at the Site under the name Sitkin Smelting and Refining (SS&R). Mr. Sitkin operated a second facility in Lewiston, Pennsylvania, under the same name [now a National Priorities List (NPL) Site]. In 1977, SS&R entered into a contract with Dow for silver extraction from silver nitrate, s ilver oxide, and oil-soaked alumina. In October of the same year, Polaroid shipped film to SS&R for metals extraction. By April 1978, SS&R was doing similar business with Kodak as well.

-American Brass. Inc.: In 1978, SS&R filed for bankruptcy; Commercial Technology (Comtec) of Dallas, Texas, bought out Sitkin's creditors, acquired the company, and reorganized it as ABI. Comtec remained ABI's parent corporation. ABI was owned by Lewis Sitkin, but was operated by Lewis Sitkin's son, Joseph H. (Jack) Sitkin. The operation at ABI involved the smelting of non-ferrous scrap material, such as discarded automobile radiators and plumbing scraps from scrap metal dealers and industrial sources, producing brass ingots for sale to plumbing materials manufacturers.

ABI operated from 1978 until December 1992. While in operation, ABI developed a history of violations and enforcement activity from both the Alabama Department of Environmental Management (ADEM) and EPA, while regulated under the Resource Recovery and Conservation Act (RCRA).

Environmental compliance problems were first identified in the mid-1980s and continued until the closure of the facility in December 1992. During this period, numerous RCRA violations were recorded by both ADEM and EPA Region 4 leading up to the inclusion of the Site on the NPL on May 10, 1999. There are no RCRA activities currently pending at the Site.

Field work for the Remedial Investigation (RI) has been conducted in two formal phases; a primary RI, conducted during September 1999 through August 2000, and a supplemental RI, conducted during November 2002 and February 2003.

A Feasibility Study (FS) for the Site was completed on May 24, 2004. The purpose of the FS was to investigate the various alternatives for remediating the contamination documented as part of the RI activities.

The Site is currently unused north of the southern railroad tracks, where operations were conducted (a sod operation currently operates south of the  southern railroad tracks but not in any areas where excavations are planned). It is bordered by mixed use properties, including agricultural and residential areas. The residential area to the east is separated from the Site by Arnold Faulkner Road.

A mixture of residential and commercial land use is deemed the most anticipated potential future land use for the Site. This is based on the past land use at this property and on the City of Headland's redevelopment plans.

Groundwater from the Lisbon aquifer is used as a drinking water source for private wells in the area, although it is not thought that the upper portion of the Lisbon aquifer is currently used by any of the nearby residents. It is possible that the upper portion of the Lisbon aquifer is used for irrigation purposes in the area.

The headwater wetlands for both Cedar Creek and Dunham Creek provide habitat for a variety of plants and wildlife. In addition, it is possible that both streams are used for recreational fishing in the area.

A Record of Decision addressing Operable Unit 1 (OU1) was completed in August 2006.

On May 4, 2006, the Proposed Plan for Remedial Action (RA) was presented to the public at the Headland City Hall. The proposed remedy was selected in the Record of Decision dated August 24, 2006. The selected Remedial Action for the Site consists of the following components:

-Decontamination & demolition of all of the buildings, pavements, and structures, with recycling of materials where possible;

-excavation of contaminated soils and sediments;

-confirmatory sampling of the excavated areas to ensure that cleanup goals have been met;

-off-site disposal of excavated materials;

-backfill and re-vegetation of the excavated areas;

-wetlands restoration in the excavated areas of Dunham and Cedar Creeks;

-monitored natural attenuation of the groundwater beneath the Site;

- engineering controls to control surface water runoff, dust, and air quality; and,

-in stitutional controls as necessary to restrict future groundwater use.

The Remedial Design for the final remedy was completed in 2007. In the spring of 2008, a Value Engineering (VE) Study was also conducted for this Remedial Action.

Funding for the Remedial Action was provided by EPA Headquarters in September 2008 and it is anticipated that this cleanup work can be completed in 2009. An EPA Region 4 contractor, Environmental Restoration, has been tasked with the work assignment for this RA, while the design contractor, Black and Veatch Special Projects Corporation, has been retained for engineering support. Field activities were begun in November 2008.

An Explanation of Significant Differences (ESD) was issued to inform the public of its Site activities and to explain two differences in the selected remedy for the Site.

An ESD addressing Operable Unit 01 of the American Brass Inc. Site was completed in April 2009.
