The American Creosote Works (ACW) Site is a former wood preserving facility that pressure-treated wood products with creosote oil and coal tar solutions. The approximately 120 acre site is located in Louisville, Winston County, Mississippi off of Highway 15 at the intersection of South Railroad Avenue and Baremore Street. The lead agency for the CERCLA regulatory response at the site is EPA. The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ) is the support agency.

The ACW Site is currently inactive and is overgrown with scattered to dense vegetated areas. Timber, owned by Boydston Lumber, lies west of the ACW Site as do several private residences. Residential areas are located to the west, northwest, and northeast of the site. Land use to the east of the site is mixed industrial and residential.

The facility was reportedly constructed in 1912 and operated under various names and ownership until 1998. The facility pressure-treated poles, piling lumber, bridge timber, cross-ties, and posts with creosote oil and coal tar solutions. Creosote was the primary preservative used in the process; however, the facility also reportedly used pentachlorophenol (PCP) sometime during the period from 1985 to 1988. Until the 1980s, the facility utilized three unlined lagoons or ponds that received discharges of creosote waste. Over the years, the largest of these ponds leaked creosote over and through an earthen dike and into Hughes Creek.

During a site inspection conducted by the Mississippi Bureau of Pollution Control (MBPC) in October 1984, inspectors discovered two uncontrolled waste sites (sludge lagoons) west of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) regulated surface impoundment. The first sludge lagoon was estimated to be 1 acre in area and contained approximately 6 feet of creosote sludge. The second sludge lagoon was estimated by the MBPC inspectors to be 20 acres in area containing approximately 6 to 8 feet of creosote sludge covered by an addit ional 2 to 3 feet of water. The MBPC inspectors noted that the earthen dike around the southwest end of a larger surface impoundment was seeping and there was evidence of recent spills into Hughes Creek. The creek banks were heavily stained with creosote and creosote was observed on the water surface. The MBPC contacted the Region 4 EPA Emergency Response and Removal Branch (ERRB) who subsequently initiated an emergency response at the site beginning on October 24, 1984.

Between October 24, 1984 and February 22, 1985, EPA conducted removal activities at the facility. The surface water was pumped from the lagoons. Then EPA excavated the creosote sludge and highly contaminated soils from the lagoons. The excavated sludge was solidified and stabilized with kiln dust. Deep pockets (up to 10 feet in depth) of creosote were excavated from some areas within the former lagoons.

Approximately 70,000 cubic yards (yd3) of creosote sludge and highly contaminated soils were excavated and solidified with cement kiln dust. The solidified material was placed in an onsite unlined storage cell and then covered with about 2 to 3 feet of clay. The final dimensions of the storage cell were 475 feet by 375 feet in area and 12 to 13 feet in depth. The cap was graded so that surface water run-on/run-off would flow around the storage cell. Topsoil was placed on the cap, and the area was seeded with grass. One groundwater monitoring well was installed up-gradient of the storage cell, and three groundwater monitoring wells were installed down-gradient of and around the storage cell. The ACW facility continued to operate after the 1984-1985 emergency removal action was completed until 1998 when the facility was closed.

On January 28 and 29, 1999, the Superfund Technical Assessment and Response Team (START) conducted a site investigation at the facility. During the site investigation, START personnel discovered that a containment area sump was overflowing and two secondary containment  cells were filled with a black liquid with only half an inch of freeboard before an overflow would occur. In addition, the inspector noted that there were nine tanks containing liquids, miscellaneous drums, and an abandoned laboratory building containing various chemicals. The EPA On-Scene Coordinator (OSC) determined that an emergency action was necessary to stop the overflow of creosote waste from the containment areas and process tanks abandoned on site. On January 29, 1999, the EPA Emergency and Rapid Response Services (ERRS) contractor pumped 55,000 gallons of liquid from the tanks and containment cells into three 20,000-gallon frac tanks. START personnel also conducted air monitoring and collected two soil, three sediment, and three miscellaneous water samples.

On May 17, 1999, START arrived at the site to begin the removal action. Activities focused on wastewater treatment and the removal and disposal of sludges in the secondary containment areas and tanks, and contaminated surface and subsurface soils. Removal activities took place in three phases.

Phase I involved data collection through an interim action by the ERRB and the Remedial Branch of the EPA. Phase II involved removing, solidifying, and stockpiling the sludge, and disposing of the tank materials. Wastewater treatment, sludge solidification, and tank decommissioning were completed on September 3, 1999. A total of 20 tanks were decommissioned, 176,000 gallons of wastewater were treated, 192 tons of metal were recycled, 200 tons of hazardous debris and 60 tons of nonhazardous debris were disposed, nine lab packs were transported off site for disposal, and 4,000 yd3 of solidified waste was stockpiled for onsite disposal.

The final phase involved constructing a temporary storage cell for the waste and waste encapsulation. The holding cell was located adjacent to the south side of the 1984 burial area. The cell measured 149 feet east-west by 55 feet north-south and had a depth of 7 feet with 2  to 1 sloping side walls. The excavation was lined with 40-mil low density polyethylene (LDPE) liner. About 1 foot of clay was placed on the top of the liner prior to adding the waste material. A 40-mil LDPE liner was then placed over the top of the full cell and welded to the bottom liner to fully encapsulate the waste. About 1 foot of clean clay was placed over the top of the liner for protection and the cell area was graded to optimize drainage and reduce surface water run on. A 6-foot chain-link fence was installed around the cell marking the completion of the remedial action (RA) activity on April 20, 2000.

A third EPA Removal Action, December 2006 to May 2007, was taken at the site to address a continuing release of creosote to Hughes Creek in an area just north of Baremore Street. This action consisted of the installation of a line of sheet piling adjacent to the creek.

The City of Louisville replaced the Baremore Street bridge culvert in Hughes Creek during the winter of 2003. During this work, the contractor encountered contaminated sediments in Hughes Creek. The City of Louisville notified the EPA that their construction contractor had encountered the contaminated material. EPA's ERRB mobilized to the ACW Site and excavated the contaminated soil/sediments within the work area to allow the culvert replacement project to continue. ERRB stockpiled approximately 700 to 900 yd3 of contaminated soil/sediment onsite over the 1984-1985 EPA emergency removal action landfill area. The excavated material generated during this work was covered with a geomembrane cap.

The City of Louisville replaced the South Church Street bridge over Hughes Creek during July 2005. During this work, the contractor used the approximately 720 yd3 of the excavated soil and sediment as fill material at a nearby residential area. Following complaints from the residents, the City of Louisville had the contractor remove the material from the residential area and transport the fill bac k to the ACW site. This material was stockpiled on top of the 1984-1985 EPA emergency removal action landfill area. The stockpiled material generated during this work was left uncovered.

The anticipated future land use for the ACW Site is commercial/industrial. This assumption is based on the 80 year history of the site being used as a wood treating facility and the fact that the property is zoned commercial.

Contamination has been detected in the Hughes Creek Flood Plain Sands (surficial aquifer) and the upper portions of the Lower Tuscahoma Formation (Middle Wilcox aquifer). These aquifers are not extensively used as potable water sources because of low productivity; however, it is possible that portions of these aquifers could be used for irrigation. The City of Louisville's municipal water supply wells are screened at a depth of 300 to 350 feet below land surface (bls) within the Gravel Creek Sand Member (Lower Wilcox aquifer). It is important to note that the 150 foot thick Grampain Hill Member which consists of multiple layers of low permeability clay and silt hydraulically separates the Gravel Creek Sand Member from the Lower Tuscahoma Formation. The maximum depth of contamination was found in the upper portions of the Middle Wilcox aquifer at a depth of only about 37.5 feet bls.

Water bodies associated with the ACW property consist of a large lake (Railroad Lake) to the northwest, and two riverine drainage features: Hughes Creek to the west and southwest; and an unnamed tributary to Hughes Creek to the east and southeast. Both Hughes Creek and the unnamed tributary are identified as intermittent; however, onsite observations and interviews with local residents contradict this classification and seem to suggest that a substantial flow of water is present in Hughes Creek year-round. The unnamed tributary flows to the southwest until its confluence with Hughes Creek; Hughes Creek flows south toward Tallahaga Creek approximately 10 miles downstream, whi ch then flows into the Pearl River. Based on the topography of the area and on direct observation during site reconnaissance, wetlands exist throughout the entire ACW Site (e.g., along Hughes Creek and in areas surrounding Railroad Lake). Some wetland habitats are located down-gradient of potential contaminant sources and thus they could be influenced by contamination transported from those source areas. The surface water in the immediate vicinity of the site is not currently being used for any community purpose; however, Railroad Lake was once used for fishing and recreational purposes by the local residents. Downstream of the site, Hughes Creek is likely used for fishing, irrigation of farm land, and for watering cattle.

A Record of Decision addressing Operable Unit 1 was completed in September 2007.

The Chemfax, Inc. Site is located in Gulfport, Harrison County, Mississippi. It occupies 11 acres and is bordered by Three Rivers Road to the east and by Irby Steel and Creosote Road to the south. Located to the north is County Barn Road and Bernard Bayou, and to the west is a rail line and the abandoned Alpine Masonite facility. Emergent and forested wetlands comprise part of the Site, which is located within the southeast quadrant of the interchange where Highway 49 meets Interstate 10. The Site is a former industrial facility.

Due to the contamination documented by the Preliminary Assessment (PA), Site Investigation (SI), Listing Site Investigation (LSI), and Expanded Site Investigation (ESI) activities, the Site was proposed to the National Priorities List (NPL) in May 1993. At this time, the Site has not been finalized on the NPL.

Chemfax, Inc. was established in March, 1955 and produced synthetic hydrocarbon resins and waxes from petroleum products. The primary operation at the time business ceased in 1995 was a paraffin blending process in which different grades of paraffin wax were heated together to a liquid state, blended, and then cooled with water. Cooling water was obtained from an on-site industrial well. Historically, condensed cooling water was stored in an on-site holding pond and re-used.

The site is currently unused. However, the Mississippi Department of Transportation has indicated its desire to locate a rail spur across part of the site, in order to eliminate one of the two aging rail crossings at Highway 49.

Based on past and anticipated future use of this Site, and current zoning for the Site and the property adjacent to the site, a commercial land use is the most appropriate potential future use for this Site. The Site and adjoining properties are commercially zoned. Under this classification, various industries are permitted including light industrial operations, etc.

Typically, EPA expects that the vast majority of sites wit h current commercial uses will continue to be used as commercial or industrial sites. Future commercial land use is likely to be a reasonable assumption where a site such as this one is currently used for commercial purposes, is located in an area where the surroundings are zoned for commercial use, and the property is expected to continue to be used for commercial purposes.

In cases where a remedy is designed to be protective for a future commercial land use, it is normally necessary to include institutional controls to ensure that the future land use is restricted to a non-residential land use. However, the remedy set forth in this decision document will not include future institutional controls since the Site soils do not pose an unacceptable risk to the lifetime resident, and the groundwater will be cleaned up to levels protective for a residential land use.

Although currently unused in the area, the surficial groundwater at the Site is considered Class II, i.e., a current or potential source of drinking water. The performance standards for Class II groundwater are maximum contaminant level's (MCL's) and non-zero maximum contaminant level goal's (MCLG's). Data from the RI indicates that soils and sediments are present on-site, which could cause groundwater contamination in the future due to rainfall infiltration and leaching of contaminants to groundwater.

A Record of Decision (ROD) addressing operable unit 1 (OU1) was completed in November 2002.

Operational History
The Davis Timber Company conducted timber processing and wood preserving operations at the facility from 1972 until 1987, when the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ) ordered Davis Timber Company to discontinue treatment operations. According to MDEQ, Davis Timber Company declared bankruptcy in 1990. The property was then operated by Lamar Industries, which conducted debarking operations. The site is currently not in operation.

The Site is approximately 30 acres in size and consists of a scragg mill, a pole peeler and debarker, a closed holding pond (Former PCP/Waste Bark Impoundment), an office, a treating cylinder, a closed cooling pond, an oil separator, two aboveground oil storage tanks, two aboveground pentachlorophenol (PCP) solution storage tanks, and a storage yard. The area surrounding the Site is mainly rural. No other industries or companies are located in the vicinity of the Site that could have contributed to the PCP/dioxin contamination in West Mineral Creek, East Mineral Creek, or Country Club Lake. 

The Davis Timber Company produced treated pine poles, pilings, and timber. Facility operations have included bark removal, treatment of wood with PCP, and product storage. In addition, a scragg mill was operated at the facility to salvage timber unsuitable for poles or piling. The facility received raw wood by truck. The materials were then weighed and stocked in the open yard for debarking. Logs were cut to length and prepared for treatment. Poles or piles then were pulled into a treating cylinder for pressure processing. The timber was conditioned with steam. After sap fluids, steam condensate, and residual oil were removed from the cylinder walls, the timber was treated with a five percent PCP solution and diesel oil or a light-cycle oil. Following treatment, excess preservative solution was removed from the treating cylinder by a vacuum process. Steam was then introduced to clean the poles. Treated materia ls were removed from the cylinder for drying and storage on the open yard prior to shipment.

The process wastewater containing PCP was discharged into an on-site storage/cooling pond approximately 2 acres in size. Other waste products produced by the facility include bark and wood fiber from the debarker and peeler; oil, steam condensate, and wood sap extract from steam seasoning; and preservative containing PCP that was spilled in the vicinity of the tanks and treating cylinder. In 1980, the on-site holding pond was reportedly closed, backfilled, and capped with approximately 6 to 8 inches of clay.

Regulatory and Enforcement History; Previous Investigations
The Site has been the subject of numerous previous investigations. These investigations are briefly summarized in this section.

Between December 1974 and January 1987, the Mississippi Bureau of Pollution Control (MBPC) documented six fish kills in Country Club Estates Lake, a 66-acre lake located approximately 1 mile downstream of the facility. Several of the fish kills were attributed to releases of PCP from the Davis Timber Company.

On January 14, 1975, subsequent to the first fish kill, Mississippi Air and Water Pollution Control Commission (MAWPCC) issued an Order of the Commission to Davis Timber Company, finding the facility guilty of causing pollution of Mineral Creek. MAWPCC subsequently fined the facility $250. The order required that the facility immediately cease any and all discharges from its facility and stated that at no time in the future was any wastewater to be discharged from the facility unless MAWPCC had issued a valid permit.

On January 28, 1977, MAWPCC informed Davis Timber Company that, on the basis of the company's history of improperly containing its process wastewater, the commission intended to issue an order to the facility requiring treatment of the wastewater and installation of a wastewater disposal system. MAWPCC also informed the facility that the commission did  not intend to issue a discharge permit until the facility contracted an engineering firm to provide recommendations for a wastewater treatment system. Davis Timber Company then retained Batson and Brown, Inc., Consulting Engineers. Batson and Brown prepared an engineering report on March 31, 1977, presenting design plans and changes in the facility's wastewater treatment system. On April 12, 1977, MAWPCC issued Davis Timber Company a five-year permit (No. 77-7017) to operate a wastewater disposal system with no discharge. On May 17, 1982, the permit was renewed for a five-year period. In 1979, MAWPCC issued a commission order that required the facility to take the following steps: operate the spray evaporation system to the maximum extent possible; eliminate all stormwater drainage into the on-site storage pond; install and operate a dry kiln and replace the existing steam preconditioned kiln, so that no process wastewater generated during the operation of the dry kiln is discharged to the on-site storage pond or to waters of the state; install and operate additional means of evaporating or otherwise disposing of the contaminated water that entered the on-site storage pond; submit a plan for reducing the surface area of the storage pond to less than one-half its existing size and complete that reduction; maintain at least 2 feet of freeboard within the storage pond at all times; and submit a plan for the disposal of the contaminated water that entered the storage pond.

On October 19, 1979, Davis Timber Company informed MAWPCC that the evaporator was operational and the underground pipe leading from the treatment cylinder to the storage pond had been cemented and that the pond did not receive any other process wastewater. Davis Timber Company informed MAWPCC that all oil draining from the treatment cylinder would enter a holding pit connected to a boil-off system through a newly installed pipe, and that facility personnel had begun filling the storage pond with ba rk and dirt obtained from the facility property.

On February 6, 1980, MBPC personnel inspected the facility and found it to be non-compliant with the commission order, which required that a minimum of 2 feet of freeboard be maintained in the storage pond at all times. MBPC noted that there was only 6 inches of freeboard in the storage pond at the time of the inspection and that a small amount of seepage was noted from one section of the dam associated with the storage pond. In addition, the spray evaporation system was not in use, as was required under the commission order.

On October 6, 1981, MBPC conducted an inspection at the facility, and noted that the facility had begun treating timber with both oil-borne and waterborne PCP. Davis Timber Company reported that it generated approximately 2,000 gallons of wastewater per week from the oil-borne process; however, wastewater generated from the water-borne PCP process could be recycled completely. The wastewater was evaporated by steam in an evaporating tank preceded by an oil-water separator tank. Davis Timber Company personnel informed MBPC that the storage pond had been filled in completely and capped with 6 to 8 inches of clay. Davis Timber Company also reported that a small pit located next to the evaporation tank also had been covered. In addition, on January 16, 1981, a citizen of Country Club Estates contacted MBPC and reported that Davis Timber Company personnel had been observed discharging a dark brown substance from a hose into a ditch and culvert at the south end of the facility property at 11:30 p.m.

In January 1982, a former employee of the facility contacted MBPC, alleging that wastes containing PCP that had been removed from the on-site storage pond had not been hauled to the City of Hattiesburg sewer system, as the president of Davis Timber Company, Mackie Davis, had told MBPC, rather the wastes had been buried on Mr. Davis's personal property. In April 1982, MBPC personnel asked Mackie Dav is about the incident; however, Mr. Davis denied the allegations. Mr. Davis said that MBPC could inspect his property personally although an inspection could not be made until May, since Mr. Davis was to be out of the country until that time. The former employee contacted MBPC one week after MBPC questioned Mr. Davis about the improper disposal of the contents of the storage pond, stating that he had been rehired by Davis Timber Company and that the information he had supplied earlier was false. The former employee told MBPC that he felt he had been laid off unfairly and had provided the original information to MBPC to cause trouble for Davis Timber Company. However, records indicate that MBPC was skeptical of the former employee's second story, because MBPC personnel had flown over Mr. Davis's personal property in February and observed that, in the exact location reported by the former employee, a large hole had been recently backfilled. MBPC conducted an inspection of the facility on April 22, 1982. MBPC personnel noted that runoff water in the drainage ditch located at the west end of the property was oily, discolored, and black in appearance. Personnel also noted that the on-site storage pond had been filled in, although the facility had not built dikes around its storage units.

MBPC personnel inspected the facility on December 2, 1983, and noted the following problems: discharge from a bleed-off line from the barometric condenser; discharge of an air compressor cooling water; oil stains around the sides of a spill containment pond that received runoff from the facility; and discharge from polyvinyl chloride (PVC) piping that drained the pump-priming water. MBPC personnel also noted that foundations were being poured for the construction of a new treating cylinder.

On January 18, 1984, Davis Timber Company notified MBPC that the facility had corrected the violations noted during the December 2, 1983, inspection and informed MBPC of changes it was making in  its wastewater treatment system. Davis Timber Company informed MBPC that the new treatment cylinder would be approximately 4 feet by 63 feet and would generate 187 gallons of wastewater per charge. Davis Timber Company stated that it intended to treat only three charges of posts, lumber, and building poles per week. Davis Timber Company also stated that it intended to try a system that another wood-treating facility used in treating foundation piling. Facility personnel stated that the new process would reduce waste to 100 gallons per charge and that it had ample capacity in the evaporation system to handle the amount of wastewater that the new treating cylinder would generate.

In December 1989, MDEQ petitioned the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR), to conduct a public health assessment at Country Club Estates Lake on behalf of the residents of Country Club Estates. ATSDR classified Country Club Estates Lake as a public health hazard because concentrations of PCP and chlorinated dibenzodioxins (dioxins), and dibenzofurans (furans) detected in the lake exceeded public health guidelines.

On September 18, 1990, MBPC collected one sediment sample each from East Mineral Creek and West Mineral Creek, and one sediment sample from the southwest comer of Country Club Estates Lake. MBPC personnel also collected a surface soil sample from an area of stained soil located adjacent to the wood treating cylinder. Analytical results revealed high levels of dioxins and furans in all three sediment samples and the on-site surface soil sample. PCP was detected in two of four sediment samples and in the on-site soil sample. No background or control samples were collected for comparison.

On February 19, 1991, MBPC collected three sediment samples, and one on-site surface soil sample from the same locations from which samples collected on September 18, 1990, had been collected. Analytical results revealed dete ctable levels of dioxins and furans in all four samples. However, no background or control samples were collected for comparison.

On October 15, 1991, MBPC conducted a phase II site investigation (SI) at Davis Timber Company and collected a control sediment sample upstream of the storage pond on West Mineral Creek and one sediment sample downstream of the storage pond on West Mineral Creek. Personnel collected a background subsurface soil sample north of the facility and a subsurface soil sample from the closed storage pond. Analytical results revealed elevated levels of PCP in the closed on-site storage pond, and in the sediment sample collected from West Mineral Creek. In addition, elevated levels of dioxins and furans were detected in the sediment sample collected from West Mineral Creek. Subsurface soil samples were not analyzed for dioxins or furans.

MDEQ conducted an expanded site investigation (ESI) in February 1995, and collected two subsurface soil samples and nine sediment samples. Tables summarizing the sample locations and rationale and analytical results were prepared; however, no formal report was submitted. Elevated levels of dioxins and furans were detected in analyses of subsurface soil sample DT-SB-02. PCP and dioxins were detected in analytical results of subsurface soil sample DT-SB-01. Dioxins and furans were detected at elevated levels in sediment samples collected from Country Club Estates Lake. PCP was not detected at levels above the detection limit in analyses of sediment samples collected from Country Club Estates Lake. Dioxins and furans were detected in sediment samples collected from the intermittent West Mineral and Mineral creeks. PCP was also detected in sediment samples collected from West Mineral Creek downgradient of the facility. However, PCP was not detected in sediment samples collected from Mineral Creek downgradient of Country Club Estates Lake.

In June 1995, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Region 4, Office  of Health Assessment prepared an ecological risk review of the Site to determine if there were potential ecological effects on aquatic and terrestrial biota from releases of contaminants to the surface waters of the Mineral Creek watershed. Analyses of fish tissue and sediment samples collected between 1987 and 1995 were evaluated for the ecological risk review. Analytical results of several samples exceeded many of the screening values, indicating a potential for ecological impacts; however, further investigation was recommended in order to fully characterize effects related to the Site.

Remedial Investigations/Feasibility Studies
The Remedial Investigation (RI) was conducted by EPA's Science and Ecosystem Support Division (SESD) between May 2000 and September 2001. During this period, SESD collected 30 subsurface soil samples, 6 groundwater samples, 51 sediment samples, 11 surface water samples, 27 surface soil samples, and multiple fish tissue samples (individual and composite). The Site was divided into 49 grids measuring-200 feet (ft) by 200 ft except in the central-northern portion of the Site which was divided into 100-ft by 100-ft grids. A 3- to 5-point composite surface sample was collected from each grid and a subsurface sample was collected from the center of each grid at a depth of 18 to 24 inches.

Contamination was delineated based on those constituents detected at concentrations exceeding EPA Region 9 Preliminary Remediation Goals (PRGs) and/or Federal Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) for surface water and groundwater; or human health risk-based Region 4 PRGs (e.g., for dioxins/furans in soil and sediment). Risk-based remediation goals derived from Site-specific data are identified by the Human Health Risk Assessment (HHRA) for residential, industrial and recreational receptors and the ecological risk assessment (ERA). Arsenic, aluminum, thallium, and iron are identified in soil as Chemicals of Potential Concern (COPCs) assuming residential us e of the property in the RI; however, they are not Chemicals of Concern (COCs) when considering the property will likely be utilized for recreational, not residential purposes. As a result, COCs for the Site are limited to PCP and dioxin/furans.

RI results indicate the main COPCs for the Site are 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-/7-dioxin toxicity equivalents quotient (dioxin TEQ), PCP, arsenic, and iron. Thallium and aluminum were also detected above screening criteria (Region 9 PRGs); however, these are not thought to be Site-related. Thallium was detected in the offsite control sample over 0.7 miles west of the Site. A summary of RI sampling results of the primary COPCs, including the range of detected concentrations (in parentheses), follows:

Surface Soils. COPCs in surface soil collected from 0 to 6 inches below land surface (bls) include the following detections: PCP at an estimated 1.6 to 120,000 micrograms per kilogram (ug/kg), aluminum [2,000 to 11,000 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg)], arsenic (1.8 to 3.9 mg/kg), iron (1,100 to 12,000 mg/kg), and thallium (4 to 21 mg/kg). Dioxin TEQ in surface soils ranged from 0.4 nanograms per kilogram (ng/kg) to 8,600 ng/kg. Twenty of the 27 surface soil samples exceeded Region 9 commercial/ industrial PRGs for dioxin TEQ; however, only two exceeded the human health risk-based cleanup criteria for this Site. These constituents were present above screening criteria in two onsite areas near the former cooling pond.

Subsurface Soils. Subsurface soil samples were collected from five intervals: 18 to 24 inches bls, 4 to 5 ft bls, 9 to 10 ft bls, 14 to l5 ft bls, and 19 to 20 ft bls. PCP was detected in one subsurface soil sample at 1,300 ng/kg at 18 to 24 inches bls near the shop at the north-central portion of the Site. Also, a specific subset of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), called benzo(a)pyrene equivalents (BAPEs), was identified in samples from three locations at 18 to 24 inches bls near the debarker, pole  peeler, and southwestern comer of the Site. BAPE concentrations ranged from 97.5 to 179 pg/kg (below the commercial/industrial screening criteria).

Site wide, detections of dioxin TEQ in subsurface soils ranged from an estimated 4 ng/kg to an estimated 33,000 ng/kg, or parts per trillion (ppt). Only three samples outside of the impoundment area had detections of dioxin TEQ. These three samples were all in the 18- to 24-inch interval and ranged from an estimated 4 ng/kg to an estimated 49 ng/kg. These were collected from the central and southwestern portion of the Site. Each of these exceeded Region 9 industrial/commercial PRGs; however, all were below the industrial/ commercial cleanup goal for this Site. The other dioxin TEQ detections in subsurface soil were in and around the impoundment area.

Former PCP and Waste Bark Impoundment Area. PCP was detected in all subsurface soil samples (ranging from an estimated 970 to 760,000 (ug/kg) collected from the impoundment area. Five of these samples exceeded both industrial/commercial and residential PRGs. PAHs and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) also were detected in one sample and three samples, respectively. PCBs and two pesticides exceeded the residential PRG value in one of two samples. Metal concentrations exceeded PRGs for aluminum, arsenic, iron, and thallium in one of two samples. In all eight subsurface soil samples analyzed from the impoundment area, dioxin TEQ was detected at concentrations exceeding both residential and industrial/ commercial PRGs. Dioxin TEQs in the impoundment area ranged 61 to 33,000 ng/kg. Contaminant concentrations above cleanup goals are generally four ft bls in the impoundment area, with the highest concentrations between 9 and 15 ft bls.

In liquid samples collected inside the impoundment area, PCP was detected in all five samples at concentrations ranging between an estimated 3 to 510 micrograms per liter (pg/L) and exceeded the Federal MCL value for PCP. It was initially tho ught these wells were installed into groundwater; however, reevaluation of aerial photographs indicates temporary wells were installed in the impoundment. This resulted in sampling liquid contained in the impoundment, and not groundwater. It is unlikely groundwater is present in appreciable quantities. The Site rests on a thick clay unit that minimizes downward migration of contaminants or precipitation. 

Sediment. PCP (an estimated 120 to 1,800 pg/kg) was detected in six sediment samples from Beaver Pond and West Mineral Creek. PAHs were found in two of the samples; 12 samples for dioxin/furan TEQ exceeded the Region 4 Sediment Screening Values (SSVs).

In East Mineral Creek, PCP (an estimated 14 to 8,200 pg/kg) was detected in 13 sediment samples. PAHs were found in six samples and pesticide concentrations greater than Region 9 screening values were found in 18 sediment samples. Dioxin TEQ (an estimated 0.94 to 6,300 ng/kg) exceeded the Region 4 screening value in 30 samples.

Sediment from Country Club Lake was sampled and analyzed. None of the sample results for COPCs exceeded risk-based screening levels. Since that time, water in Country Club Lake was drained in 2007, exposing the submerged sediment to the air. The sediment results were compared to surface soil criteria, and none of the results exceeded soil screening criteria. The Lake was refilled in 2008.

Surface Water. Five of six surface water samples exceeded the HHRA calculated child resident screening value for dioxin TEQ (0.0003 to 0.19 [nanograms per liter] ng/L, estimated). Ground water. Appreciable quantities of groundwater have not been observed at the Site. Of the four permanent monitoring wells installed outside the impoundment area, only one produced an adequate quantity of water to collect a groundwater sample. No volatile organic compounds (VOCs), PCP, or PAHs were detected in the groundwater sample collected from this well outside the impoundment area. Temporary monitoring wells wer e installed and sampled in the initial field investigation. After evaluation of historical aerial photographs it is believed these temporary monitoring wells were installed within the footprint of the impoundment and the fluid sampled was not groundwater but fluid remaining within the impoundment.

Sampling for the Ecological Risk Assessment. A sampling event took place in July 2004 to collect additional data to complete the ERA. Samples collected included surface soils, sediment, and surface water. In addition, fish were collected from the Beaver Pond, West Mineral Creek, and a reference location. No fish were found in East Mineral Creek. Soils and sediments were sent back to the SESD laboratory for toxicity and bioaccumulation tests. Toxicity tests included a seed germination test using the lettuce seed (Lactiica sativa), soil toxicity test using the earthworm (Eiseniafoetida), and sediment toxicity test usmg the sediment worms {Lumbriciilus variegatiis) and freshwater amphipod {Hyalella azteca).

Current and Future Land Use
Current Land Use
The area surrounding the Site is mainly rural; however, residential areas have been expanding from Hattiesburg east of the site. The southern edge of the property is adjacent to the Longleaf Trace rails to- trails project, which extends from Hattiesburg northwest 41 miles to its terminus in Prentiss, Mississippi. The Longleaf Trace is Mississippi's premier running, biking, hiking and equestrian trail. Country Club Lake is nearby. In 2007, the lake was drained to repair the dam and spillway at the northern edge of the lake. As of August 2008, the dam had been repaired and the lake was being refilled with water.

In 1990, MDEQ conducted a ground water well survey around the Site area (MDEQ, 1995). This survey identified two actively utilized wells within a one-mile radius of the Site. One private well was identified approximately 4,000 feet southeast of the Site (at 287 Gravel Pit Road) and one public supply well (Arnold  Supply Line) was located over a mile southeast of the Site. During a site visit in December 2004 it was discovered that the private well off Gravel Pit Road was no longer used (the owner hooked into the public system); however, the public supply well was still in operation.

As an update to assess current ground water use, an additional well survey and hydrology assessment of the Site area, was completed in October 2005. The survey queried well records from the MDEQ Office of Land and Water Resources and the USGS. Results of this survey determined that there were no wells utilized for domestic or public supply in the Site area except for the Arnold Supply line well located over a mile southeast of the Site.

Future Land Use
The Site's anticipated future land uses could include commercial, light industrial, recreational, and public land uses. The Site's location and proximity to the region's growing residential and commercial areas, and its proximity to the Longleaf Trace, means that the Site is well suited to a wide range of public, recreational and ecological land uses including parks, community centers, walking trails, educational areas, sports fields and wildlife habitat. These land uses would be compatible with the Site's changing surroundings, and could meet multiple community needs.

A ROD addressing the Davis Timber Site was completed in September. 2009.

The Picayune Wood Treating Site (PWTS) is the location of a former wood treating facility that used creosote and pentachlorophenol (PCP) in the treatment process. The 30-acre site is located at 403 Davis Street in the city of Picayune, Pearl River County, Mississippi. 

The site once included a sawmill, veneer mill, a wooden box factory, and a tung oil extraction facility. Abandoned buildings and concrete foundations of these former facilities are located near the northern and southern property lines. The main process area was located near the eastern portion of the site. It included the creosote, PCP, and diesel storage tank area; oil/water separator tanks; the treatment vessels; and the treatment building. The closed cooling water impoundment and the biological treatment storage tanks were located to the north of the main process area. The central portion of the site was the Product Storage Area. The closed trench impoundments are in the western portion of the site.

Most of the structures on the property have been demolished. The site is generally flat, and is mostly gravel roads, tall grass, and vegetation. Progressing eastward across the property, the terrain becomes increasingly more difficult to navigate due to fallen trees (associated with Hurricane Katrina), piles of scrap metal and concrete debris, and treated timbers. Mill Creek, considered to be the eastern boundary of the site, is entrenched to a depth of roughly 5 to 7 feet. Fencing marks the boundary of the property to the north, west, and south.

The plant was constructed around 1945 by Crosby Forest Products, Inc., to produce treated wood, primarily utility poles and foundation pilings. Crosby Wood Preserving, Inc. purchased the plant and other manufacturing operations in 1963. In 1973, Wood Treating, Inc. (WTI) purchased the wood preserving facility and approximately 30 acres of land. Operations ceased in 1999.

Prior to 1982, the chemicals used in the wood treatment process were coal tar,  creosote and PCP in a petroleum carrier. After 1982, only creosote was used. The following description of wood treating operations was obtained from the Groundwater Quality Assessment.

The wood preserving process used at PWTS required a conditioning cycle followed by the impregnation cycle. The conditioning cycle removed sufficient natural moisture and saps to allow injection of the required quantity of preservative chemical. This plant used a steam/vacuum conditioning cycle. In this cycle, the wood to be preserved was placed in the pressure impregnation retort and heated to 245 degrees Fahrenheit by saturated steam for a period of 10 to 16 hours. Condensate, contaminated with residual preservative from the retort and sap extractives from the wood, was continuously bled from the retort.

At the end of the steaming period, the retort was vented to the atmosphere and a vacuum of 23 inches mercury minimum, was applied as rapidly as possible for a period of 2 to 3 hours. Prior to 1985, a direct contact barometric condenser was used to condense any condensable vapors removed during this time. The cooling water for the condenser was stored in an unlined cooling water surface impoundment constructed in 1946. The cooling water collected all condensable organic vapors which left the retort during the vacuum phase. In 1985, process equipment was changed to replace the barometric condenser with a surface condenser. The large volume of direct contact cooling water was replaced by a small volume of non-contact cooling water in a tank and a cooling tower. The condensable vapors were then collected in a condensate tank and pumped to the wastewater treatment system.

After completion of this conditioning cycle, the retort was filled with preservative and the wood was impregnated by raising preservative pressures to 150 to 200 pounds per square inch gauge (psig). The wood was removed from the retort and the cycle begun again.

The wastewater stream from the steaming cycle a nd the condenser cooling water were contaminated process wastewaters. Sludge generated from the treatment of process wastewaters was defined as hazardous waste by 40 Code of Federal Regulation (CFR) 261.32 as K001: "Bottom sediment sludge from the treatment of wastewater from wood preserving processes that use creosote and/or pentachlorophenol." Other waste stream sources included drips, spills, and other loses of preservative, and spent preservative that was no longer suitable for use in the treatment process.

The plant had two areas that were used to manage process wastewater and/or sludge from the treatment of these waters. The recycled cooling water was stored in an unlined surface impoundment. This impoundment was not designed or operated as a "wastewater treatment" unit. Some sludges did accumulate in the bottom of the impoundment. The State of Mississippi determined that this impoundment contained K001.

Since the early 1970's, the steaming condensate process wastewater stream was treated by gravity oil/water separation followed by chemical flocculation and sedimentation. The flocculated wastewater was discharged to the City of Picayune sanitary sewer system. In 1975, the northern-most "trench impoundment" was dug. The flocculation sludge from the wastewater treatment system, along with some creosote tank bottoms from the wood preserving operations, was placed in this impoundment. Subsequently, between 1975 and 1980, two additional trench impoundments were dug. They were also used for the storage/disposal of the same wastes. No wastes were added to these impoundments after 1980.

Changes were made in 1980 which allow recycling of the flocculation sludge to the creosote preservative system. Process equipment changes were completed in 1985 to allow removal of the barometric condenser which eliminated the need for the cooling water impoundment.

The Mississippi Department of Natural Resources (MDNR) and the Mississippi Department of Environmental Qualit y (MDEQ) inspected the PWTS several times between 1981 and 1998. Deficiencies and Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA); violations noted during the inspections included: failure to control entry into the surface impoundments and trenches; old sand filter bed not in compliance with the RCRA; incomplete closure plans for hazardous waste disposal units; failure to properly locate and sample monitoring wells; failure to properly inspect impoundments for leaks, deterioration, or failure; failure to maintain operating records; failure to operate groundwater pumping systems for recovery and treatment of contaminated groundwater; and failure to install a drip pad in the process area.

Groundwater contamination was discovered beneath the two closed impoundments in 1985. As a consequence of this discovery, WTI closed the cooling water pond and trench impoundments that were used to manage wastewater and/or sludge generated during the treatment operations. The former cooling water pond dates from the earliest days of site operations and was located in the eastern portion of the site. The trench impoundments were constructed in the western portion of the site between 1975 and 1980. The cooling water pond and trench impoundments were closed by removing all pumpable sludges, solidification of the remaining sludges, and capping with a "very impermeable" cap.

In April 1988, the EPA issued a RCRA Facility Assessment (RFA) report that identified ten solid waste management units (SWMUs) and one area of concern (AOC). The EPA issued a Hazardous and Solid Waste Amendment (HSWA) post-closure permit to WTI on September 22, 1989. As part of their permit requirements, a Corrective Action Plan (CAP) was implemented for remediation of the groundwater contamination. In October 1991, WTI installed six recovery wells as part of a groundwater pump and treat system. WTI operated the corrective action system to recover non-aqueous phase liquid (NAPL) and contaminated groundwater. The s ystem has been dismantled and is no longer operable.

On June 10, 1994, WTI submitted final amendments to the RCRA Facility Investigation (RFI) Plan and the EPA approved the plan on July 12, 1994. On January 9, 1995, WTI issued the Draft RFI Report. On November 11, 1996, the facility submitted the Final Phase I RFI. On April 1, 1997, the facility submitted an Interim Measures Remediation Plan (IMRP) to address the concerns raised by the EPA during the RFI. WTI proposed reclamation of useable fluids and sludge from the wood process, and on-site bioremediation of the contaminated soils. The EPA approved the IMRP on July 29, 1997; however, in December 1997, WTI requested a postponement of the remedial activities due to litigation with the previous owner and operator. In January 1998, the EPA notified WTI that implementation of the Phase II RFI work plan should begin within 30 days; however, on February 25, 1998, WTI requested a postponement of the Phase II RFI until a settlement could be reached between the current and former owners. A second lawsuit was filed by the insurers of the facility to contest the insurance coverage. WTI ceased operations in 1999.

Since 1999, EPA has been the lead agency in charge of ensuring the contamination at the PWTS is addressed through the Superfund program to be protective of human health and the environment. The MDEQ is the support agency representing the interests of the State of Mississippi. The investigation and cleanup of the Site has not been funded by the Potentially Responsible Parties (PRPs) at the site, since there are no financially viable PRPs.

On October 19, 1999, the EPA conducted a reconnaissance and sampling investigation to evaluate and characterize the risks posed by the facility. The EPA inspectors observed that the site was not completely fenced and contained several areas of concern. Trespassers, primarily school children on their way to and from school, were observed on the site. The interior surfaces of t he operations building were thickly coated with creosote, and the building contained 2 to 3 feet of standing water mixed with creosote. Areas throughout the site contained stained soils and puddles of sludge. Waste product was observed around the biostorage tanks, central processing area, on-site drainage ditches, and off-site in Mill Creek. Several of the on-site tanks were leaking creosote and liquid waste product.

From October 1999 through 2001, the EPA conducted an emergency response action. Product was removed from all tanks, vats, and ditches where waste product leaked or had the potential to leak. Liquid waste was either removed or treated on-site. Small drums and containers were inventoried and grouped according to their hazard category, while the larger tanks were demolished and recycled. The remaining sludges were stabilized using fly ash. After the sludges were stabilized, all of the containers and treated materials were staged together and covered with a polyethylene liner. Approximately 175 cubic yards (yd3) of asbestos was also removed from some of the tanks and pressure vessels, and disposed of in the Central Landfill in McNeil, Mississippi. The stabilized sludges, etc. remain onsite; however, a removal action under the direction of EPA's Emergency Response and Removal Branch (ERRB) is pending that will transport this material to an appropriate treatment facility.

The PWTS was added to the National Priorities List (NPL) in 2004. The NPL is a list of priority releases for long-term evaluation and remedial response, and was promulgated pursuant to section 105 of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA) of 1980, as amended.

The PWTS is located in an industrial complex where a chromated copper arsenate (CCA) facility and a paint blending company are currently operating. These facilities are located near the site, outside the site boundaries to the north and southwest, respectively. Additional land use sur rounding the site includes residential, commercial, and industrial areas to the north; a public park, day care center, and residences to the south; commercial and industrial areas to the east; and Southside Elementary School and residences to the west. 

Prior to September 2007, the site was zoned Industrial-2 (I-2). Approved uses for properties zoned I-2 include any industrial use involving manufacturing, processing, assembling, fabricating, bottling and/or packaging of materials or heavy commodities. The property was recently rezoned to Open Space-1 (OS-1). Approved uses for properties designated OS-1 include parks, recreation centers, and open fields. The final remedy is fully compatible with the new zoning designation.

The Miocene aquifer system is the most widely used aquifer in south Mississippi and supplies the City of Picayune. The City of Picayune maintains five municipal water supply wells that serve approximately 10,683 persons. The City of Picayune drinking water wells are completed at depths of 1,042 feet or greater. The three nearest public water supply wells from the site are City of Picayune Well 1, City of Picayune Well 2, and City of Picayune Well 3, which are located within 0.25 to 0.5 mile east of the site. City of Picayune Well 4 is located 1.75 miles northeast of the site, and City of Picayune Well 5 is located 0.6 mile south of the facility, in addition to the City of Picayune's municipal water supply wells, Dixie Utilities and the Nicholson Water & Sewer Association provide potable water to the community. These two utilities have a total of four water supply wells located within 2 to 3 miles of the site and are completed at depths ranging from 365 to 490 feet. The Miocene aquifer system is separated from the Citronelle or surficial aquifer by a massive clay layer. This clay layer prevents contamination in the Citronelle aquifer from impacting public water supply wells.

The uppermost aquifer at this site is the Citronelle aquifer. The  Citronelle aquifer is not currently being used as a drinking water source in the site vicinity. There are no known private wells in the site vicinity. Further, a public ordinance prohibits the existence of private drinking water wells within a 3-mile radius of the site. However, since the potential exist for the public ordinance to be cancelled in the future residential exposure to groundwater obtained from the Citronelle aquifer was evaluated. It is anticipated that the city ordinance will remain in place and the City of Picayune, Dixie Utilities, and Nicholson Water & Sewer Association will continue to provide drinking water in the future.

The surface water runoff from the Site leads to Mill Creek. There is no official state designation for Mill Creek. As such, the state has informed EPA that Mill Creek has a fish and wildlife designation.

A Record of Decision addressing Operable Unit 1 was completed in September 2007.

The Sonford Products Superfund Site Operable Unit (OU) 1 (Site) is located at 3506 Payne Drive, in Flowood, Rankin County, Mississippi. The Site is identified in CERCLIS as MSD865556388. The Record of Decision (ROD) is issued by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the lead agency for site activities, and the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ), the support agency. EPA has not located a potentially responsible party who is available or financially viable to conduct the remediation. Thus, EPA is currently handling the Site as fund lead. 

The Site is comprised of two separate parcels, the Sonford Products parcel and the adjacent undeveloped parcel. The Site including both parcels is approximately six acres in size. The former Sonford Products parcel is relatively flat, mostly covered with pea gravel and clear of vegetation, and actively used for industrial purposes. This parcel is currently leased by a company that manufactures concrete septic tanks. The septic tanks along with heavy machinery are used and stored at the Site. The Site is bounded on the west by Gulf South Pipeline right of way, the pipeline is comprised of a 12-inch steel high-pressure natural gas pipeline installed in the 1940's. The gas pipeline is bounded on the west by an active rail line, and beyond the rail line lays an older neighborhood of homes and trailers in a mixed state of repair. The direction of groundwater flow is west - northwest toward the residential area. Groundwater flow crosses both the gas line and rail line right of ways. The active rail line separates the Site from the adjacent residential area.

The other parcel immediately south of the Sonford Products parcel is an undeveloped lot. The undeveloped parcel is heavily forested and is not in use. A chain link fence surrounds the perimeter of both parcels. Both properties are surrounded primarily by forested wetlands and light industrial /commercial businesses in both northern and eastern directions.

From 1972 to 1985, two separate chemical processing plants operated under the company name Sonford International and Sonford Products. The operations of both companies involved turning pentachlorphenol (PCP) into liquid formulations. Sonford International operated at the Site from 1972 to 1980 and produced a water-soluble product, sodium pentachlorophenate, used for the short termed protection of wood products from mildew. Sonford Products operated at the Site from 1980 to March 1985. Sonford Products produced an oil-soluble PCP product used for the long-term protection of wood products. In addition to the PCP product, Sonford Products also produced products for the control of pests and products to control the growth of mold and sap stains in freshly cut lumber.

On September 3, 1980, a Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) Notification for a Part A permit was filed by Sonford Products, which resulted in the facility being classified as a RCRA  generator where the hazardous wastes were required to be shipped off-site within 90 days.

Mississippi Beaurau of Pollution Control (MBPC) conducted a hazardous waste inspection on December 31, 1980, at the facility. This inspection identified waste and waste quantities generated during the facility's operations including 550 pounds of PCP and 6,000 pounds of sodium pentachlorophenate. The waste product generated during the production of PCP was a sludge, which was stored in drums at the facility and transported for disposal at Chemical Waste Management in Emelle, Alabama. The sodium pentachlorophenate was also stored on-site in drums and then transported to another Sonford Products facility in St. Paul, Minnesota for reuse.

On April 18, 1985, approximately 2,000 gallons of PCP were spilled into the wetlands on the parcel immediately south of the facility. Mississippi Department of Natural Resources (MDNR) responded to the spill and began remediation of the wetland area. The wetland was contaminated with PCP, mercury, lindane, and phenylmercuric acetate. On April 21, 1985, EPA assumed responsibility for the response action at the Site. Remediation of the wetland included the excavation and removal of approximately 2,500 cubic yards of impacted soils. The contaminated soils were transported to a chemical waste disposal facility in Emelle, Alabama. The remediation efforts also included the disposal of more than 10,000 gallons of oil and treating solution at an incinerator in South Carolina and the treatment and disposal of approximately 100,000 gallons of existing wastewater. EPA response action for the 2,000 gallon PCP release was completed on May 10, 1985.

In June of 1985, MBPC prepared a Preliminary Assessment (PA), which detailed site operations, releases, and response actions at the Sonford Products facility. The Site was assessed as a medium priority for further inspection. On July 10, 1985, a desktop Site Inspection (SI) was prepared by MBPC, which included documentation of site operations, past site activities, enforcement / response actions, and ownership data.

From April 1985 until January 1989, the Sonford Products facility was unoccupied. In September 1989, a PA Reassessment was prepared for the Sonford Products facility by MBPC. No sampling occurred in preparation of this report but based upon previous sampling results from previous investigations MBPC recommended no further remedial action for the Site. In January 1989, Sunrise Truck Lines began leasing the property. Sunrise Truck Lines transported non-food dry commodities, which were not stored on-site. The actual length of time Sunrise Truck Lines leased the property is unknown. More recent changes in site conditions prompted the need for an updated PA/SI. These changes included the addition of a multifamily residential structure with people living and working at the Site. Currently, no one resides at the Site; but, there are still employees working on-site.

In 2004 Weston Solutions, Inc., a contractor for the EPA, prepared a PA/SI for the Site. The PA/SI was prepared in order to determine if the Site had the potential to be placed on the National Priorities List (NPL). The results of the updated PA/SI supported a listing of the Site on the NPL. EPA listed the Site on the NPL in March 2007.

As a result of the former chemical processing operations, the soil, groundwater, surface water, and sediment at and closely surrounding the Site are contaminated. The Site is located in Flowood, Mississippi, a rapidly growing suburb of Jackson, Mississippi. The Site is comprised of two separate parcels, the Sonford Products parcel and the adjacent undeveloped parcel. The Site including both parcels is approximately six acres in size. The undeveloped parcel contains no structures, and is located between the Sonford Products parcel and the Custom Products facility.

The former Sonford Products parcel is relatively flat, clear of vegetation, and actively used for light industrial purposes. The undeveloped parcel is heavily forested trees and is not currently in use. Two separate vehicular access points to the Site are located at Payne Drive and Custom Drive. The properties are surrounded primarily by forested wetlands and some light commercial and industrial uses. The Site is bounded on the west by Gulf South Pipeline right of way, comprised of a 12 inch steel high-pressure natural gas pipeline installed in the 1940's. The gas pipeline is bounded on the west by an active rail line, and beyond the rail line lays an older neighborhood of homes and trailers in a mixed state of repair. There are no signs of new residential development in the proximity of the Site. Public water and electricity are available at the Site, but the nearest public sewer line appears to be located on the other side of the railroad tracks.

The former Sonford Products property is zoned Light Industrial District (I-1) and the adjacent forested property is zoned Land Conservation District (L-C). Because the property zoned L-C is less than five acres, single-family detached structures and similar structures are prohibited; however, crop cultivation is permitted. The most likely future use at the Site is industrial. According to the City of Flowood representatives, the L-C zoning is a transitional designation for areas of the City where the best future use has not yet been determined. According to the City's Comprehensive Plan, these areas often do not have "current utilities or access to adequate public facilities." The City intends to rezone these areas when public utility systems are expanded to adequately serve them and the demand for development increases. The area the properties are located within is primarily surrounded by industrially or commercially zoned land. The adjacent neighborhood of older homes and trailers to the northwest of the Site is zoned R-2. The Site is also located in a flood zone. Any future development at the Site would need to address requirements outlined in the City's flood ordinance.

Flowood appears to be a relatively prosperous community with significant new commercial and residential construction underway. The Site is located in an area of town that is not currently experiencing any new construction and is not likely to be targeted for growth in the foreseeable future. The City of Flowood representatives stated that light industrial uses were the most desirable and the anticipated future use of the property.

A ROD addressing OU1 was completed in September 2009.

A ROD addressing OU2 was completed in September 2010.
OU2 addresses the contamination present in the surface soil, the sediment, and the surface water. Contact with the Contaminants of Concern (COCs) present in the surface soil, sediment, and surface water pose, an unacceptable risk to human health because concentrations of contaminants are present in media above levels that pose risks above the 1 x 10^-4 cancer risk or a hazard quotient of 1. The Selected Remedy for OU2 is necessary to protect public health or welfare or the environment from actual or threatened releases of hazardous substances into the environment. An ecological risk assessment (ERA) evaluated the risks to ecological populations in contaminated media. The results of the ecological risk assessment indicated that sediments pose an unacceptable risk to ecological receptors from site contaminants.

The Flowood site is located in the town of Flowood, Rankin County, Mississippi along Highway 468 on the east side of the Pearl River, east of Jackson, Mississippi. The site encompasses approximately 225 acres of property and consists mostly of wetlands and lowlands of the alluvial plain of the Pearl River.

Two manufacturing facilities have existed at the Flowood site since at least the 1940's. The northernmost facility is currently occupied by the Stone Container Corporation. The facility to the south, currently owned by Rival Manufacturing Company, was used for the manufacture of ceramic tiles from the 1950's through the early 1970's. A former owner of this facility, the Marmon Group, began using the facility to manufacture stoneware cooking pots in the mid 1970's. Rival Manufacturing continues this operation. The United Gas Pipe Line Company also owns a portion of the property which comprises the Site.

State officials first became aware of the presence of hazardous substances in an onsite canal during a routine industrial wastewater inspection in the fall of 1982. In January 1983, the site was reported to the EPA by the State of Mississippi. Investigations performed indicated that soils and sediments containing lead existed at five areas around the site: the slough/canal area, the small drainage ditch, the wash area, the drainage ditch/Lake Marie area, and the cow pasture ponded area. The site was added as a "Superfund" site in September 1983, at the request of the State of Mississippi. EPA and the Marmon Group signed a Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (RI/FS) Consent Agreement in January 1986. The final RI report was issued in August 1987 and the Final FS was issued in April 1988. The ROD was signed in September 1988. The major components of the selected remedy included excavation and solidification/stabilization of 6,000 cubic yards of contaminated soils and sediments. The treated material was to be backfilled into the excavated slough/canal area  and covered.

A consent agreement between EPA and the Potentially Responsible Parties (PRPs) was reached in September 1989. The Consent Decree became final in February 1990 at which time the preparation of design plans commenced.

 The site was added as a "Superfund" site in September 1983 and an Explanation of Significant Differences (ESD) for the Flowood Superfund Site was signed in September 1993.

The Newsom Brothers/Old Reichold Chemicals, Inc., Site is located in Marion County, Columbia, Mississippi. The 81-acre Site is bordered on the north by residences along Bullis, Wade, and Pearl Streets, and on the east by residences along Chinaberry and Park Avenues. The Illinois Central Gulf Railroad parallels most of the site's southwestern border. Further to the southwest, across the railroad, lies a moderately developed commercial area. Scattered residences are also located to the south. A chain-link fence surrounds the entire facility.

The Site's main processing facilities were located in the west-central portion of the Site. Of significance are an extensive system of concrete drains that apparently served to collect and drain spilled wastes and rainwater, two 100,000-gallon storage tanks which reportedly contained diesel oil, several smaller tanks and boilers, one incinerator and one boiler building used to heat "Dowtherm". The extent of the area of runoff (Old Processing Area) drained by the concrete drainage system is approximately 300,000 square feet.

North of the processing area is a 20-acre field sparsely covered with short grass. The southeast quadrant of the Site contains three ponds (North, East and Horseshoe), a pecan orchard, and the remnants of a wood chip pile. The fourth pond located in the extreme south was filled in 1984 during an EPA emergency response action.

Several areas of buried material were identified during the remedial investigation of the Site. Buried drums were found in the North Pond and Pecan Orchard areas. EPA returned to the site in November 1987 to remove these drums. During this removal action, additional areas of buried materials were discovered and investigated through additional field work.

In 1989, EPA issued a cleanup plan (a Record of Decision, or ROD) for OU-1. The plan included removing aboveground and underground storage tanks and debris; draining on-site ponds; digging up contaminated soil and sediment and disposing of the material at an off-site facility; placing clean fill in the dug-up areas; digging up tar-like waste materials and treating the materials off site; disposing of treated materials at an off-site facility; monitoring groundwater; and preventing erosion at the site.

In 1997, EPA issued a cleanup plan (a ROD) for OU-2. The plan included EPA�s decision that no cleanup activities were necessary to address groundwater contamination. The plan required a three-year plan to confirm groundwater contamination did not exist. Following completion of the monitoring plan, EPA and MDEQ would evaluate groundwater contamination.
