The Waverly Groundwater Contamination Site is located in Lancaster County in southeastern Nebraska, in and near the city of Waverly. The Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC), an agency within the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), operated a grain storage facility in Waverly between 1952 and 1974. The facility consisted of storage structures (approximately 100 bins and 13 Quonset huts) on concrete foundations. The fumigant "80/20" was used at the facility between approximately 1955 and 1965. The fumigant was reported to have been composed of 80% carbon tetrachloride and 20% carbon disulfide.

The EPA sampled the Waverly municipal drinking water system in July 1982 as part of a nationwide survey. The analytical results indicated contamination of the public water supply (PWS) wells 1 and 3 with carbon tetrachloride and chloroform at concentrations of up to 200 parts per billion (ppb) and 7.5 ppb, respectively. Subsequent samplings of PWS 3 in 1983, 1984, 1985, and 1986 confirmed continuing high levels of carbon tetrachloride and chloroform. The site was placed on the National Priorities List (NPL) in October 1984.

After the discovery of contamination, the city of Waverly relegated PWS 1 and PWS 2 to standby status and PWS 3 was removed from service. Between 1982 and 1987, four additional PWS wells were sited south of the site. Two of these wells are two miles southwest of town, outside the known extent of the contaminated plume associated with the site.

In May 1986, the EPA developed an Engineering Evaluation and Cost Analysis (EE/CA) report outlining an Expedited Response Action (ERA). The ERA included (1) pumping and treating the groundwater with air stripping technology, and (2) soil gas extraction. Design of the system was completed in May 1987, and a public meeting was held in Waverly with the mayor and city council to receive their comments on the proposed ERA system.

The EPA began operation of the current ERA systems at the site in February 1988. A  compliance agreement between the CCC/USDA and the EPA subsequently went into effect in May 1988. In June 1988, the CCC/USDA took over the operation and maintenance of the ERA. In September 1990, the EPA issued the Record of Decision (ROD) for the Waverly Groundwater Contamination Site. The CCC/USDA is responsible for implementing the response actions described in the ROD for the Waverly site.

In April 2004, a five-year review was conducted to assess current site conditions as required under CERCLA ? 121(c) and Section 300.430 (f)(4)(ii) of the National Oil and Hazardous Substances Pollution Contingency Plan (NCP). This review included additional groundwater and soil gas sampling activities at targeted areas around the site. The results of this targeted investigation have found that the remaining carbon tetrachloride plume is restricted vertically within the upper aquifer (30 to 40 feet below ground surface), and that the plume is approximately 900 feet long and 250 feet wide, with the majority of the plume located under 141st Street. The local groundwater flow direction has been shown to move primarily to the northeast.

As the plume continues to move to the northeast it will be continually tracked by monitoring wells that are currently being installed along 141st Street. Additional monitoring wells need to be placed on the land located at the southeast corner of 141st Street and Waverly Road.

The property east of 141st Street and south of Waverly Road, across from the Hedrick property, has recently been purchased for the construction of a housing development. Monitoring well placement will be negotiated with the new land owner. The additional monitoring wells placed on this property are based on the natural groundwater flow to the northeast. This groundwater flow direction could potentially move the remaining small plume under homes being planned for this development.

Recent groundwater and soil gas sampling data indicate that the relatively low concent rations of carbon tetrachloride in the plume, and the depth of the plume, do not present a health threat through either direct exposure or vapor intrusion to a future resident in this proposed new housing development. Additionally, there will be no exposure to contaminated ground water since all the new homes in the new addition will receive their water from Waverly's municipal wells.

A ROD addressing Operable Unit 1 (OU 1) was completed in September of 1990.  An ESD pertaining to the OU1 ROD was completed in March of 2005.

CITY HAS FOUND VOC CONTAMINATION IN 1 OF ITS DRINKING WATER WELLS. CLEBURN ST WELL SHUT DOWN DUE TO PCE CONTAMINATION.


The Cleburn Street Well Site is located in Grand Island, Hall County, Nebraska and is situated approximately two miles north of the Wood River and approximately seven miles northeast of the Platte River. The Cleburn Street Well site encompasses a portion of the downtown area, and is surrounded by a variety of light industries, commercial businesses, and residential dwellings. The site is located in the Great Plains physiographic province and in the middle of the Platte River Basin. Surface topography is generally flat with natural surface drainage flowing in a northeasterly direction. Much of the surface water runoff from the site is controlled by man-made surface features such as storm sewers and gutters. The Platte River flows southwest to northeast and is situated approximately seven miles south of Grand Island. Groundwater flows in a northeasterly direction in the vicinity of the site. The Cleburn Street Well site consists of a former municipal water supply well, the Cleburn Street well, and surrounding groundwater and soils containing volatile organic compounds (VOCs), primarily tetrachoroethylene (PCE).  Results of the Remedial Investigation (RI) completed in 1993 indicate four separate source areas including three dry cleaning facilities and a former solvents distribution facility. This ROD (EPA/ROD/R07-96/083) addresses the three dry cleaning source areas only. The solvents facility source area will be addressed in a separate ROD following additional investigation. The three dry cleaning source areas which are the subject of this ROD include the former One Hour Martinizing facility, the Liberty Services facility, and the Ideal Cleaners of Grand Island facility. Results of the RI indicate that the primary source area responsible for contamination of the Cleburn Street municipal well is the former One Hour Martinizing facility. Extremely  high contaminant levels were found in the shallow subsurface soils and groundwater in the vicinity of this facility. The Liberty Services and Ideal Cleaners source areas exhibit lesser degrees of contamination and are not believed to be related to contamination of the Cleburn Street well.

A ROD addressing OU1 was completed in June 1996.

OU 2:
The Site is comprised of five operable units (OUs) and covers an area of approximately 144 city blocks. OU 1 is the area of subsurface soil contamination at the former One Hour Martinizing (OHM) facility. OU 2 is the area of groundwater contamination at the facility. OU 3 is the area of groundwater contamination at Liberty Cleaners. OU 4 is the area of groundwater contamination at Ideal Cleaners. OU 5 is the area of soil and groundwater contamination at the Nebraska Solvent Company. This Record of Decision (ROD) Amendment documents the selected amended remedial action for OU 2 at the facility to address the remaining residual source materials within the saturated soils and associated downgradient groundwater plume contaminated with tetrachloroethylene (PCE), trichloroethylene (TCE), carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) and chloroform (CHCl3). The facility is currently being used as an auto mechanic shop as well as a church.

The first ROD was signed in June 1996. The selected remedy for OU 1 included soil vapor extraction (SVE) and treatment by carbon adsorption to address contamination in subsurface soils at the facility source area and groundwater extraction and treatment (GET) using air stripping to address groundwater contamination at the facility source area and groundwater plume designated as OU 2. The selected remedy for Liberty Cleaners (OU 3) and Ideal Cleaners (OU 4) included monitored natural attenuation (MNA) and SVE as a contingency. The 1996 ROD also included groundwater monitoring and institutional controls (ICs) for OUs 1, 2, 3 and 4. A separate ROD was signed for the Nebraska Solvent Company (OU 5) in September  2001 and included SVE and air sparging. The 2001 ROD for OU 5 was amended in 2009 to enhance the SVE and air sparging systems.

The EPA, the lead agency for the Site, began additional investigation activities in 2006 at the facility (OU 2) to further delineate remaining residual contamination at the source area and the groundwater contaminant plume While the existing GET remedy at the facility has been largely effective in containing the plume, it has not addressed the groundwater at the source area or downgradient plume to a substantial degree, and does not appear to be adequate to meet the remedial action objectives (RAOs) established in the 1996 ROD. Historical results from the long term remedial action (LTRA) sampling events indicate that groundwater contamination has not been decreasing in the monitoring well network, particularly in wells with high concentrations of PCE at the source area beneath the facility. Based on the additional information developed since the 1996 ROD was issued, the EPA selected the amended remedial action to address the remaining residual contamination.

The Site is located in Grand Island, Hall County, in east-central Nebraska. The city of Grand Island has an estimated population of 48, 520 and lies just north of the Platte River. The Site consists of an aquifer contaminated with industrial chemicals, primarily chlorinated volatile organic compounds (VOCs). 

PCE contamination was first discovered at the Site in March 1986 when the Nebraska Department of Health detected PCE in the Cleburn Street well at a concentration of 21.9 micrograms per liter (ug/L). The well was subsequently closed for drinking water purposes the following month. Until 1992, groundwater pumped from the Cleburn Street well was discharged to the city's storm sewer system for direct discharge to the Wood River. In 1993, the discharge of the groundwater was redirected to the city's sanitary sewer for treatment in the publically owned treatment works (POTW). T o alleviate flooding problems in the Eddy Street underpass, the city has infrequently operated the Cleburn Street well and an additional dewatering pump which is located within the Eddy Street underpass.

The EPA became involved with the Site in 1987 when the agency conducted a Preliminary Assessment. A Site Inspection was subsequently conducted that year which included a soil gas investigation to locate potential source areas. The soil gas investigation consisted of obtaining air samples from the pore spaces in the soil above the saturated zone at depths of approximately 1 to 5 feet below ground surface (bgs) at 73 sample locations. Four potential source areas were identified. Based on the findings of the EPA-lead studies, the Site was proposed for listing on the National Priorities List (NPL) on July 29, 1991, and was placed on the NPL on October 14, 1992.

The preliminary investigations identified four separate source areas: three dry-cleaning facilities and a former solvent distribution company. The primary source of contamination impacting the Cleburn Street well was the facility located on the southwest comer of 4"' and Eddy Street, near , the Eddy Street Underpass, where high contaminant concentrations were observed in both shallow subsurface soils and groundwater. Between 1990 and 1992, the EPA conducted a search for potentially responsible parties. A series of CERCLA section 104(e) information request letters were sent to several parties associated with potential sources identified during the soil gas investigation. The EPA determined that OHM, a Missouri corporation, used PCE which likely caused releases. OHM was the owner and operator of the facility for a period that extended sometime after 1949 through March 1989. Although the EPA identified subsequent owners as potentially liable, the agency did not identify any who were viable, including the current owner and the current operator. Based on this search, the EPA initiated a fund-lead remedial invest igation/feasibility study (RI/FS) in 1991.

Because of the four distinct source areas and varying degrees of contamination, the EPA subdivided the Site into the following OUs: OU 1 - subsurface soil of the facility,
OU 2 - groundwater emanating from the facility, OU 3 - groundwater emanating from Liberty Cleaners, OU 4 - groundwater emanating from Ideal Cleaners, and soil and groundwater associated with OU 5 - Nebraska Solvent Company. Currently, all municipal wells in the vicinity of the Site have been disconnected from the public water supply and the city has passed an ordinance prohibiting groundwater use or the installation of wells within the affected area around the Site.

The EPA initiated a fund-lead RI/FS for three of the four source areas, including the facility, in September 1991. Phases I and II of the RI field sampling activities were conducted in 1992 and 1993, and the RI Report, including a baseline human health risk assessment (HHRA), was submitted to the EPA in May 1993. At the EPA's direction, a Phase III was later conducted to delineate the extent of contamination detected in the previous Phase I and Phase II investigations. During these RI efforts, PCE concentrations in groundwater at the facility source area were greater than 170,000 ug/L. Based on this, the EPA conducted a non-time-critical removal action in 1993 to prevent the contamination from impacting additional downgradient municipal supply wells until a permanent remedy could be selected and implemented. An engineering evaluation/cost analysis was prepared to support the removal action, which consisted of installation of one groundwater extraction well at the facility and disposal of the groundwater into the city POTW. The removal action continued until the permanent GET system was constructed in 1998 as the OU 2 remedy.

In June 1996, the EPA signed a ROD for OUs 1 through 4 detailing the selected remedies for treating the affected media. The selected remedy for OU 1 and OU 2 con sisted of the following: In situ soil treatment by SVE and treatment by carbon adsorption, GET by on-site air stripping, ICs to restrict groundwater use and prevent exposures, groundwater monitoring, and air monitoring of emissions from the air stripper and emissions control if necessary. The selected remedy for Liberty Cleaners (OU 3) and Ideal Cleaners (OU 4) consisted of groundwater monitoring for 10 years, ICs to restrict groundwater use and an SVE and treatment system as a contingency. A separate ROD was signed for OU 5 in September 2001 and included SVE and air sparging. The 2001 ROD for OU 5 was amended in 2009 to enhance the SVE and air sparging systems.

The Remedial Design for OU 1 and OU 2 was completed and approved in September 1997. The design included plans and specifications for the installation of both an SVE and GET system. Construction of the systems began in March 1998 and was completed in August 1998. The SVE system consisted of four wells that withdraw contaminated vapors from subsurface soils. The wells were installed with a screened interval of 8 to 18 feet bgs. The contaminated vapors were treated via granular activated carbon (GAC) adsorption units. The GET system consists of three extraction wells to withdraw contaminated groundwater, which is treated in an air stripper. Extraction well 1 was installed with a screened interval of 13 to 57 feet bgs. Extraction wells 2 and 3 were installed with a screened interval of 24 to 49 feet bgs. Treated water from the GET system was discharged into the Wood River via the Grand Island storm water system under a National Pollutant Discharge Elimination Permit.

The EPA collected performance monitoring samples at OU 1 and OU 2 from August 1998 through April 2000. Responsibility for operations and maintenance activities at the OU 1 SVE soil remediation system was transferred from the EPA to the Nebraska Department of Environmental Quality (NDEQ) in 2000. In August 2006, the SVE soil remediation system  was shut down by NDEQ because the soil vapor concentrations were significantly less than initial concentrations and appeared asymptotic. NDEQ concluded that the SVE system had remediated the area of contaminated soil. In February 2007, the EPA notified NDEQ that its obligations to operate the OU 1 remedy were complete and that any further work with regard to the SVE system would be conducted by the EPA as part of the OU 2 groundwater restoration remedy.

The existing GET remedy for the facility has been largely effective in containing the plume but has not addressed the source area or downgradient contaminant plume to a substantial degree and does not appear to be adequate to meet RAOs established in the 1996 ROD. Historical results from the LTRA sampling events indicate that groundwater contamination was not decreasing in the monitoring well network, particularly in wells with high concentrations of PCE beneath the facility. Based on this information, from November 2006 through December 2011, the EPA conducted a series of additional investigations as part of a Focused RI/FS, honing in on groundwater contamination associated with OU 2. These investigations included a source area investigation, a hydrogeologic investigation, an evaluation of the silt layer, an in situ chemical oxidation injection evaluation treatability study, an expanded groundwater profile sampling and a vapor intrusion evaluation. These additional investigation activities are described in detail within Section 5.0, Site Characteristics, of this ROD Amendment.

A Record of Decision Amendment for the Cleburn Street Well Superfund Site OU-2 was completed in September 2012.

OU 5:
Operable Unit (OU) 5 is the former Nebraska Solvent Company Facility. OU5 is located northwest of the intersection of Lincoln Street and the railroad right-of-way on property owned by the Union Pacific Railroad (UPRR).

The contaminated media at OU5 are soil and ground water. Some on-site soils contain contamination  which is a source of contamination in the ground water. This source continually releases chlorinated contamination into the upper portion of the ground water of OU5. In addition, light hydrocarbon contamination has been found sporadically floating atop the ground water. The chlorinated contamination, both in the soil and ground water, and the hydrocarbon contamination will be referred to in this record as volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Based on the site investigation, the EPA has concluded that the presence of these contaminants is, most probably, the result of activities at OU5 by the Nebraska Solvent Company. The Nebraska Solvent Company facilities were located on property owned by the Union Pacific Railroad (UPRR). Nebraska Solvents Company is no longer in business. However, under the Superfund law, the current owner of contaminated property is responsible for the clean up. The UPRR is the owner of the property that comprises OU5 and is referred to as the PRP. This property is located generally northwest of the intersection of Lincoln Street and the UPRR rail lines in east central downtown Grand Island, Nebraska. The subject property consists of two parcels (west and east) and attached to this ROD. The west parcel was leased by the Nebraska Solvent Company from 1936 to 1973 for above ground tank storage and distribution of organic solvents including PCE for industrial use, primarily, in the dry cleaning industry. Prior to 1973, bulk petroleum storage tanks located at the west parcel were used for the storage of cleaning solvents. The west parcel occupies an area approximately 75 feet by 175 feet just south of the Thompson Company grocery distribution facility and is leased by Toba, Inc. of Grand Island. This parcel is currently unoccupied and is composed of soil fill with no asphalt or concrete paving.

The east parcel was leased by the Nebraska Solvent Company until 1973 for warehousing, handling, and truck loading cleaning solvents, mostly in drums. This  occupies an area approximately 100 feet by 125 feet. It is currently leased by the city of Grand Island's street department. It now consists of a maintenance office building and a small sign shop in the former Nebraska Solvent Company warehouse plus a portion of the concrete paved maintenance yard. A municipal water well, the Lincoln Street Well, was located directly northeast of the east parcel. In May 1994, the city of Grand Island terminated use of the well following the detection of PCE in the ground water at concentrations exceeding the maximum contaminant level (MCL) as established by the Safe Drinking Water Act. The well was plugged and abandoned in August 1997 by the city of Grand Island. PCE was first detected in the drinking water wells of Grand Island, Nebraska, in April 1984 by the Nebraska Department of Health (NDOH). In 1986, NDOH found low levels of PCE in the Lincoln Street Well and higher levels in the Cleburn Street Well, which is located approximately 1,400 feet northeast of OU5. In September 1988, the EPA conducted a soil gas survey over a large area of downtown Grand Island. It was discovered that PCE existed in the soil near the former Nebraska Solvents Company facilities. The subsequent Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (RI/FS) at the Cleburn Street Well Site was conducted by the EPA and published on January 27, 1993. The RI/FS confirmed the presence of contamination in both the soil and ground water near the former Nebraska Solvent Company facilities and concluded that a plume or plumes of contamination in the ground water were emanating from there.

UPRR, under EPA's oversight via a July 1998 Administrative Order on Consent, completed the remedial investigation (RI) Site Characterization Summary report. This RI confirmed and defined the source, magnitude, and locations of the VOC contamination in both the soil and groundwater at OU5. The investigation discovered a new contamination-Light Nonaqueous Phase Liquids (LNAPLs)-in the wes t parcel. LNAPLs were determined to be light mineral spirit hydrocarbons.

A feasibility study (FS) was completed in 2000. The FS included a pilot study by UPRR in the west parcel to substantiate the effectiveness of a soil vapor extraction (SVE) system to remove contamination from the soil. The selected remedy included a SVE system for the soil cleanup and an air sparging (AS) system for the groundwater cleanup, monitoring of both media, LNAPL removal from the groundwater, and an institutional control barring drinking water wells in the Site area via a Grand Island city ordinance. 

A ROD addressing OU5 was completed in September 2001.

Construction of the remedial action, which included five SVE wells and eighteen AS wells, was completed in June 2004. The SVE/AS systems were in operation from June 2004 to November 2007 at which time the systems were temporarily turned off for assessment of rebound within the areas of influence. The systems have performed well as expected. In 2005, the east parcel was in compliance. In 2006, a permanganate injection program to accelerate the degradation of VOCs in the groundwater was approved by EPA and the Nebraska Department of Environmental Quality (NDEQ).

Currently, all but one groundwater monitoring well in the east parcel and one in the west parcel have met the remediation level of five micrograms per liter. LNAPLs have also shown no reappearance after a pilot study was performed using the MicroBlaze solution infusion. The groundwater remediation generally has been successful; however, the soil in the west parcel still is a concern-specifically, the shallow soil.

The SVE system was in operation for over three years. Various off-gas treatments were used to limit air emissions. The SVE system effectively and efficiently removed most VOCs (including chlorinated solvents) and LNAPLs from the subsurface soil to the water table. However, a shallow zone of compacted silt and clay-rich soil from the surface to approximate ly four feet below ground surface (bgs) in the west parcel has not been sufficiently remediated by the SVE system. This is due to high compaction and low soil permeability limiting the ability of the system to pull air through this layer of the soil.

To address the impacted shallow soil and complete the Site's remediation in an effective and efficient manner, UPRR proposed to modify the SVE system remediation. EPA determined the modification to incorporate soil excavation and thermal treatment was a fundamental remedy change that would warrant a ROD Amendment.

A ROD amendment addressing OU5 of the Cleburn Street Well Site was completed in March 2009.

The Bruno Cooperative Association/Associated Properties (Bruno Co-op) site is located approximately 60 miles west of Omaha, Nebraska, and is situated in the northeast portion of Butler County in the small agricultural community of Bruno. The site was formerly used for grain storage by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).

At the site, groundwater is contaminated with chemicals which are constituents of grain fumigants including carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, and 1,2-dichloroethane. The disposal practices principally included the direct introduction of grain fumigation chemicals into rodent burrows for eradication purposes and thus minimized the aerial extent of surface applications. These practices served to limit the area of soil contamination by introducing the contaminants at depth through dispersal in rodent burrows.

The community of Bruno was served by two public water supply wells that had to be taken out of operation due to elevated levels of grain fumigant constituents in public drinking water. Two new water supply wells were located in an area hydraulically upgradient from the contaminated portion of the aquifer in order to restore drinking water to the community. The EPA provided bottled water to approximately 150 residents as an interim measure until the new water supply wells were operational.

Groundwater contaminants were initially discovered by the Nebraska Department of Health in the mid-1980s and verified throughout the 1980s and 1990s by the EPA, the Nebraska Department of Environmental Quality (NDEQ), and several contractors. The USDA and their contractors also found groundwater as well as soil contamination in the early to middle 1990s. The soil impacts were at depth and principally related to the fluctuating water table. Surficial soils were deemed to be relatively free of contaminants and vadose zone soils did not warrant inclusion in the cleanup plan due to the low levels of constituents that were present. The majority of the s oil contaminants had been flushed to the groundwater system over time due to the highly permeable nature of the soils, shallow depth to water, and long time frame following release of the contaminants.

A Record of Decision (ROD) was issued in 1998 by EPA with support of NDEQ and the community of Bruno. The ROD specified the following cleanup plan for the Bruno Co-op site: install a groundwater extraction system to pump the contaminated groundwater from the shallow drinking water aquifer; pump the contaminated groundwater from all depths (the approximate 100 feet of the shallow, unconsolidated, Pleistocene age aquifer is contaminated and hydraulically interconnected); treat the impacted groundwater by means of conventional air stripping technology; discharge the effluent water to a surface tributary of Skull Creek; allow for beneficial re-use by incorporating a point-of-use hookup on the effluent water discharge piping; abandon the contaminated former public water supply well #36-1 in accordance with state requirements; and return public water supply well #65-1 to use as a source of drinking water for the Village of Bruno (Village) in times of high demand.

Implementation of the ROD was delayed in order to conduct an evaluation of a relatively new type of groundwater extraction technology that involved below-ground air stripping and recirculation of the extracted groundwater as opposed to conventional above-ground air stripping and surface discharge of treated groundwater. The potential advantage of the new technology was to return the pumped water to the aquifer and perform the cleanup in an in-situ manner. However, the evaluation determined that the new technology resulted in neither improved cost efficiency, nor a reduced remediation time frame. Additionally, several potential design problems were identified during the evaluation. Thus, the engineering evaluation indicated the groundwater circulation well technology was not an optimum choice for the Bruno Co- op site and the original remedy was deemed to be the most effective and efficient. In the process of conducting the evaluation, costs of the selected remedy were re-analyzed. The updated cost estimate represented a significant difference in costs (increase) from the original 1998 ROD estimate and was the basis for the first Explanation of Significant Differences (ESD) in 2000. A second ESD addressing OU 1 was complete din September 2005.

MUNICIPAL WATER SUPPLY WELLS LOCATED IN CITY ARE            CONTAMINATED WITH TCE. 

The Tenth Street Site, also known as the Columbus Water Supply is located in the south-central portion of the city of Columbus, Nebraska. The Loup River is about 1.2 miles south of the site and flows east. Current land use at the site includes mostly occupied, single-family residences, as well as some commercial facilities, light industry, schools, and parks. The 10th Street Site consists of a volatile organic compound (VOC)-contaminated groundwater plume located beneath a mixture of commercial and residential properties in the city of Columbus, Nebraska. The city's southern well field consists of seven wells located near the city's water treatment plant on 10th Street. VOC contaminants have been detected in five of the seven municipal wells in the city's southern municipal well field and in the city's water distribution system. The U. S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is the lead agency for the site and the Nebraska Department of Environmental Quality (NDEQ) is the support agency. The sources of funding for cleanup of this site will be the Superfund trust fund and state funds received through the NDEQ. Capital construction costs, operational and functional costs, and long-term response costs which involve up to 10 years, will all be funded at 90 percent by the Superfund trust fund and 10 percent by the NDEQ.

The 10th Street Site first came to the attention of the Nebraska Department of Health, now the Nebraska Health and Human Services System (NHHSS), in November 1983 when VOCs were detected in a routine sampling event of the city's municipal wells. Follow-up analysis of the municipal wells also detected trichloroethene (TCE) at concentrations exceeding the maximum contaminant level (MCL) for TCE of 5 micrograms per liter (?g/l). The MCLs are established by the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA). In April 1987, the site was referred to the EPA for investigation. The 10th St reet Site was proposed for the Superfund National Priorities List (NPL) in October 1989 went final on the NPL in August 1990. On May 17, 1990, general notice letters were sent to the two drycleaners identified by the EPA as potentially responsible parties (PRPs): Jackson Services, Inc. and Liberty Cleaners inviting them to conduct or finance a Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (RI/FS). Both parties declined and claimed inability to perform or finance the RI/FS.

An RI/FS was conducted by the EPA between 1990 and 1993. Potential contaminant sources and the extent of groundwater contamination were investigated during the RI/FS. A network of monitoring wells was installed to monitor contaminants in the groundwater. During the RI/FS, the extent of groundwater contamination was generally thought to be restricted to the vicinity of the southern municipal well field. An EPA ROD was signed for the site in February 1995. 

A ROD addressing OU1 was completed in February 1995.

During post RI/FS sampling events, it was recognized that contaminant concentrations in municipal and monitoring wells had been decreasing. Therefore, the EPA selected sampling of municipal and monitoring wells and institutional controls to limit exposure to contamination from the 10th Street Site. The remedy also included a contingency for extraction of contaminated groundwater with treatment, if necessary and discharge to the Loup River (approximately ? mile south of the 10th Street Site). Follow-up quarterly groundwater monitoring by the EPA in 1997 to 1998 indicated that increasingly higher concentrations of tetrachloroethene (PCE) and TCE were detected along the northern boundary of the monitoring well network installed during the 1990-1993 RI/FS. In response to the results from the 1997-1998 quarterly sampling events, a series of removal assessments (RAs) were conducted to further investigate the 10th Street Site. Screening results of groundwater and soil samples collected during the  Phase 1 RA indicated that VOC contamination appeared to be originating from a current dry-cleaning business, OHM, located on the southwest corner of U.S. Highway 30 and 25th Avenue. Delineation of the shallow VOC-contaminated groundwater indicated that the contaminant plume initially flows to the southeast; following the ambient groundwater flow direction; however, due to pumping of the municipal wells, the groundwater flow direction is modified and the contaminant plume is drawn in a south-southwest direction toward the wells. In September 1999, the EPA installed additional monitoring wells to monitor the contaminant plume upgradient of the initial study area. Through a fund-lead removal action, the EPA initiated treatment of highly contaminated soil and groundwater at the OHM source area in October 2000. The source area treatment system consists of air sparging (AS) and soil vapor extraction (SVE). Additionally, the EPA is currently conducting a treatability study upgradient of the southern municipal well field with two types of in-well stripper (IWS) treatment systems.

The EPA issued a general notice letter to the owner and operator of OHM on February 8, 1999. Demand letters were issued to representatives of Jackson Services, Liberty Cleaners, and OHM on September 12, 2000. The EPA is in the process of pursuing cost recovery against all three PRPs. The operation and maintenance period for this groundwater action will begin after 10 years of long-term response, which NDEQ will fund 100 percent. In February 2001, the EPA prepared a second RI that incorporated the data gathered from RAs and 1999-2000 quarterly groundwater monitoring results. The EPA is currently completing the FS to determine the site-wide remedy to address all contaminated soil and groundwater at the site. This Interim Action ROD addresses contaminated groundwater in the vicinity and upgradient of the city of Columbus' southern municipal well field and at the One Hour Martinizing (OHM) source ar ea.

An Interim ROD addressing OU2 was completed in September 2001.

In May 2005, EPA prepared a second FS, entitled "Revised Final Feasibility Study Report" that incorporated the existing GET and AS/SVE systems into the alternatives considered for the site-wide remedy for contaminated soil and groundwater. These alternatives are presented in this final ROD.

A ROD addressing Operable Unit 02 at the 10th Street site was completed in September 2005.

The Ogallala Groundwater Contamination Site is in Ogallala, Keith County, in west central Nebraska. The City of Ogallala has an estimated population of 5,100 and lies just north of the South Platte River. The Ogallala Groundwater Contamination Site consists of an aquifer contaminated with industrial chemicals, primarily chlorinated volatile organics. Contamination was discovered in 1989 when the Nebraska Department of Health (NDOH) sampled the Ogallala public water supply system during routine sampling. Contamination was present in five of the town's nine water supply wells. Under a State of Nebraska Administrative Order, the City of Ogallala installed a new well field in 1993 northeast of the city. Depth to groundwater at the site ranges from 9 to 17 feet below ground surface (bgs). In 1990, the Nebraska Department of Environmental Quality (NDEQ), the support agency, conducted a soil-gas investigation to determine sources for the groundwater contamination. Based on this survey, several source areas were identified. The contamination present at the Tip-Top Dry Cleaners is referred to as the "east-PCE" plume and was subsequently identified as Operable Unit (OU) 2. The contamination from other sources was identified as OU 1 and is being addressed by a remedy selected in a Record of Decision (ROD) issued by EPA in 1999. Based on current information, current exposure to the contaminants is not occurring because of the installation of the new well field northeast of Ogallala.

The EPA, the lead agency, has been investigating the source of groundwater contamination in the Ogallala area since 1994. Prior to 1994, the NDEQ, the support agency, led the investigation. Due to the volatile organic compounds (VOCs) present in four of the nine municipal supply wells, EPA designated the contaminated area as the Ogallala Groundwater Contamination Site. The Ogallala Groundwater Contamination Site covers the business corridor along Highway 30 and an area north of Highway 30 which s tarts at the Tip-Top Cleaners and moves in an east-south-easterly direction to East G and 1st Streets. The Ogallala Groundwater Contamination Site was placed on the National Priorities List (NPL) in 1994.

The Ogallala Groundwater Contamination Site is composed of two OUs. OU 1 is the area with several sources of groundwater contamination extending from the American ShuiZuki Corporation plant site beneath Highway 30 to east of the city limits. OU 2 is the groundwater contamination migrating from the Tip-Top Cleaners.

Operable Unit 1 (OU1):

OU1 includes a plume of tetrachloroethylene (PCE) and trichloroethylene (TCE), located in the western portion of the site, in the Alluvial formation of the Ogallala aquifer and a second plume characterized by carbon tetrachloride (CT) and TCE contamination, located in the center of the site and present in the upper Ogallala formation.   A Record of Decision (ROD) addressing OU1 was completed in April 1999.

OU 2:

The tetrachloroethene (PCE) plume extends from the Tip-Top Dry Cleaners approximately 2,800 feet downgradient to the southeast to East G Street. The absence of PCE's breakdown products indicates that biodegradation of PCE in the groundwater at OU 2 does not appear to be occurring.

During 1995-1996, EPA installed 25 groundwater monitoring wells and conducted groundwater, surface water, and sediment sampling and analysis during the remedial investigation (RI). Results of the RI identified the Tip-Top Dry Cleaners as the likely source area for PCE that was detected in soils and groundwater in the northeastern portion of the site. In 2000, NDEQ conducted additional groundwater sampling to characterize the PCE plume at 35 direct-push sample locations. At each location, groundwater samples were collected from multiple depths. This allowed NDEQ to develop a vertical profile as well as the horizontal profile of the PCE contamination. The highest concentrations were found at a location immediately east of the Tip-T op Cleaners building.

In 2001-2002, EPA conducted an in-situ chemical oxidation treatability study using a dilute solution of sodium permanganate. The study was intended to evaluate the ability of this oxidant to effectively treat the PCE in the alluvial aquifer and to evaluate this technology as a potential treatment option that would be evaluated in the Feasibility Study (FS). Overall results of the treatability study indicated that the injection of the oxidant could be a relatively fast and effective method for significantly reducing the PCE concentrations in the aquifer.

Between January 2003 and August 2005, the EPA performed a time-critical removal action (TCRA) to reduce the PCE present in the aquifer to reduce the risk of exposure to indoor vapor intrusion. Ten injection events were conducted with several groundwater monitoring events before and after chemical treatment. The EPA injected sodium permanganate at strengths of 5 to 10 percent at 43 locations. The volume of oxidant varied from 50 to 100 gallons per injection location. The most recent injection was conducted in August 2005. The EPA used Superfund monies to support this work effort.

OU 2 of the Ogallala Groundwater Contamination Site starts at the Tip-Top Cleaners located at 116 West 5th Street. The PCE plume migrated in a narrow channel to the east-southeast from the source area. The area affected by the PCE contamination is a mixture of residential and commercial properties. Future use of the site is anticipated to be similar to current uses. There are no land use activities which are being restricted due to the contamination in the groundwater. Access is unrestricted and will not be changed in the future. There are no surface water resources currently within the PCE plume migrating from the source area. The groundwater in the vicinity of OU 2 has been designated as a Class GA Groundwater Supply by the State of Nebraska. A Class GA Groundwater is a groundwater supply which is currently be ing used as a public drinking water supply or is proposed to be used as a public drinking water supply. Contamination detected at OU 2 caused the state to designate the site as a Remedial Action Class 1 (RAC-1), requiring the "most extensive remedial action measures" to clean up the groundwater to drinking water quality suitable for all beneficial uses. The City of Ogallala enacted an ordinance to restrict use of the groundwater for potable water purposes in the Ogallala Groundwater Contamination Site area. These actions are necessary in order to minimize the threat to human health until such time as the project goals are achieved. The selected remedial action is necessary in order to ensure that the contaminated groundwater is cleaned up and the aquifer returned to full beneficial use within an acceptable timeframe. Nebraska Title 118 states that the timeframe for required action (including cleanup) will be the period of potential exposure to the contamination in the absence of any remedial action or 20 years, whichever is less.

A ROD addressing OU 2 was completed in February 2006.

The 110-acre property formerly owned by Garvey is located in the NWl/4 of Section 23, T7N, RlOW, approximately seven miles west ofthe Adams County/Clay County line in the southwest portion ofthe city of Hastings, Nebraska. The 110-acre property, consisting of an 88-acre parcel and a 22-acre parcel, is bounded on the north by U. S Highway 6 and business and residential properties, on the east by the Burlington Northern and Santa Fe railroad frack, on the west by Marion Road, and on the south by farmland. Garvey owned and operated a grain elevator facility on the 22-acre parcel along the eastem boundary of the property. The contamination associated with the Garvey Elevator Superfund Site (Site) consists of volatile organic compound (VOC)-contaminated soils and groundwater beneath the 22-acre parcel and an associated groundwater contaminant plume approximately three miles long that extends from the property in an east-southeasterly direction.

EPA has organized the Site into two Operable Units. Operable Unit 1 (OU 1) is designated as the area of soil and groundwater contamination that is generally within the boundaries ofthe 22-acre parcel on which the grain storage facility formerly owned by Garvey was operated. OU 1 is commonly referred to as the source area. OU 2 is the associated groundwater contaminant plume that extends east-southeast from OU 1 approximately three miles, in the direction of groundwater flow.

The land usage at OU 1 is light industrial (I-l). OU 1 is currently the location of an active, 8-million-bushel-capacity, grain storage facility. The grain storage facility is currently owned and operated by Ag Processing, Inc. (AGP). AGP also owns the 88 acres bounding OU 1 on the north, west, mid south. AGP, as purchaser ofthe property and under the terms of a 2005 Agreement among EPA, Garvey and AGP agreed to execute and record in the Recorder's Office of Adams County, an easement, running wdth the land (CERCLA Docket No. 07-2005-0268). The easement w ould grant access for response activities at or near the Site and grants the right to enforce land/water use restrictions that EPA determines necessary to implement, ensure noninterference with, or ensure the protectiveness of the response actions to be performed at or near the Site. The land use east of OU 1 and in those areas above the downgradient groundwater plume is a mix of agricultural, residential, and commercial. It is anticipated that current land usage at and in the immediate vicinity of OU 1 will remain unchanged for the foreseeable fiiture. The nearest residential developments are approximately 1 mile to the northeast and east. However, isolated residences lie within 1/8 to 3/4 of a mile from OU 1.

Groundwater in the area is heavily utilized in areas within and surrounding the Site for domestic, irrigation, and commercial uses. Garvey previously utilized a private water well to meet its water supply needs at the grain storage facility. In March 18,1996, Garvey was connected to the municipal water supply and capped its private water well sometime in 1996. There are currently no water supply wells at OU 1. The majority of land in areas above the groundwater plume is outside the city limits of Hastings, and until 2008, a majority of the residential properties in these areas were not served by municipal water from the city of Hastings. Beginning in 2008 and under authority pursuant to the CERCLA removal program, EPA extended more than 1 1/4 miles of municipal water lines to connect all but one residence/business whose private water wells have been impacted. To address the sole residence not currentiy connected to the municipal supply, EPA is maintaining a whole-house, carbon filtration system to treat the water from its private well.  

The groundwater in the vicinity of OU 1 has been designated as a Class GA Ground Water Supply by the state of Nebraska. A Class GA Ground Water is a groundwater supply which is currently being used as a public drinking  water supply or is proposed to be used as a public drinking water supply. Contamination detected at OU 1 caused the state to designate the Site as a Remedial Action Class 1 (RAC-1), requiring the "most extensive remedial action measures "to clean up the groundwater to drinking water quality suitable for all beneficial uses. The selected remedial action is necessary in order to ensure that the contaminated groundwater is cleaned up and the aquifer retumed to beneficial use within an acceptable time frame. Nebraska Title 118 states that the time frame for required action (including cleanup) will be the period of potential exposure to the contamination in absence of any remedial action or 20 years, whichever is less.

This section ofthe Interim Record of Decision (ROD) provides the history ofthe Site and a brief discussion of EPA and the State's removal, remedial, and enforcement activities. The "Proposed Rule" proposing the Site to the National Priorities List (NPL) was published in the Federal Register (FR) on April 27,2005. The "Final Rule" adding the Site to the NPL was published in the FR on September 14, 2005.

The former Garvey property contains an active 8-million bushel capacity grain storage facility currently owned and operated by Ag Processing, Inc. (AGP). Garvey owned the grain storage facility from its constmction in 1959 until 2005. Garvey operated the grain storage facility from 1959 until April 1,1998, at which time a put through agreement with AGP became effective. In September 2005, Garvey, AGP, and EPA entered into an Agreement that allowed AGP to purchase the entire 110-acre property with an EPA covenant not to sue, provided AGP satisfactorily performed its obligations under the Agreement and subject to certain reservations of rights by EPA (CERCLA Docket No. 07-2005-0268). The effective date of deed transfer to AGP was October 7, 2005.

The property formerly owned by Garvey consisted ofa total of 110 acres; but historically, only a 22-acre p arcel was used for grain storage facility operations. The majority of the remaining 88 acres of property are used to cultivate crops. The grain storage facility at the Garvey terminal consists of a concrete elevator head house and silos, flat storage building, steel grain storage bins, and associated buildings (maintenance shop, office building, and chemical storage shed). The area surrounding the grain storage facility is rural with a sparse distribution of residential properties north, east and west of the site.

Garvey utilized a liquid mixture of carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) and carbon disulfide (CS2) as a grain fiimigant from 1959 to 1985. This fiimigant mixture is known as 80-20 fiimigant. Some formulations ofthe 80-20 fiimigant may also have contained a minor amount of ethylene dibromide (EDB), also known as 1,2-dibromoethane, CCl4, CS2, and EDB are CERCLA hazardous substances and are categorized as volatile organic compunds (VOCs). In 1960, Garvey installed a 3,000-gallon, above-ground storage tank (AST) north ofthe silos to store the liquid. The fumigant was fransferred via piping from the AST to the silos' grain application gallery on top ofthe silos. The section of piping between the AST and the side of the silos was buried. The piping exited the subsurface at the side ofthe silos and extended up the north side ofthe silos to the application gallery. In the mid-1970s, a release of carbon tetrachloride at the ground surface was noted in the area where the trucks drove over the underground piping. The buried portion ofthis delivery pipe was excavated and found to be broken in two places: one near the AST and one near the grain elevator. The piping was completely replaced at the time. Leaks and drips were reported to have occurred during the operation period ofthe AST and piping. Staining in the area beneath the valve ofthe AST was also observed. Garvey ceased use ofthe liquid fumigant in 1985 and the AST and underground piping were removed in 1986.

The  grain storage facility located on the 22-acre property is currently owned and operated by Ag Processing Inc. (AGP). AGP has operated the grain storage facility since April 1998. A ban on the production and import of carbon tefrachloride in developed countries, including the United States, tookeffect on January 1, 1996. 

The former Garvey grain elevator first came to the attention of Nebraska Department of Environmental Quality (NDEQ) in July 1994, when, in written correspondence, Garvey notified NDEQ of a release of organic solvents and the presence of groundwater contamination at its grain storage facility. The release of CCl4 and methyl ethyl ketone was reported to have been discovered on June 16,1994, but the date of occurrence was reported as unknown. Garvey also reported the results of Phase I activities of direct push soil sampling and installation and sampling of five monitoring wells. The results indicated CCl4 was detected in the soil and groundwater samples. The CCl4 concentrations in the groundwater exceeded EPA's maximum contaminant level (MCL) for CCl4 of 5 micrograms per liter (ug/l). Ih October 1994, Garvey reported to NDEQ that according to its sampling results, its monitoring wells, water supply well serving the grain storage facility, and several nearby private water supply wells were contaminated with CCl4 at levels that exceeded the MCL and were as high as 300 ug/l. In December 1994, Garvey notified NDEQ that it was beginning site assessment activities in accordance with Nebraska Title 118. Garvey installed an additional 18 monitoring wells.

In April 1995, Garvey met with NDEQ to present some preliminary site characterization results and to petition for entry into the Voluntary Cleanup Program (VCP), which is authorized by the Nebraska Remedial Action Plan Monitoring Act (RAPMA). The site characterization results indicated the presence of CCl4 soil gas contamination in the unsaturated zone across approximately one-third ofthe 22-acre active  portion ofthe property. The results also indicated a contaminated groundwater plume more than 1 mile in length, with a source area clearly defined at the 22-acre active portion ofthe former Garvey property. The only contaminant of concen identified was carbon tefrachloride, the highest concenfration of which was observed to be 29,943 ug/l in monitoring well MW-3B. Garvey also described its efforts of altemate water provisions (i.e., reportedly either a new well in an uncontaminated portion ofthe aquifer or hookup to the municipal water supply) for private water supply well users. The potential need to install a soil vapor extraction (SVE) system to address soil contamination in the unsaturated zone was discussed. In June 1995, NDEQ notified Garvey of its acceptance in the VCP.

In September 1995, Garvey met with NDEQ to present additional site characterization results and groundwater modeling results, and to propose actions to address the soil and groundwater contamination on its property. Garvey described a groundwater model they developed and applied to evaluate different scenarios for addressing the groundwater at the Site. In an October 1995 Site Characterization Report, Garvey summarized its investigations. The report described activities conducted by Garvey, in 1994 to characterize the nature and extent of VOC contamination in the soil and groundwater beneath the Site. Soil sampling at the grain storage facility detected only frace quantities of VOCs. Soil gas sampling, conducted primarily from a depth range between 9 and 18 feet (ft) below ground surface (bgs), identified potential source areas at numerous locations across the Site. This sampling was supplemented with limited soil gas vertical profiling at three additional locations. The entire area from the north side ofthe silos to the north side of the shop area, and frending east and west along the entire length ofthe silos had carbon tetrachloride concentrations in soil gas exceeding 10,000 ug/cubic m eter. It was estimated that the soil gas contamination was spread across more than 500,000 cubic feet at the grain storage facility and that more than 55 million cubic feet of soil was impacted. Of the 36 monitoring wells on the Site, CCl4 was detected in 15 of the wells at concenfrations greater than 1.0 ug/l. The highest measured concentrations of CCl4 were found in the immediate vicinity ofthe elevator, with the highest measured of 29,943 ug/l. CCl4 was detected only in the dissolved phase. In a well located approximately 5,500 east-southeast ofthe elevator, CCl4 was detected at 80 ug/l.

In late 1997, the city of Hastings notified NDEQ that CCl4 was detected in municipal well #13 located 1,500 ft northeast ofthe former Garvey property at 5 ug/l, which is equivalent to the MCL. In November 1997, the city of Hastings reassigned municipal well #13 for emergency use only, and it has been effectively shut-down since that time.

In January 1999, Garvey completed constmction of and began operating a groundwater extraction and treatment (GET) system and an SVE and treatment system. The systems were intended only to treat contaminated soils at the source area and prevent groundwater migration from the source area. The systems were not designed to address that portion of the groundwater contaminant plume that had already migrated off to the east-southeast of the grain storage facility. The GET system consisted of five wells screened in the shallow aquifer (RW-1 through RW-5) and three wells screened in the intermediate aquifer (RW-6, RW-7, and RW-8). The wells were fitted with variable frequency pumps designed for a maximum pumping rate of 40 and 100 gpm, for the shallow and intermediate wells, respectively. Extracted groundwater was treated by an air stripping tower. After treatment, the treated water was reinjected into two deep injection wells located to the west ofthe elevator. The SVE system consisted of five wells screened in the unsaturated zone from approximat ely 20 to 50 ft bgs (SVE-1, SVE-3, SVE-4, SVE-7, and SVE-8) and three wells screened in the unsaturated zone from about 60 to 110 ft bgs (SVE-9, SVE-10, and SVE-11). The SVE system was constincted with a blower capacity of 200 standard cubic feet per minute (scfm) for the shallow wells, and a 600 scfm blower for the deep wells. Based on pilot study testing, the SVE wells had an expected radius of influence (ROI) of 25 to 30 feet in the shallow unsaturated zone and a ROI of 150 to 180 feet in the deeper unsaturated zone. The extracted soil vapors were treated by a catalytic oxidation unit and scmbber prior to discharge to the atmosphere.

In May 2002, Garvey notified NDEQ that that they would not sign the NDEQ RAPMA Memorandum of Agreement (MOA), which would have required cleanup of not only the source area, but also the groundwater contaminant plume stretching eastward from their grain storage facility. Following this development, in October 2002, NDEQ requested EPA's assistance in performing a removal site evaluation to identify the full extent of the groundwater contaminant plume. NDEQ had several concems, including the fact that additional private drinking water wells might be impacted and that Garvey was unwilling to perform the necessary work. EPA recommended NDEQ consider performing a Preliminary Assessment/Site Investigation (PA/SI) under their cooperative agreement with EPA. Subsequent to NDEQ's request, Garvey was no longer active in the VCP.

In April 2003, NDEQ conducted a PA/SI of the Site and prepared a Hazard Ranking Score (HRS) report to assess whether there was a potential threat to human health and the environment and to identify source(s) of groundwater contamination. Thirty-five private and business water supply wells were sampled. The results varied from nondetect to greater than 500 ug/L of CCl4. The only VOC detected in samples from the 35 water supply wells was CCI4. The PA/SI report concluded that a release of CCl4 at the grain storage fa cility had impacted the city of Hastings' municipal well #13 and several nearby private wells at levels exceeding the MCLs.

In correspondence dated December 9,2003, NDEQ expanded its October 17,2002, request for EPA assistance. NDEQ requested EPA's assistance to provide altemate water supplies to impacted private well users; evaluate the effectiveness and make recommendations for improving the source area control system; characterize the groundwater plume downgradient of the Garvey, grain storage facility; and evaluate potential remedial altematives for the groundwater contaminant plume.

In response to NDEQ's request for EPA's assistance, EPA initiated removal actions. These actions included monitoring water quality and providing altemate water supplies to impacted private well users and operating the existing GET and SVE systems.

On April 27, 2005, EPA proposed the Site for listing on EPA's NPL. The Site was listed on the NPL on September 14, 2005.

On October 7,2005, Garvey entered into an Administrative Order on Consent (AOC) with EPA (CERCLA Docket No. 07-2005-0215). The AOC identified Garvey as a responsible party (RP) and required Garvey to perform the removal actions that were previously being conducted by EPA and to perform a Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (RI/FS). The AOC did not identify any other RPs other than Garvey. The removal and RI/FS activities were funded by Garvey through an escrow account that was established from the proceeds ofthe sale of the former Garvey property to AGP, as documented in the Agreement (CERCLA Docket No. ,07-2005-0268). The Agreement also required AGP to implement institutional controls. While the institutional controls have not yet been put into place, as required by the Agreement, the institutional controls should take the form of an environmental covenant that will include restrictions for the use ofthe property owned by AGP. These restrictions shall restrict the property owner from certain activities  including but not limited to (1) utilization of the groundwater underlying the property for human use or consumption, (2) causing or allowing a disturbance ofthe surface ofthe site, arid (3) using the property for residential purposes.

The removal activities included the identification of, monitoring of, and alternate water provisions for private residential/business wells and an evaluation of the effectiveness of the SVE and GET systems in containing the source area. Garvey was also required to conduct an RI/FS to further assess the nature and extent of groundwater contamination and to evaluate potential remedial actions to address the contamination.

During the period October 2005 to April 2008, Garvey and its confractors performed a portion ofthe activities described in the AOC. Garvey performed monitoring of private residential/business wells within and near the known extent ofthe contaminated groundwater plume and provided altemate water supplies to impacted private well users in the form of bottled water and whole-house carbon filfration systems. Garvey completed work planning to assess the performance ofthe source area SVE and GET systems. To determine the nature and extent of source area contamination in the soils, Garvey performed soil vapor sampling and soil sampling in vertical profiles at more than 17 locations across the grain storage facility. The soil vapor sampling indicated CCl4 contamination of the soil gas throughout the unsaturated zone at the grain storage facility. The lateral extent ofthe contamination varied with depth, with the broadest extent observed at approximately 80 ft bgs. Garvey performed vertically discrete groundwater sampling along a profile consisting of seven direct push sampling locations, immediately east ofthe Site and perpendicular to the direction of groundwater flow, to characterize the extent of the impact to the groundwater migrating from the source area. This investigation was followed by the targeted installation  of four multi-level monitoring wells for long-term monitoring. The characterization revealed the source area of groundwater contamination was more than 1,500 feet wide when measured perpendicular to the direction of groundwater flow.

Under the terms ofthe AOC, Garvey was to operate the SVE and GET systems. However, Garvey did not demonstrate that it could reliably maintain and operate the GET and SVE systems. The systems shut down frequently and repairs were not completed in a timely manner, Garvey initiated planning for the RI/FS, but did not complete characterization of the nature and extent of contamination downgradient of the source area.

On March 27, 2008, Garvey filed a voluntary petition for liquidation pursuant to Chapter 7 of the United States Bankmptcy Code in the United States Bankmptcy Court for the Northem District of Texas, Fort Worth Division. Following this development, in April 2008, EPA directed Garvey and its contractors to halt work at the Site.

EPA initiated fund-lead removal actions on May 19,2008, to address the immediate threat to human health posed by the contaminated private wells and to implement source control measures to prevent further impacts to the groundwater at the source area. These activities, which are ongoing, include providing altemate water systems or municipal water hookup for impacted and potential impacted residential/business private well users. It also includes source control measures of maintaining arid operating the existing SVE and GET systems and enhancing these systems as necessary.

On September 26, 2008, EPA expanded the scope of removal actions to include
fabrication of an enclosure for the existing GET and SVE systems, extension of municipal water supply main lines to impacted private well users, and connections of residences to the main lines. To date, EPA has extended approximately 1.25 miles of municipal water supply main lines and connected more than 15 residences whose private wells were impacted . With the exception of the one residence, all impacted private well users have been connected to the municipal water supply. EPA continues to maintain a whole-house carbon filtration system at the single residence still utilizing private well water.

In December 2008, EPA initiated work planning activities for fund-lead RI/FS.

To establish the basis for taking the Interim Action, in September 2009, EPA developed an Interim Data Summary to summarize the existing information collected during historic and recent PRP-, state-, and EPA-lead field investigations at OU 1. EPA developed a screening level Risk Assessment Memorandum to assess the potential human health risks based on the data contained in the Interim Data Summary.

A ROD addressing OU01 of the Garvey Elevator Superfund Site was completed in June 2010.

The Parkview Well Superfund Site is in Grand Island, Hall County, in east central Nebraska. The city of Grand Island has an estimated population of approximately 44,000 and lies just north of the Platte River within the flood plain. The Parkview Well Superfund Site consists of an aquifer contaminated with industrial chemicals, primarily chlorinated volatile organics. The Site covers the area bordered to the west by Highway 30, to the south by Husker Highway, to the north by Stolley Park Road, and to the east in the area of Pioneer Boulevard. The Southern Plume starts at the 3304 Engleman Road South property (an industrial location) near the northwest corner of the intersection of Engleman Road South and Husker Highway. The plume moves in an east-northeasterly direction through commercial, industrial, and residential areas into the Parkview Subdivision and adjacent areas. The Northern Plume starts at the CNH America, LLC (CNH) facility and does not exceed Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) outside the facility boundary to the east. The Parkview Well Superfund Site was placed on the National Priorities List (NPL) on April 19, 2006.

Operable Unit No. 1 (OU 1) is the area of groundwater contamination that includes the Parkview Subdivision and private and municipal drinking water wells impacted or threatened by the groundwater contamination plume.

Groundwater contamination problems were first recognized during sampling of Parkview Well No. 3 by the Nebraska Health and Human Services System (NHHSS) in 1999. At that time, 1,1-Dichloroethene (1,1-DCE) and 1,1,1-trichloroethane (1,1,1-TCA) contamination were reported at detectable concentrations but below EPA's MCLs. Since 1999, the concentrations and the number of contaminants increased in the well. With increasing concentrations detected in Parkview Well No. 3, and 1,1-DCE exceeding its MCL and tetrachloroethene (PCE) approaching its MCL, in August 2001 the city removed Parkview Well No. 3 from service. Between the fa ll of 2001 and the summer of 2002, the city sampled 77 private wells and four public water supply wells in the Parkview Subdivision area. The samples were analyzed by the NHHSS and results indicated volatile organic compound (VOC) contamination in 37 wells. The most frequently detected contaminants were 1,1-Dichloroethane (1,1-DCA) (32 wells); 1,1-DCE (19 wells); 1,1,1-TCA (17 wells); and PCE (nine wells). Samples collected from three of the private wells on Pioneer Boulevard contained VOCs (1,1-DCE and PCE) exceeding MCLs.

In response to the city's data, the Nebraska Department of Environmental Quality (NDEQ) initiated a Preliminary Assessment/Site Inspection (PA/SI) of contamination in the area identified as the Stolley Park Road Groundwater Contamination Site in the summer of 2003. The PA/SI results generally confirmed the results of previous investigations, but several background samples collected from an area considered upgradient of the Stolley Park area exhibited some of the highest VOCs reported at the time. Samples collected in the Mary Lane Subdivision near North Road South and West Husker Highway and from a farmhouse well east of Mary Lane Subdivision and north of West Husker Highway reported 1,1-DCE and PCE in excess of the MCL. The Mary Lane location reported concentrations of at least 10 times the MCL for 1,1-DCE and PCE. Based on these results the city initiated a sampling program.

Between October 2003 and January 2004, an interim removal action was conducted on the CNH facility at the burn and burial areas and documented in a report entitled Final Report Interim Removal Action, dated March 2004. Following completion of the interim removal action, CNH conducted vertical profile sampling at three locations, installed and sampled three on-site monitoring wells, and conducted a round of sampling of on- and off-site monitoring wells for VOCs. As part of the interim removal action, several on-site wells in proximity to the burn and burial were requir ed to be abandoned. The results are presented in the CNH contractor 2004 Results of Supplemental Groundwater Investigation Activities Report.

In December 2004 and January 2005, EPA initiated a removal action and connected residences with PCE concentrations in their well water exceeding 5 ug/l to city water.

Site investigation activities were conducted by EPA in 2005 in support of the Remedial Investigation (RI) as well as ongoing groundwater sampling of private wells. The conclusions from the RI report indicated that the source of groundwater contamination in the Southern Plume is located at the 3304 Engleman Road South property and appears to be the result of historical releases. Provisions for an alternate water supply will be provided to each residence affected above health-based levels. Indoor air sampling did not indicate site-related contaminants within living spaces above health-based levels. Further characterization of the source area will be conducted by EPA in the near future to determine if a measurable soil source area is present at the site.

OU 1 of the Parkview Well Superfund Site consists of the downgradient plume within and near the Parkview area and private and municipal well users throughout the area of groundwater contamination. The area affected by the VOC contamination is a mixture of residential, agricultural, and industrial/commercial properties. Future land use of the site is anticipated to be similar to current uses. There are no land use activities in OU 1 which are being restricted due to the contamination in the groundwater. However, land-use restrictions may be changed in the future if groundwater-use restrictions are enacted.

Surface water resources near the groundwater VOC plume are gravel pit lakes. The Wood River is located approximately 1,500 feet to the southeast of the site.

The groundwater in the vicinity of OU 1 has been designated as a Class GA Groundwater Supply by the state of Nebraska. A Class GA Groundwater i s a groundwater supply which is currently being used as a public drinking water supply or is proposed to be used as a public drinking water supply. Contamination detected at OU 1 caused the state to designate the site as a Remedial Action Class 1 (RAC-1), requiring the "most extensive remedial action measures" to cleanup the groundwater to drinking water quality suitable for all beneficial uses. The selected remedial action is necessary in order to ensure that the contaminated groundwater is cleaned up and the aquifer returned to full beneficial use within an acceptable time frame. Nebraska Title 118 states that the time frame for required action (including cleanup) will be the period of potential exposure to the contamination in the absence of any remedial action or 20 years, whichever is less.

A Record of Decision (ROD) addressing OU1 was completed in September of 2006.

OU2:


Site investigation activities were conducted by EPA in 2005 in support of the remedial investigation (RI) for OU 1 as well as ongoing groundwater sampling of private wells. The conclusions from the RI report for OU 1 indicated that the source of groundwater contamination in the Southern Plume is located at the 3304 Engleman Road South property and appears to be the result of historical releases. Indoor air sampling did not indicate site-related contaminants within living spaces above health-based levels. Further characterization of the source area for OU 2 was conducted by EPA in 2006 and 2007 to determine if a measurable soil source area is present at the site. The data presented in the OU 2 RI report shows two areas of VOC-contaminant release at the 3304 Engleman Road South building-one area near the western side of the building and one area beneath the building. A removal action was conducted by EPA to address the highest concentrations along the western side of the building through excavation. The remaining source area and groundwater plume will be addressed as part of the selec ted remedy for OU 2. In addition to the VOCs detected in groundwater, 1,4-Dioxane was detected in the Southern Plume with a maximum measured concentration of 160 ug/l in the source area groundwater; 1,4-Dioxane will be addressed as part of the selected remedy.

EPA has undertaken several activities to identify the entity or entities that are responsible for the contamination at the site. The potentially responsible parties (PRPs) under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 (CERCLA) include:
- Current owners and operators of a facility,
- Past owners and operators of a facility at the time hazardous wastes were disposed,
- Generators and parties that arranged for the disposal or transport of the hazardous substances, and
- Transporters of hazardous waste that selected the site where the hazardous substances were brought.

PRPs are liable for: the costs the government has incurred for cleanup, damages to natural resources (for example, a fishery), the costs of certain health assessments, and injunctive relief (i.e., performing a cleanup) where a site may present an imminent and substantial endangerment.

EPA has issued numerous information requests to parties that are currently or have historically operated a business that may have used industrial solvents in and around the area of the site. In addition, EPA has performed title search activities and interviewed members of the community in order to obtain information that may help identify the source of the contamination. Further, in 2005, EPA entered into an Administrative Order on Consent with CNH that required the company perform an RI for the "Northern Study Area" of the site. EPA is continuing its PRP search efforts to identify the source of contamination in the Southern Plume.

OU 2 consists of a source area at 3304 Engleman Road South and groundwater contaminant plume migrating from the source area. OU 1 consists of the downgradient portion plume within and  near the Parkview area and private and municipal well users throughout the area of groundwater contamination. The area affected by the VOC contamination is a mixture of residential, agricultural, and industrial/commercial properties. Future land use of the site is anticipated to be similar to current uses. The 3304 Engleman Road South property is zoned as light manufacturing. There are no known land use activities in the site area which are being restricted due to the contamination in the groundwater. However, land use restrictions may be changed in the future. OU 1 includes groundwater use restrictions and OU 2 includes proprietary controls for the 3304 Engleman Road South property.

Surface water near the groundwater contaminant plume are small ornamental ponds at the golf course near the western portion of the groundwater plume and gravel pit lakes near the eastern portion of the groundwater plume. The Wood River is located approximately 2.44 miles to the south of the 3304 Engleman Road South property, approximately 1.1 miles south of the intersection of Husker Highway and Highway 281 intersection, and approximately 0.48 miles south of the distal end of the groundwater contamination plume near the east end of the Parkview neighborhood.

The groundwater in the site area has been designated as a Class GA Groundwater Supply by the state of Nebraska. A Class GA Groundwater is a groundwater supply which is currently being used as a public drinking water supply or is proposed to be used as a public drinking water supply. Contamination detected caused the state to designate the site as a Remedial Action Class 1 (RAC-1), requiring the "most extensive remedial action measures" to cleanup the groundwater to drinking water quality suitable for all beneficial uses. The selected remedial action for OU 2 is necessary in order to ensure that the contaminated groundwater is cleaned up and the aquifer returned to full beneficial use within an acceptable time frame. Nebraska  Title 118 states that the time frame for required action (including cleanup) will be the period of potential exposure to the contamination in the absence of any remedial action or 20 years, whichever is less.

A Record of Decision addressing OU 2 was completed in September 2007.

The ROD for OU 2 is intended to be the final remedy for the Site, and was signed by the EPA on September 30, 2007. This ROD addresses the remaining source materials and groundwater contaminants within and downgradient of the source area at 3304 Engleman Road South, Grand Island, Nebraska, and west of the OU 1 treatment system. The selected remedy is in-situ chemical oxidation (ISCO) coupled with Institutional Controls (ICs).

Principal threat wastes were identified in the Northern Plume source area and, as previously mentioned, are being addressed by CNH America (CNH) through the Nebraska RAPMA program with oversight by NDEQ. Principal threat wastes were identified for the Southern Plume at the 3304 Engleman Road South property. The most highly contaminated soils in the source area, which comprise a portion of the principal threat wastes, have been addressed by an EPA-lead removal action. The remaining principal contaminants exist below the water table at the 3304 Engleman Road South property will be addressed by the OU 2 selected remedy or ISCO injections.

The removal action implemented at the Site included the excavation of soil above the water table exceeding risk-based action levels with implementation of VI and groundwater monitoring. Excavation of contaminated soils was completed in 2006. Groundwater and VI monitoring continued after the soil removal was completed and is ongoing in accordance with the ROD.
