The former U.S. Radium Corporation facility, which covers 2 acres in the City of Orange, Essex County, New Jersey, is a former radium-processing plant where extraction, production, application, and distribution took place from about 1915 through 1926. Approximately 1/2 to 2 tons of ore per day was processed and disposed of on and off the property. As a result of those operations, the facility buildings and soil became contaminated with radionuclides. In addition, radium-contaminated soil and debris were identified at approximately 250 noncontiguous properties in the vicinity of the former plant and at various other locations throughout the municipalities of Orange, West Orange, and South Orange.

The U.S. Radium Corporation, formerly known as the Radium Luminous Materials Corporation, operated a facility at the High and Alden Streets Properties study area from 1915 through 1926. The U.S. Radium Corporation also operated facilities at various Satellite Properties in the early 1900s. A primary activity at the High and Alden Streets Properties was the extraction and purification of radium from carnotite ore. Because each ton of ore produced only a few milligrams of radium, large volumes of ore were required. As a result, large quantities of process wastes, or "tailings", were generated which contained radioactive elements at elevated levels. The tailings were temporarily discarded on unused areas of the facility and ultimately disposed of off-site.

In addition to the production and sale of radium itself, the U.S. Radium Corporation also manufactured a radium-based luminous paint. At one time, the company employed over 100 workers to paint instruments and watch dials with this luminous paint. Reports indicate that dial painting took place at the High and Alden Streets Properties and at several Satellite Properties. U.S. Radium Corporation discontinued radium processing operations in 1926, while continuing its dial painting business. In the 1940s, the U.S. Radium Co rporation sold its properties at High and Alden Streets, and no subsequent occupants of the properties are known to have processed or used radium.

In 1979, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) initiated a program to identify and investigate locations within New Jersey where radium processing activities had taken place.

The former U.S. Radium Corporation facility was included in this program. In May 1981, EPA conducted an aerial gamma radiation survey covering approximately 12 square miles centered on the High and Alden Streets Properties. This aerial survey located about 25 acres around the High and Alden Streets Properties where; elevated readings of gamma radiation were detected. This same survey identified areas of elevated gamma radiation in the nearby communities of Montclair, West Orange and Glen Ridge; the affected properties in these areas comprise two other Superfund sites, the Montclair/West Orange Radium site and the Glen Ridge Radium site.

In 1982, the Site was proposed for inclusion on the National Priorities List (NPL) of Superfund sites, and the Site was placed on the NPL in September 1983. Ground level surveys conducted in the early 1980s showed elevated gamma radiation and radon gas in most of the buildings on the High and Alden Streets Properties. In 1984, NJDEP performed preliminary field investigations of 31 properties near the facility. While these studies found elevated levels of gamma radiation at some properties, NJDEP found only small pockets of radium-contaminated soil, and detected no elevated radon gas levels. 

Working from U.S. Radium Corporation documents and other historical records, EPA and NJDEP initially identified 22 Satellite Properties where the U.S. Radium Corporation had conducted operations. Initial investigations of some of the Satellite Properties in 1983 and 1986 indicated elevated levels of gamma radiation, with a few instances of eleva ted radon gas in basements.

EPA initiated a full remedial investigation and feasibility study (RI/FS) in October 1989 to determine the nature and extent of contamination at the Site. By October 1992, over 160 investigations had been performed, and 63 radium-contaminated properties had been identified. As part of a removal action begun in 1991, EPA installed radon mitigation systems and gamma radiation shielding at four properties where elevated radiation levels were detected early in the RI.

In October 1992, with the investigation of the former plant site and the Satellite Properties still ongoing, EPA elected to organize the other properties into a first operable unit (OU1), and to propose a remedy for these properties. With about 160 investigations completed, it was clear that performing studies on additional properties would not assist EPA in better understanding the problem, and would unnecessarily delay the process of proposing a remedy and cleaning up the radium contaminated properties. An RI/FS report was prepared in 1993 which documented the nature and extent of contamination at the already investigated properties, and provided a detailed evaluation of remedial alternatives.

A Proposed Plan for the first operable unit (OU1) was released to the public on April 28, 1993. OU1 consisted of mostly residential properties. On September 21, 1993, a Record of Decision (ROD) was signed for the OU1 properties, selecting a remedy of excavation of radium-contaminated material from affected properties, restoration of the excavated areas, and offsite disposal of the radium-contaminated material.

A Proposed Plan for the second operable unit (OU2) of the Site was released to the public on May 23, 1995, along with an OU2 RI/FS Report. OU2 consisted of the remainder of the Site; namely, the former U.S. Radium facility at High and Alden Streets, plus four other commercial properties used by the former U.S. Radium Corporation. On August 29, 1995, a ROD was signed for  the OU2 properties, selecting essentially the same remedy as that for the OU1 properties: excavation of radium-contaminated material, restoration of the excavated areas, and off-site disposal of the radium-contaminated material.

Field work for the first group of OU1 properties was initiated in 1997. Investigations of additional area properties continued during the cleanup and, when additional radium-contaminated properties were located, designs for their cleanup were prepared.

The OU1 and OU2 remedial actions are now essentially complete. Overall, approximately 650 properties were investigated during the remedial design. Of these properties, approximately 250 were identified as requiring remediation under the selected actions. 

The OU1 and OU2 cleanup was performed in phases. Phase 1 and Phase 2 of the remedial action were completed in December 1998 and resulted in the removal of approximately 25,000 cubic yards (approximately 38,400 tons) of radium-contaminated material. 

Phase 3 was completed in October 1999 and resulted in the removal of approximately 9,000 cubic yards (approximately 14,400 tons) of radium-contaminated material. Phase 4 was completed in September 2001, included the former U.S. Radium Corporation facility located at High and Alden Streets, and resulted in the removal of approximately 34,000 cubic yards (approximately 54,400 tons) of radium-contaminated material. Phase 5 was completed in December 2002 and resulted in the removal of approximately 10,000 cubic yards (approximately 16,000 tons) of radium-contaminated material. Phase 6 was completed in September 2003 and addressed approximately 5,000 cubic yards (approximately 8,000 tons) of radium-contaminated material. Phase 7 was completed in September 2005 and addressed approximately 1,996 cubic yards (approximately 3,200 tons) of radium-contaminated material. Due to access issues, one remaining property will be addressed some time in the future.

Ground water sampling was conducted  during the initial RI/FS at the Site, but the results were not conclusive. Therefore, a full comprehensive ground water investigation was initiated in 2003, after most of the contaminated source material was removed from the Site.

The U.S. Radium Site is located in a densely populated urban neighborhood consisting of residential, commercial, and light industrial properties. The former U.S. Radium facility located at High and Alden Streets in Orange is currently vacant and fenced. The City of Orange owns the majority of the former facility area, including the area where Well P-2 is located, and at this time plans to redevelop the area for recreational use. 

Water is provided to all residents of Orange and the surrounding communities by local water supply companies which are regulated by the State of New Jersey. The overburden aquifer currently is not used for domestic or industrial water supply. While it is not expected that it will be used in the future as a source of potable water, it is classified by NJDEP as Class IIA, which means that it can be used with appropriate treatment.

A ROD addressing OU3 was completed in September 2006.

The Mannheim Avenue Dump Site (the Site) is located in a two-acre sand and gravel clearing occupying lots two and three of Block 54 in Galloway Township, Atlantic County, New Jersey. The Site lies on Mannheim Avenue between Shiller Road and Clarks Landing Road. The site is approximately 1,500 feet southeast of the Tar Kiln Branch and two miles southwest of the Mullica River and associated tidal marsh. The area immediately surrounding the Site is relatively flat woodlands of scrub pine and low bush. The area is within the New Jersey Pinelands Protection Area. A sand and gravel pit is located across the street from the Site and is owned and operated by Galloway Township. At least 82 residences lie within a one-mile radius of the Site. The Bethel Christian Day School is located within 5000 feet south of the Site. Many of these residences and facilities rely on groundwater wells for potable water supply.

The Cohansey Sand and the Kirkwood Formation form an important water-bearing unit used as a major source of potable water in the area. At the Site, this unit is an unconsolidated deposit of sands and gravels interbedded with clay. A semi permeable clay layer, approximately 3 to 5 feet thick underlies the Site at approximately 50 feet below ground surface. This layer separates the shallow zone of the aquifer system from the deeper zone. Throughout the region, this deeper zone extends to a depth of approximately 200 to 250 feet below ground surface to a low permeability clay layer, which marks the lower boundary of this aquifer system. The depth to water at the Site is approximately 35 feet. In the shallow zone, groundwater flows in a northwesterly direction towards Tar Kiln Branch. In the deep zone, groundwater flows in a northeasterly direction towards the Mullica River.

The Mannheim Avenue Dump Site was originally used as a sand and gravel excavation operation by Galloway Township for road construction material. After mining operations ceased in 1964, the excavat ed portions of the Site were used for waste disposal.

Beginning in 1964, Lenox China obtained permission from Galloway Township to use the Site to dispose of industrial wastes produced at its manufacturing facility in Pomona, New Jersey.  The drummed wastes were deposited on the floor of the excavated portion of the Site, approximately 5 feet below ground surface, and subsequently compacted into 35 waste mounds, along with other municipal wastes, and covered with soil.  Leaded porcelain fragments and household refuse was also mixed in the waste mounds.

A 1981 industrial survey report submitted by Lenox China notified the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) that hazardous wastes may have been disposed of at the Mannheim Avenue Site. The survey indicated that 55-gallon drums of trichloroethene (TCE) degreasing sludge were disposed of at the Site and in other locations. A subsequent investigation by NJDEP in 1982 revealed that many of the 55 gallon drums were exposed and deteriorating. Samples collected from the exposed drums indicated the presence of the following chemicals: TCE at 1,640 parts per million (ppm), toluene at 230 ppm, ethylbenzene at 350 ppm, methylene chloride at 220 ppm, cadmium at 22 ppm, lead at 2,600 ppm, nickel at 27 ppm, and chromium at 6 ppm.

The Site was placed on the National Priorities List in 1983. In December 1984, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) issued an Administrative Order to Lenox and the Township of Galloway to remove the waste material buried in the soil mounds at the Site, conduct soil and groundwater sampling, and excavate and remove contaminated soil from the Site. By August 1985, Lenox had completed the excavation of the waste material from the soil mounds. Approximately 25,000 pounds of degreasing sludge were separated from general trash and incinerated off site. Thirty-five mounds of soil remained, many with residual contamination.

In 1985 and 1986, Lenox conducted soil, groundwat er, limited surface water, and domestic well sampling. This sampling showed that the principal contaminants associated with the waste at the site were lead and TCE. Soil sampling revealed that lead was the predominant contaminant remaining within the soil mounds (at levels up to 48,000 ppm). Several of the mounds also contained small fragments of the asphaltic sludge waste which could not be separated from the soil during the initial excavation. These mounds were assumed to contain TCE as well as lead contaminants. Groundwater sampling on site revealed the presence of TCE (at levels up to 140 parts per billion (ppb)). Groundwater sampling from residential and school wells, and from the nearby stream, did not reveal the presence of any site-related contaminants. In June 1989, the 35 mounds of soil containing residual lead and TCE contamination were excavated and disposed off site by Lenox. 

In July 1988 and March 1989, EPA sampled the drinking water from 25 local residential wells surrounding the site and one well from the Bethel Christian School for volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and metals. No VOCs or metals were detected above EPA's drinking water standards.

In May 1988, EPA entered into an Administrative Order on Consent with Lenox, Inc. and the Township of Galloway to conduct a Remedial Investigation (RI) and Feasibility Study (FS) at the Site. 

In February 1990, Lenox, Inc.'s contractor submitted a FS report for EPA review and approval. EPA determined that this report as incomplete and inappropriate for public release, and for preparing a Record of Decision. Consequently, EPA tasked its contractor to prepare a FS Report to develop and evaluate alternatives for groundwater remediation more thoroughly. 

A Record of Decision for Operable Unit 1 of the Mannheim Avenue Dump Superfund Site was completed in September 1990.

The Myers Property Superfund Site is located on Lower Kingtown Road in Franklin Township, Hunterdon County, New Jersey, about three miles south of Clinton, New Jersey. It lies adjacent to Cakepoulin (or Capoolong) Creek to the north. The Cakepoulin Creek Trail, part of the Cakepoulin Creek Wildlife Management Area, runs through the Site along a former railroad bed. The Site includes: approximately five acres presently owned by Arkema Inc. (Arkema), a potentially responsible party for the Site, and approximately two acres of an undeveloped area south of Lower Kingtown Road owned by the State of New Jersey and designated as a wetland. The Site is presently vacant except for a water treatment facility.

Nearby properties are used for residential and/or agricultural purposes.  Cakepoulin Creek is an FW-2 trout production stream stocked by the New Jersey Department of Fish and Game. The Creek and the adjacent New Jersey-owned wetlands are all part of the Cakepoulin Creek Wildlife Management Area.

The State of New Jersey has classified the creek as Category I (a stream with high water quality in a sensitive environmental area, afforded special protection under the state's environmental laws). The majority of the Site property lies within the 100-year floodplain of Cakepoulin Creek, and a portion of the Site lies within a closed canopy hardwood wetland. The State of New Jersey has classified-the aquifer as Class II-A, a current source of drinking water, in accordance with New Jersey Administrative Code 97.9-6.5. The U. S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has also classified the aquifer as a Sole Source Aquifer in a June 1988 decision in accordance with the Safe Drinking Water Act, Public Law 93-523 ? 1423 (e), because it is the only viable source of drinking water for the local community.

Portions of the Site were used for pesticide manufacturing during the 1940s.  Four companies are known to have been involved in pesticide and/or chemical handling or manufact uring while owning and/or operating on the property: W. A. Allen Company, Elko Chemical Works, the Pennsylvania Salt Manufacturing Company and Clinton Chemical Company. The first two companies no longer exist. The Pennsylvania Salt Manufacturing Company became Pennwalt Corporation, and is now Arkema.  Clinton Chemical Company is now Witco Corporation.

The W. A. Allen Company owned the Site from 1928 to 1932, and may have operated on the property, formulating fertilizer-pesticide mixtures for residential use.  Elko Chemical Works operated a pesticide production plant at the Site from 1942 to 1945, manufacturing the insecticide p,p'dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane, commonly called DDT. The Pennsylvania Salt Manufacturing Company bought the property in 1945 and operated the plant, producing DDT, for two years.  In 1947, Pennsylvania Salt Manufacturing Company sold the property to Associated Terminal, Inc., a New Jersey Corporation.

Associated Terminal leased the Site from 1953 to 1959 to the Clinton Chemical Company, which produced anhydrous aluminum chloride. Little additional information is available regarding other on-site activities of Associated Terminal. Mr. and Mrs. Cornelius Myers purchased the property in 1971 and used it as a residence. They sold it to Arkema (then called Elf Atochem North America, Inc.) in 1993.

The Myers Site is currently vacant except for the water treatment building. The privately owned portion is fenced. While it is zoned for residential use, a deed restriction, specifying that the impacted areas of soil can not be disturbed without prior written approval, will be implemented on the land. The restriction is necessary because contaminated material below the water-table was not addressed by the soil remedy. No change in use is anticipated in the near future. The state-owned portion of the Site consists mainly of wetlands. A recreational trail that runs through the Site has been remediated and is open for public use. The ground wate r below the Site is part of an aquifer designated by the State of New Jersey for use as a potable water supply, but is not currently utilized as such. 

The Site was proposed for inclusion on the National Priorities List (NPL) in December 1982, which qualified it for funding and response under CERCLA. The Site was finalized on the NPL on September 1, 1983. In 1984, the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) requested that EPA take the lead for remedial activities at the Site. 

EPA performed a removal action in August 1984 to address the presence of badly deteriorated drums containing DDT and other materials. Deteriorated drums, solid DDT, and other organic chemicals, lead compounds, sheets of asbestos, and building debris were repacked into a total of 216 fifty-five gallon drums and removed to a hazardous waste landfill. In October 1987, a second removal action was performed to install a security fence around the perimeter of the most highly contaminated parts of the Site. 

EPA performed a Remedial Investigation and Feasibility Study (RI/FS) of the Site, which was completed in 1990. After the issuance of a Proposed Plan and review of public comments, EPA documented its remedy selection for the Site in a September 28, 1990 Record of Decision (ROD). EPA organized the work into two distinct phases, or operable units (OUs):

- Operable Unit 1: Contamination of the Site soils, sediment, buildings, and ground water
- Operable Unit 2: Final remedy to address contamination of the ground water aquifer

The soil/sediment portion of the remedy was amended in a ROD dated July 6, 2000. The ROD amendment changed the remedy from on-Site treatment and backfilling of soil/sediment to offsite disposal, with treatment as necessary to meet disposal requirements. All other aspects of the 1990 ROD remained unchanged.  To date, the soil, sediment, and building portions of the remedy have been completed and the interim ground water remedy has been implemente d. The buildings were dismantled in 1997 and disposed of at a licensed off-site landfill. A ground water extraction and treatment system, which addresses both shallow and bedrock ground water contamination, has been in operation since October 1999. A series of monitoring wells, as well as a number of area residential wells, continue to be tested regularly; no site-related contamination has been found in any of the residential wells. Finally, the soil and sediment portion of the remedy was initiated in the spring of 2003. All physical work associated with the soil/sediment cleanup was completed by July 2004, and a remedial action report was approved in June 2005. 

A Record of Decision (ROD) addressing OU2 of the Myers Property Superfund Site was completed in September 2005.

The Rockaway Township Wells site is a 2-square-mile well field area containing a cluster of three municipal wells within 100 feet of each other.  In 1979 and 1980, the wells were found to contain a variety of volatile organic compounds (VOCs).  Two gasoline service stations, freight and transit facilities, and industrial properties are located near the well field.  Groundwater contamination in the area appears to have resulted from several sources, including the gasoline stations and industrial facilities.  
Monitoring wells in the area indicated widespread contamination by chlorinated solvents and fuel components.  In 1980, a treatment system for the wells was installed and included an air stripping system and an activated carbon system.  Only one of the three wells is currently in operation.  The operative well serves approximately 12,500 people.  The valley fill aquifer is the only water supply source capable of meeting the Township's water demand.The 185-acre Rockaway Township Wellfield Site is located in Rockaway Township, Morris County, New Jersey and has been developed by commercial business and light industry including service stations, restaurants, a hotel, plastic manufacturers, truck/transit companies, and commercial office complexes.  The Rockaway Township Wellfield serves as the source of potable water for approximately 12,000 residents in Rockaway Township.  Rockaway Township overlies a designated sole source aquifer.  Water samples in 1979 and 1980 first indicated the presence of (TCE) and other VOCs.  The Township installed an activated carbon adsorption treatment system.  The water then developed an unpleasant taste and odor.  On October 10, 1980 the Township declared a water emergency.  An air stripper was subsequently installed at the site for additional treatment.  Currently the only treatment system in operation is the air stripper.

The Rockaway T ownship Wells Site (also known as the Rockaway Township Wellfield Contamination Site) is located in both Rockaway and Denville Townships in Morris County, New Jersey. Rockaway and Denville Townships are situated in the center of Morris County, approximately 10 miles north of Morristown and 20 miles northwest of Newark in the north-central portion of the state.

The Site, located immediately north of Interstate 80, is an area of approximately 185 acres, which lies in the center of a Y-shaped valley in an otherwise hilly area of the New Jersey Highlands. The area has been developed by commercial businesses and light industries including service stations, restaurants, hotels, plastic manufacturers, truck/transit companies, and commercial office complexes. The Denville Technical Park is located within the Site.

Near the center of the Site are the Rockaway Township Wells, which serve as the source of potable water for approximately 14,000 residents in Rockaway Township. The Wellfield originally consisted of municipal wells PW4, PW6 and PW7, which are located on the northeast side of Green Pond Road, south of White Meadow Brook, and west of the New Jersey Transit railroad tracks. In 1983 PW4 was sealed. At present, PW6 and PW7 are intermittently pumped at an average rate of approximately 1.3 million gallons per day (mgd), and a maximum of approximately 1.8 mgd. 

The municipal wells are situated in glacial sediments, which have been deposited in a large bedrock valley. The "valley fill" has a thickness of up to 200 feet near the center of the Beaver Brook valley and primarily consists of sands and gravels, with abundant cobbles and boulders. Within the sands and gravels, prominent clay lenses and boulder zones occur. The municipal wells are screened in sand and gravel deposits at a depth of 130 feet to 160 feet below the ground surface (bgs).

Prior to the construction of the municipal wells in the mid to late 1960's, the predominant direction of ground water flo w in the aquifer was thought to be south-southwest. However, water levels measured in monitoring wells throughout the area indicate that the influences from the Wellfield dominate local ground water flow. Within the local area, ground water flows toward the Wellfield and is thought to be recharged by natural precipitation falling on the area, ground water drainage along the valley walls, ground water flowing from areas upgradient of the Site, and infiltration from surface streams. This area of Rockaway and Denville Townships overlie the Rockaway River Basin Area Sole Source Aquifer. The USEPA designates areas as sole source aquifers under the Safe Drinking Water Act to protect principal drinking water sources.

Water samples collected from the Rockaway Township Wells in late 1979 and early 1980 indicated the presence of trichloroethene (TCE) and other volatile organic compounds (VOCs). The Township installed an activated carbon adsorption treatment system in response to this contamination. In October 1980, the treated water developed an unpleasant taste and odor. Analysis showed it to be contaminated with di-isopropyl ether (DIPE) and methyl tertiary butyl ether (MTBE), both gasoline additives. On October 10, 1980, the Township declared a water emergency and advised residents to avoid consumption of the water until an air stripping unit was installed for additional treatment of the water prior to distribution. An air stripping unit was subsequently installed. Currently, Rockaway Township uses only the air stripping unit for water treatment. The water treated with the air stripping unit meets the New Jersey and Federal Safe Drinking Water Act requirements without the need for supplementary treatment. However, to ensure a safe drinking water supply, Rockaway Township uses the carbon adsorption treatment system whenever the air stripping unit is taken out of operation for maintenance or repair.

In 1982, the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP)  requested that USEPA consider this Site for inclusion on the National Priorities List (NPL) of Superfund sites because a public water supply was impacted and the source of the contamination to the Wellfield was unknown. USEPA placed the Site on the NPL on September 1, 1983.

Following the discovery of contamination in the Wellfield, NJDEP conducted an area wide industrial survey to identify potential sources of these hazardous substances. The survey, along with additional information, revealed that petroleum hydrocarbon products were present in the ground water at the Shell Gas Station and the Town and Country Gas Station, which are both located on Green Pond Road to the west of the Wellfield. Chlorinated VOCs were present in ground water at the Denville Technical Park.

In June 1986, pursuant to the New Jersey Spill Compensation and Control Act (Spill Act). NJDEP issued Directives to Morton Thiokol Incorporated (then owner of the Denville Technical Park property), Shell Oil Company and the Town and Country Gas Station requiring payment to NJDEP to conduct a remedial investigation/feasibility study (RI/FS), and payment to Rockaway Township for the operation and maintenance of the air stripping unit. In May 1987, pursuant to the Spill Act, NJDEP entered into an Administrative Consent Order (ACO) with Morton Thiokol Incorporated and Shell Oil Company in which the two companies agreed to make the above payments. The RI Report was finalized in November 1988. The Town and Country Gas Station never complied with the Directive.

Based on the information from the 1988 RI Report, NJDEP determined that additional studies were necessary and began a Phase II RI. In April 1989, NJDEP issued Directive II to the Town and Country Gas Station requiring payment to NJDEP to conduct the Phase II RI/FS. The Town and Country Gas Station never complied with Directive II. In September 1989, NJDEP issued Directive III to Thiokol Corporation, Motion International Incorporated and Shel l Oil Company requiring payment to NJDEP to conduct the Phase II RI/FS, and payment to Rockaway Township for the continued operation and maintenance of the air stripping unit. The Phase II RI Report was finalized in September 1992. The FS Report was finalized in December 1992.

From April 1988 through April 1995, Thiokol Corporation and Shell Oil Company split the operation and maintenance costs of the air stripping unit. In 1995, NJDEP notified Shell Oil Company that it had satisfied its obligation since gasoline-related contaminants were no longer being detected in the Rockaway Township Wells. Thiokol Corporation and its successors continue to pay the operation and maintenance costs of the air stripping unit. Based on the RI and FS Reports, the USEPA signed, and NJDEP concurred with, a Record of Decision (ROD) on October 5, 1993. The 1993 ROD documents the selection of the ground water remedy for the Rockaway Township Wells Site. 

In addition, the 1993 ROD stated that a subsequent decision document was planned to evaluate the need for remediation of soils and contaminant sources. 

Town and Country Gas Station operated on Green Pond Road in Rockaway Township. In June 1984, the property was leased to Exxon Company, U.S.A. (Exxon).

In January 1984, Exxon installed four monitoring wells on the property as a condition imposed by Rockaway Township on Exxon's application for facility plan approval. The results of the monitoring showed the presence in the ground water of hazardous substances including benzene, toluene, ethyl benzene, xylene and petroleum hydrocarbons. Water level measurements showed that the ground water flow was towards the Rockaway Township Wells, as influenced by the pumping of the Wellfield.

In April 1984, Exxon removed three underground storage tanks (USTs) on the property. Exxon also collected soil samples that indicated the presence of petroleum hydrocarbons. On July 17, 1984, NJDEP issued a letter to Town and Country Gas Station requ iring a complete hydrogeologic study and remedial measures for soil and ground water. Town and Country Gas Station never complied with the NJDEP requirements. 

In June 1985, Exxon removed 2,500 cubic yards of contaminated soil from the property in accordance with New Jersey regulations in effect at that time. Exxon then installed five new 10,000 gallon fiberglass reinforced plastic USTs for the storage of gasoline, medium diesel fuel and waste oil. Exxon also installed a storm water collection system. The storm water flows across the facility into a catch basin connected to an oil-water separator. Oil from the oil-water separator is pumped into the waste oil UST and disposed of at a licensed facility, while the water is discharged to the municipal storm sewer in accordance with a NJDEP discharge to surface water permit (No. 0061816). The USTs were upgraded in 1992 to meet regulatory requirements. According to NJDEP records, there have been no documented releases from the five USTs, and the storm water collection system is currently in compliance with the permit. The soil and ground water contamination present at the Town and Country Gas Station have been addressed under New Jersey rules and regulations, including the regulations implementing the Underground Storage of Hazardous Substances Act.

Shell Oil Company (Shell) operates a gas station on Green Pond Road in Rockaway Township.

In 1979, approximately 1,000 gallons of unleaded gasoline were discharged to the subsurface as a result of an UST failure. The leaking UST was replaced in 1980. In 1980-1981, Shell installed 11 monitoring wells on and around the property. The results of the monitoring indicated the presence of hazardous substances including benzene, toluene, TCE, DIPE and MTBE. Water level measurements showed that ground water flow was towards the Wellfield, as influenced by the pumping of the Wellfield. Shell contributed money towards the installation and operation and maintenance of the air str ipping unit installed on the Rockaway Township Wells.

In 1991, Shell installed and activated a soil vapor extraction (SVE) system to address the contamination present in the soil at its gas station in accordance with NJDEP rules and regulations.

On March 2, 1995, NJDEP informed Shell that, pursuant to Paragraph 38 of Directive III, it was no longer required to pay Rockaway Township for the operation and maintenance of the air stripping unit since the on-site contamination appeared to be under control and gasoline-related contaminants are no longer being detected in the municipal wells. 
Shortly after, however, monitoring well data from the Shell facility began to again show increasing concentrations of MTBE. In December 1996, it was discovered that the remote fill and vent lines at the gas station had separated from the tanks at the joints, resulting in another release of gasoline. The remote fill and vent lines were repaired at that time. NJDEP's Underground Storage Tank Program required Shell to reactivate the SVE system in December 1996, which Shell had deactivated in 1994 without NJDEP's approval. The SVE system operates in accordance with an NJDEP Air Pollution Discharge Permit. Shell also installed and activated a ground water pump and treat system on-site and a second ground water pump and treat system off-site. The off-site system was activated in September 1997 at 130 gallons per minute (gpm) and the on-site system was activated in December 1997 at 30 gallons per minute. Both ground water systems operate in accordance with a NJDEP Discharge to Surface Water Permit. The treated ground water from both systems is combined prior to discharge to the drainage ditch, which flows to White Meadow Brook, which in turn flows into Beaver Brook.

The on-site ground water extraction system has a similar treatment train to the off-site system, including an air stripping unit, total dissolved solids filters and granular activated carbon treatment units. In March 2 000, NJDEP approved Shell's request to deactivate the on-site system because the concentrations of contaminants in the ground water were below the New Jersey Ground Water Quality Criteria.

Rockaway Township conducts biweekly monitoring of municipal wells PW-6 and PW-7 for MTBE. Although monitored, MTBE has rarely been detected in the wells. When MTBE has been detected, it has been significantly below the New Jersey Safe Drinking Water Act Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) of 70 parts per billion (ppb). Benzene and toluene have not been detected in the wells.

The soil and ground water contamination present at the Shell Oil Company Gas Station are being addressed under New Jersey rules and regulations, including the regulations implementing the Underground Storage of Hazardous Substances Act.

In 1953, the United States government purchased 52.7 acres of property in Denville Township and established the Naval Industrial Reserve Plant. A number of buildings, including Buildings 1, 2 and 3, were constructed and utilized for the research, development and manufacture of rocket engines and associated components. In that same year, the United States government leased the facility to Reaction Motors Company who continued the same operations. In 1958, the Thiokol Chemical Corporation (Thiokol) purchased the Reaction Motors Company and continued the operations at the facility pursuant to government contracts. In 1964, the United States government sold the property, including Block 62101, Lots 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 and all buildings, to Thiokol. In 1968, Thiokol began to close down its operation at the facility and started leasing portions of the buildings to various businesses.

In 1973, Thiokol sold Lots 2 and 4, including Building 7, to the International Paper Realty Company. W.P. Realty acquired Lots 2 and 4 and Building 7, from International Paper in 1977. W.P. Realty purchased from Thiokol the buildings on Lots 1, 3 and 5 in 1978 and the property in 1996, operating as  the Denville Technical Park.

Thiokol described some of the tenants, which operated or currently operate at the Denville Technical Park, in the Preliminary Assessment dated September 1996. Many of the tenants were and are subject to the requirements of the New Jersey Industrial Site Recovery Act.

In December 1989, Thiokol removed seven USTs from the Denville Technical Park. The USTs contained gasoline, No. 2 and No. 6 fuel oils, waste oil and ammonia. Several of the USTs had leaked so contaminated soil was removed along with the USTs. In 1990, as required by NJDEP, Thiokol performed a subsurface investigation associated with the leaking USTs, in accordance with the New Jersey regulations in effect at that time. As part of this investigation, five shallow monitoring wells (MW-1 through MW-5) were installed near the former UST locations. Ground water sampling results showed elevated levels of VOCs at each of the well locations.

In June 1995, Thiokol removed a 1,000-gallon waste oil UST (Waste Oil) located between Buildings 1 and 2. No soil delineation or remediation was conducted during the UST excavation since it was located in an area of known soil contamination, which was to be addressed as part of the Superfund action. With NJDEP approval, the excavated soil was returned to the excavation that had been lined with polyethylene sheeting prior to backfilling. Base and sidewall soil samples indicated elevated levels of petroleum hydrocarbons ranging from 490 parts per million (ppm) to 16,400 ppm. A variety of VOCs were also detected in the soil samples at levels ranging from less than 0.3 ppm to 2,000 ppm.

With the signing of the October 5, 1993 ROD, NJDEP determined that the replacement of the deteriorating air stripping unit at the Rockaway Township Wells should be expedited. In April 1994, pursuant to the Spill Act, the Water Pollution Control Act and the Solid Waste Management Act. NJDEP entered into an ACO with Thiokol, in which Thiokol agreed to repla ce the air stripping unit. The air stripping unit was replaced and has been operational since May 1995.

In March 1996, NJDEP entered into a second ACO with Thiokol, in which Thiokol agreed to pay for the full cost of the operation and maintenance of the Rockaway Township air stripper, to implement the ground water remedy required in the 1993 ROD, and to investigate and remediate contaminant sources at the Denville Technical Park.

Several industrial establishments that operated or currently operate at the Denville Technical Park were subject to regulation pursuant to the New Jersey Industrial Site Recovery Act, which requires the owner/operator to clean up environmental contamination prior to the sale of the business or property. A list of the industrial establishments can be obtained from NJDEP, although many were identified in the 1996 Preliminary Assessment. For the majority of the industrial establishments NJDEP issued Non-Applicability Determinations or Negative Declarations indicating that remedial actions were not required. Two industrial establishments, Avionic Products Company (Avionics) and Lockheed Electronics Company (LEC), however, were required by NJDEP to conduct remediation as follows.

Avionics (Case No. 86540) was required to investigate its drum storage area adjacent to Building 2. In 1987-1988, Avionics investigated the soil and found it to be contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons, cadmium and silver. Sediments in a nearby catch basin were contaminated with the same hazardous substances. Approximately 39 cubic yards of contaminated soil and sediment were excavated and disposed of at a licensed disposal facility. Upon final inspection of the remedial action, NJDEP issued a letter requiring No Further Action to Avionics in April 1988.

LEC (Case No. 89846) was required to investigate its Raw Materials Storage Area, Hazardous Material Storage Area and Empty Drum Storage Area. Two samples were collected beneath the Raw Materials Storage A rea, one sample was collected from the Hazardous Materials Storage Area and one sample was collected from the Empty Drum Storage Area. Samples were collected at a depth of one foot below the surface. Chemical analyses of the soil samples detected only one hazardous substance, TCE. It was found in a sample collected from the Hazardous Material Storage Area at a concentration well below the New Jersey Soil Cleanup Criteria (NJSCC).

LEC was also required to investigate its air handling unit located in the eastern side of Building 2. Two surface soil samples were collected below drainage valves on the unit. Analytical results indicated the presence of elevated levels of petroleum hydrocarbons and zinc. Approximately 24 tons of contaminated soil were excavated from this area and disposed of at a licensed disposal facility. Upon final inspection of the remedial action, NJDEP issued a letter requiring No Further Action to LEC in January 1992.

In response to a request by the property owner of the Denville Technical Park, USEPA issued an Administrative Determination in 1997 that Block 62101, Lot 4 and a portion of Lot 1 were not considered to be part of the Rockaway Township Wells Site. In 1998, USEPA issued a second Administrative Determination that Block 62101, Lot 2 was not part of the Site. Both Determinations were made based on information and conditions known to USEPA, including sampling data, and a finding that the low levels of hazardous substances detected on these lots have not resulted in or threaten to result in a release or a threatened release of hazardous substances, pollutants or contaminants under CERCLA which would require remedial action at the property.

The area has been developed by commercial businesses and light industries including service stations, restaurants, hotels, plastic manufacturers, truck/transit companies, and commercial office complexes. It is unlikely that this development scenario will change in the future.

The ground water i s drawn from the Rockaway River Basin Area Sole Source Aquifer as a drinking water source for approximately 14,000 residents in Rockaway Township. The surface waters of the White Meadow Brook and the Beaver Brook flow into the Rockaway River and are not used for drinking water. The ground water will continue to be the source of drinking water for the foreseeable future. Wetlands associated with these brooks exist in the vicinity of the Site.

A ROD addressing Operable Unit (OU) 2 was completed in October 2002.

The Evor Phillips Leasing site is located on Lot 7, Block 6017A in Old Bridge Township and comprises approximately six acres. The site is located on Cheesequake Road just off Old Water Works Road and Bordentown Road. This area is primarily commercial/industrial.

The Evor site was used for various commercial/industrial operations between 1969 and 1986. It is alleged that bulk acids and caustic solutions were discharged directly onto the ground. In addition, it is alleged that hundreds of drums containing chlorinated solvents, aromatic hydrocarbons, ammonia, benzene, toluene, xylene, ketones and alcohols were disposed of at the site. 

In 1982, the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) requested that the site be placed on the National Priorities List (NPL). The Evor site was included in the September 8, 1983 revision to the NPL.

In 1986 a Remedial Investigation (RI) and Feasibility Study (FS) was initiated to determine the nature and extent of contamination at the Evor site. Two field investigations were conducted to categorize on-site contamination and were completed in April 1987 and April 1990, respectively. The RI concluded that there is contaminated groundwater leaving the Evor site. Following the remedial investigation, a feasibility study was conducted. During 1992, the feasibility study was completed and a proposed plan was developed which recommended a groundwater pump and treatment system, and recharge of the treated water back to the groundwater. 

A Record of Decision (ROD) was issued by the EPA on September 30, 1992, which described the selected remedy to be implemented. The ROD identified two operable units for the project. They are as follows: 

The Operable Unit #1 (OU1) remedy included the extraction of contaminated groundwater underlying the site with on-site treatment and recharge of the treated water, excavation of buried drums and debris in the drum disposal areas with off-site disposal at an appropriate facility, a nd environmental monitoring to evaluate the effectiveness of the remedy. 

The Operable Unit #2 (OU2) ROD will address the final remedies for on-site soils and groundwater, including a comprehensive study to assess the impact of the site on nearby municipal well fields.

Following negotiations with NJDEP, the PRPs provided assistance to NJDEP and its contractor in the design of the groundwater extraction and treatment system. Construction was completed by NJDEP's contractor in 1999. Subsequently, it was decided to discharge the treated water to a local wastewater treatment plant. 

This change was documented in an Explanation of Significant Differences  (ESD) addressing OU1 was completed in May 2002.

An Administrative Consent Order was entered into by NJDEP and several PRPs in 1996 related to the performance of an RI associated with the source of the contamination at the site, the demolition of the office buildings and furnaces, and the removal of buried drums and underground storage tanks. The RI effort culminated in the completion of an RI report for the soil entitled Supplemental Remedial Investigation Report (SRI Report).

In 2002, a number of PRPs entered into another Administrative Consent Order with NJDEP to conduct further investigation and remediation of the site. These efforts included additional investigation of the soil and the preparation of a risk assessment report entitled Site-Specific Risk Assessment Report (SSRA Report) and an FS report entitled Focused Feasibility Study Evor Phillips Leasing Company (FFS Report). Based upon EPA's review of the FFS Report, in combination with an assessment of the contamination at the site, it was concluded that further expansion and refinement of the potential remedial alternatives were necessary. This was accomplished in EPA's August 2008 Supplemental Feasibility Study Report for Soil (SFS Report).

The PRPs are currently performing a groundwater investigation at the site. It is anticipated that the i nvestigation will be completed and a remedy decision related to the on- and off-site groundwater will be made in the near future.

The property, which has been used for industrial purposes, is currently unoccupied and unused. The property is zoned as Special Development (SD3), the purpose of which is to establish areas that will provide new development opportunities for large-scale service and light manufacturing uses with appropriate supporting facilities. Properties within one mile of the site include a mix of Essential Services, Residential, Environmentally Sensitive/Recreation, and Special Development (SD3) properties.

To facilitate the integration of the reuse of the site into an actual remedy, the PRPs' consultant and the Old Bridge Housing and Redevelopment Agency discussed potential redevelopment options for the site prior to the development of remedial alternatives in an FFS. During these discussions, a preference was expressed toward a light commercial/industrial type operation. As part of the FFS report, the PRPs prepared a conceptual site redevelopment plan which includes the construction of warehouses on the property consistent with the property's zoning. Such redevelopment is consistent with the land use and zoning.

The PRPs' consultant has indicated that based upon very preliminary discussions, several parties have expressed an interest in redeveloping the site. A recent discussion with the Old Bridge Housing and Redevelopment Agency reinforced this future-use strategy as appropriate for the property.

Although the groundwater underlying the site is designated Class II-A (potable water and conversion to potable water through conventional water supply treatment, mixing or other similar technique), since the area is served by municipal water, it is unlikely that the groundwater underlying the property will be used for potable purposes in the foreseeable future.

Surface water runoff from the site is limited due to the relatively flat topogra phy, the presence of slight depressions, and the sandy soil underlying the site, which promotes infiltration of stormwater. Therefore, it is unlikely that the site, through surface water runoff, affects the nearest surface water bodies (the Sayreville recharge pond, which is located approximately 0.25 mile from the site, and Pricketts Brook, a tributary to Tenants Brook, which are both located approximately 1 mile from the site).

A ROD addressing Operable Unit 2 was completed in September 2008.

The Evor Phillips Leasing Company Site is located in a commercial/industrial area of Old Bridge Township, Middlesex County, New Jersey. The Site is an unoccupied 5.8 acre plot of land located approximately one mile west of U.S. Route 9 and 1.5 miles northeast of U.S. Route 18. The Site slopes gently toward the southwest, with a slight depression in the southwestern part of the property. Most of the buildings and facilities associated with previous Site operations have been demolished and removed. Two buildings on the Site support a groundwater extraction and treatment system. The Site is surrounded by eight-foot chain-linked fencing. The surrounding area is largely industrial. The Site is bounded to the north and south by railroad tracks. The CPS/Madison Industries Superfund site is located approximately 800 feet southwest of the Site. The Sayreville municipal well field is located approximately one quarter mile west of the Site and the Perth Amboy municipal well field approximately one mile south.

From 1970 to 1986, activities at the Site included industrial waste treatment, oil recovery, and metal reclamation operations that resulted in widespread contamination at the Site, including groundwater contamination. During the early 1970's, two treatment ponds were used at the Site for the neutralization of acidic and caustic wastewater. During the 1970s and into the 1980s, nineteen horizontal furnaces were used to recover silver by incinerating photographic film s.

In 1973, the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) filed a complaint against several companies demanding that they obtain a permit and certificate to operate the waste treatment facility located at the Site. The parties continued to operate the waste treatment facility without obtaining the appropriate permit. In 1975, the waste treatment facility was shut down pursuant to a court issued consent judgment and the contents of the treatment ponds were removed and disposed off site.

In 1983, the State of New Jersey excavated and removed approximately 40 drums from the Site and performed other stabilization measures. The Site was listed on the National Priorities List (NPL) in September 1983.

A remedial investigation and feasibility study (RI/FS) was conducted by the State of New Jersey from 1986 to 1992. The RI sampling results indicated that volatile organic compounds (VOCs), including 1,2-dichloroethane (1,2-DCA) and trichloroethene (TCE) , arid heavy metals, such as copper, nickel, and zinc, had contaminated the groundwater, at the Site. Based upon the results of the RI/FS, a Record of Decision (ROD) was issued by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in 1992, selecting an interim remedy for the first Operable Unit at the Site that included the removal and disposal of buried drums and the extraction, and treatment of the contaminated groundwater, followed by reinjection of the treated water. NJDEP designed and installed an on-site groundwater extraction and treatment system in 1993. Construction of the groundwater pump and treatment system was completed by NJDEP in 1999. The groundwater extraction and treatment remedy was an interim containment action until a final remedy could be selected.

An administrative consent order was entered into by the State of New Jersey and several potentially responsible parties (PRP) in 1996 for the performance, of an RI to identify additional sources of contamination at the Site. The administrativ e consent order also called for the demolition of office buildings and-furnaces, and the removal of buried drums and underground storage tanks located at the Site.

From January 1996 to May 1997, a group of PRPs unearthed hundreds of buried waste Containers. The excavated containers and associated contaminated soil were disposed off-site. From February to April 1997, EPA performed a portion of the removal activities because chemical warfare agents were alleged to be present in one area of the site. This allegation was not correct. During EPA's removal action, 34 drums, 300 small containers and associated contaminated soil were excavated and disposed off-site;

In 2002, following negotiations with NJDEP, a group of PRPs assumed responsibility for the operation and maintenance of the interim groundwater extraction and treatment system at the Site. Subsequently, it was decided to discharge the treated water to a local wastewater treatment plant rather than re-inject it back into the groundwater. This change was documented in an Explanation of Significant Differences that was issued in 2002. The interim groundwater treatment system continues to operate at the Site.

In .2002, a number of PRPs entered into another administrative consent order with NJDEP to conduct further investigation and remediation of the Site. In 2008, EPA assumed the lead responsibility for the Site. A Supplemental Soil FS Report, addressing soil sources of groundwater contamination at the Site, was completed by EPA in August 2008. In September 2008, an OU2 ROD was issued, selecting the final soil remedy for the Site. The OU2 remedy consists of excavation, and off-site disposal of contaminated soils exceeding impact-to-groundwater cleanup goals, and the on-site capping of soils exceeding nonresidential cleanup goals. The remedy selected for OU2 includes institutional controls to restrict excavation below the soil cap. In September 2009, a PRP group entered into a consent decree with EPA to per form the remedy selected in the OU2 ROD. The OU2 remedy is currently being implemented by the PRPs with EPA oversight, and is expected to be completed in October 2012.

In 2010, the same PRP group entered into an administrative order on consent with EPA to conduct the RI/FS for on-site groundwater contamination. An on-site groundwater RI report was completed in February 2011. The FS report was completed in February 2012. The results of the groundwater RI and FS reports are summarized below.

A Record of Decision addressing Operable Unit 03 of the Evor Phillips Leasing Site was completed in September 2012.
