The Franklin Burn Superfund Site is comprised of seven non-contiguous parcels of land in Franklin Township, Gloucester County, New Jersey. Each of the seven parcels is known as a subsite. The subsites are referred to as Subsite 1 through Subsite 7. Subsites 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6 are clustered within 2500 feet of each other just north of Marshall Mill Road. They are reached via dirt roads, which extend from Marshall Mill Road. Subsites 1, 5 and 6 are just south of, and adjacent to, an intermittent stream known as Hayes Branch. Subsites 2 and 7 are within a few miles of the aforementioned sites in a north and northeast direction, respectively. Subsite 2 is located just east of Lincoln Road, and Subsite 7 is east of Stanton Road.

The subsites are generally flat open fields and brush covered areas which are bordered by forested areas. At each of the seven subsites, scrap copper wire and possibly other electrical components were placed on the ground surface and burned to remove the plastic coatings and insulation so that the remaining copper could be recovered for sale. The burning process took place on open unprotected ground and resulted in the generation of contaminated ash and debris piles and soil, which contained hazardous substances. The hazardous substances included heavy metals, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and dioxins and furans.

Soils, sediment and associated isolated small pools of surface water and groundwater were the media affected by the release of these hazardous substances. At Subsites 1,5, and 6, site-related contaminants have come to be located in wetland areas, which border the northern flank of the former burn areas.

The subsites range in size from 480 square feet (Subsite 6) to 15,000 square feet (Subsite 2). The locations where contaminated soil and ash were present comprised just over 2.5 acres of surface area.

Currently, all the subsites are undeveloped. One former residence, located adjacent to Subsite 5, burned down some time durin g the spring of 2000. Abandoned and/or demolished cinder block and wood structures are present at Subsites 6 and 7.

Based on site environmental characteristics, including the surface and near-surface waste disposal practices, the Franklin Burn Site was managed under the EPA Superfund Accelerated Cleanup Model (SACM) initiative, as a SACM Pilot project. The SACM paradigm was introduced in 1992 to create improved removal and remedial program coordination, thereby streamlining the traditional Superfund response process. SACM utilized removal authorities created under CERCLA to conduct early response actions at the site, thereby reducing the primary risks of human and ecological exposure through direct contact with contaminated ash and soils. Baseline and future human health and ecological risks associated with residual contamination, and the potential need for longer-term actions were evaluated during remedial program investigations.

The site appears to have been active as a burn area beginning in the early 1960's until the 1980's. The burning took place on open ground (at the land surface) where no containment was in place.

In 1986, the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) investigated Subsites 1 and 2 and detected heavy metals in soils, including cadmium at 197 parts per million (ppm), chromium at 121 ppm, copper at 63,700 ppm, lead at 13,700 ppm, nickel at 131 ppm, and zinc at 924,800 ppm.

NJDEP referred the first of the Franklin Burn subsites to EPA in February 1989. Investigations by both agencies identified a total of seven burn sites in the area. Since assuming the lead role in the investigation of the site, EPA with support from various EPA contractors, has conducted numerous investigatory and removal activities, and prepared a number of site-related reports.

The site was proposed for listing on the National Priorities List in October 1995, and was included on the list in June 1996.

In 1989, EPA conducted soil removal asse ssments including analysis with field and fixed-based laboratory equipment for Subsites 1 and 2. In 1990, investigation of the groundwater pathway began. EPA Superfund pre-remedial activities, including the preparation of a Preliminary Assessment and Site Inspection, were completed for Subsites 1 and 2 by 1991.

During 1992 and 1993, extent of contamination studies were conducted at Subsites 3,4, 5 and 6, and the identity of Subsite 7 was confirmed. This work included a determination of extent of soil and ash contamination both prior to and after removal activities. Screening for metals in soil and ash was conducted using a Field Portable X-ray Fluorescence (FPXRF) spectrometer. The FPXRF indicated that lead, copper, zinc and other metals were present at elevated concentrations. The maximum concentrations of contaminants in screening sample data included lead at 42,000 ppm, copper at 140,000 ppm, and zinc at 260,000 ppm. The screening study confirmed that most of the contamination was confined to the piles and upper few feet of soil and within the perimeter of the visible ash contamination. A minimum of 10 percent of the samples analyzed by FPXRF were chosen for confirmatory analysis by atomic absorption (AA) or inductively coupled plasma (ICP) spectrometry.

From November 1992 through May 1993, EPA time-critical removal actions were conducted which included the excavation and stockpiling of contaminated ash and soil at Subsites 1,2 and 3, and excavation and off-site disposal of contaminated ash and soil from Subsites 4, 5, 6 and 7. Within the SACM framework, the stockpiled soils that were excavated from Subsites 1,2 and 3 were targeted for off-site disposal, thus eliminating the necessity of a feasibility study for remediation of these wastes. A total of approximately 10,063 tons of contaminated soils, ash and debris was excavated. Off-site disposal of all excavated and stockpiled materials was completed by the spring of 1997.

As a result of the removal acti ons, the levels of contamination have for the most part been decreased to values below the EPA established preliminary remediation goals (PRGs). Exceptions (areas where residual contamination exists above the PRGs) are noted in the RI report. These areas include subsurface residual contamination locations at Subsites 5 and 6 where excavation activities were discontinued when the groundwater table was encountered at a shallow depth. At these subsites, excavation activities extended to the groundwater table and a textile membrane was installed prior to backfilling with clean fill. All areas with residual contamination have been backfilled with two to four feet of clean fill.

In 1994, the SACM Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (RI/FS) work plan was finalized. RI goals included review of existing removal program data and collection of additional data to address the stockpiled soils at Subsites 1, 2 and 3, performing a groundwater contamination investigation, and completing human health and ecological risk assessments.

Twenty monitoring wells and six piezometers were installed and sampled as part of the remedial investigation activities. Seven residential wells, which were located in close proximity to the subsites, were also sampled. All groundwater samples were analyzed for volatile organic, semi-volatile organic, pesticide/PCB, dioxin and furan, phenolic, and inorganic constituents.

Following the additional soil and groundwater data collection and removal of the primary waste material and adjacent contaminated soils, EPA prepared a draft RI report. The report focused on the potential for groundwater contamination and health effects associated with the low-level subsurface residual soil contamination that was present below the water table interface. The RI report was submitted in August 1997.

Samples collected during the RI investigation identified a few areas with elevated levels of contamination. The RI sampling indicated high metals readings in se diment at Subsite 6, elevated dioxin and furan congeners in groundwater in an up-gradient monitoring well at Subsite 7, elevated residual metals in soil readings at Subsite 7, and a potential for elevated noncarcinogenic risk in the home produce ingestion pathway at a number of subsites. Further investigation and sampling was conducted in the elevated contamination areas to confirm the presence and level of contamination or absence of contamination in these locations.

In December 1998, sampling was conducted to confirm the distribution of residual metal contamination (e.g., copper exhibited the highest concentrations) in the wetland area of Subsite 6. This effort included the collection of three environmental samples at and around a previous location where copper significantly exceeded the PRG. This re-sampling failed to confirm the previous result. Instead, copper was measured at background levels and well below the PRG. This effort confirmed the discontinuous and haphazard nature of contaminant distribution in the wetland.

In February of 2000, the up gradient monitoring well at Subsite 7 was re-sampled. All dioxin and furan congeners were found to be well within acceptable limits.

In July 2000, seven soil samples were collected from Subsite 7. Samples were collected adjacent to previously excavated areas where copper concentrations (maximum of 5,400 ppm) were below the PRG but significantly in excess of the New Jersey Residential Soil Cleanup Criteria of 600 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg). This follow-up sampling effort indicated that copper concentrations were all below the New Jersey criteria with the exception of one copper reading of 672 ppm at the northern end of the subsite, which was slightly above the New Jersey ecological effects-derived soil criteria. In addition, all copper concentrations are well below EPA's generic soil screening (residential scenario) guidance value of 2,900 mg/kg.

In September 2000, site-specific vegetation and soil sam pling were conducted to determine plant uptake values for use in the human health risk homegrown produce pathway analysis. The data collected during this investigation indicated that risks associated with this pathway are within acceptable levels. A detailed description of the homegrown produce study is included in the section entitled "Summary of Risks."

Early on in the State's investigation process, site owners and/or potential responsible parties were directed to further sample and remediate the subsites. According to responsible party legal representatives, these individuals were not financially able to comply with the above-noted directives. EPA confirmed this conclusion and site activities including cleanup actions were completed utilizing Superfund monies. No potential responsible parties have been involved in the investigatory or remedial processes conducted at the site.

The Franklin Burn site is located in a predominantly rural community with approximately 105 people living within one-quarter mile. An elementary school, church and housing development are within one-half mile of the site. Franklinville, a town with a population of approximately 20,000 lies about 2.5 miles west.

Currently, none of the subsites are developed. One former residence, located adjacent to Subsite 5, burned down sometime during the spring of 2000. Abandoned and/or demolished structures are present at Subsites 6 and 7.

With the exception of Subsite 2, all of the subsites are located off unimproved roads, and currently have limited access. Subsite 2 is east of Lincoln Avenue, a. paved local road. The subsites are vegetated with trees, low bushes, and grasses. Wetlands associated with Subsites 1, 5, and 6 are of limited access based on the density of vegetation and their distant location from existing roadways.

Since residential use is allowed in accordance with the local zoning, the site risks were evaluated with this in mind. Residential exposure was also assumed in th e development of the PRGs during the removal activities performed by EPA.

Surface water and groundwater are not currently utilized at any of the subsites.

The proposed land use at all seven subsites is characteristic of the undeveloped and agricultural nature of Franklin Township. In accordance with Franklin Code Article X1B, Subsites 1, 3, 4, 5,6 and 7 are located in one-acre minimum Rural Agricultural (R-A) Districts. Subsite 2 lies within a similar Franklin Code Article XIV Residential (R-l) District. Some portions of Subsites 1, 5 and 6 lie within Franklin Code Article XXIX areas zoned as Flood (F) Districts. Structures, which would unduly obstruct the natural passage of floodwaters, are not allowed in F Districts. Although no development plans are currently approved for the site, the subsites most likely will continue to be zoned as R-A, R-l and F districts.

No future use of surface water is anticipated at the subsites. The future use of groundwater is not determined at this time.

A Record of Decision (ROD) addressing operable unit (OU) 1 was completed in May 2004.

The Welsbach/General Gas Mantle Contamination site (Welsbach Site) is a multi-property site centered around two former thorium gas mantle manufacturing companies in the cities of Gloucester City and Camden, New Jersey. Approximately 100 residential, commercial, and industrial properties make up the Welsbach Site. The Delaware River, Newton Creek, and Martins Lake are adjacent to some of these radiologically-contaminated properties. 

Between the 1890s and 1940s, the Welsbach Company (Welsbach) manufactured gas mantles at its facility in Gloucester City, New Jersey. Welsbach was a major manufacturer and distributor of gas mantles until the electric light replaced gas lighting. Beginning around 1895, Welsbach imported monazite ore to use as its source of the radioactive element thorium. Welsbach extracted thorium from the ore and used it in its gas mantle manufacturing process. Thorium causes the mantles to glow more brightly when heated. Just after the turn of the century, Welsbach was the largest producer of gas mantles and lamps in the United States, making up to 250,000 mantles per day. Welsbach went out of business in 1940.

A second gas mantle manufacturing company, General Gas Mantle Company (GGM), located in Camden, New Jersey, was a small competitor to the Welsbach Company. GGM operated from 1912 to 1941. There is little information on its activities. It appears that GGM only used refined thorium in its gas mantle manufacturing processes.

Both Welsbach and GGM went out of business in the early 1940s. To date, EPA has been unable to identify any successor companies.  

The Welsbach Site properties and the surrounding areas consist of industrial, commercial, and residential zoning districts. Study Area 1 is located in an industrial-zoned section of Camden with residential properties east of the former GGM facility. In Study Area 2, the former Welsbach Facility is situated in an industrial-zoned section of Gloucester City with residential properties to  the immediate east. An original Welsbach building, the Armstrong building, is still present on the property.  Study Area 3 consists of residential properties, a private swim club, and a land preserve. Study Area 4 consists entirely of residential properties in the Fairview section of Camden. Residential properties, vacant land and two municipal parks near Temple Avenue and the South Branch of Newton Creek in Gloucester City comprise Study Area 5. Study Area 6 consists of residential properties and vacant land in a residentially zoned area of Gloucester City. The Gloucester City Board of Education planned to build a new middle school on the vacant land in the area, including the former Popcorn Factory parcel.  No significant changes in land use are anticipated, except in the area of the former GGM facility where some residential areas may be rezoned for commercial uses. 

A separate study area was created to investigate surface water, sediment and wetlands.  EPA conducted the investigation of surface waters, sediments and wetlands in Study Areas 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6 of the Welsbach Site. EPA did not include Study Area 4 in this investigation because the soil contamination in this area is in very small and isolated locations.

The State of New Jersey classifies Newton Creek and the South Branch Newton Creek as "fresh water-non-trout" (FW2-NT). The State has also classified Martins Lake as FW2-NT. The FW2-NT water classification refers to fresh waters that are generally not suitable for trout because of the waters' physical, chemical or biological characteristics, but are suitable for a wide variety of other fish species. Designated uses of FW2-NT waters include: maintenance, migration, and propagation of the natural and established plant and animal life; primary and secondary contact recreation; industrial and agricultural water supply, and public potable water supply after treatment. 

The State of New Jersey classifies the portion of the Delaware River adjacent t o Study Area 2 as "Zone 3." Designated uses for Zone 3 include agricultural, industrial and public water supply after treatment; maintenance of resident fish and other aquatic life; migration of fish; secondary contact recreation; and navigation. EPA anticipates no significant changes to the classifications of the Delaware River, Newton Creek or Martins Lake. 

EPA initially identified the Welsbach Site in 1980 during an archive search conducted as part of an investigation of the U.S. Radium Corporation Superfund site located in Orange, New Jersey. Historical U.S. Radium Corporation files indicated that U.S. Radium purchased radiological materials from Welsbach during the 1920s. In May 1981, EPA sponsored an aerial radiological survey of the Camden and Gloucester City area. The survey covered a 20-square-kilometer area surrounding the locations of the former Welsbach and GGM facilities. The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) evaluated the data from the aerial survey and identified five areas with elevated gamma radiation levels. The elevated areas included the locations of the two former gas mantle manufacturing facilities and three mainly residential areas in both Camden and Gloucester City. In 1993, EPA re-analyzed the data from the aerial survey, which subsequently led to the identification of a sixth area, located in Gloucester City, with elevated gamma radiation levels

In the early 1990s, NJDEP conducted follow-up radiological investigations at more than 1,000 properties located throughout the original five Study Areas. During these investigations, NJDEP identified radiological contamination at the two former gas mantle facilities and at residential, commercial, and industrial properties located near the two facilities. Based on these data, NJDEP conducted some interim remedial measures which included installing concrete, steel, and/or soil shielding inside homes and yards, installing radon mitigation systems at selected properties,  and relocating one resident and one business. 

In March 1995, EPA prepared a Hazard Ranking System (HRS) report for the Site, and in June 1996, EPA placed the Welsbach Site on the National Priorities List (NPL). EPA, as the lead agency, prepared this decision document with support from NJDEP. Site-related activities are being federally funded. From September 1997 to January 1999, EPA conducted a remedial investigation and feasibility study (RI/FS) to investigate the radiological contamination at a number of residential and industrial properties at the Welsbach Site. On July 23, 1999, EPA signed a Record of Decision (ROD) for Operable Unit 1 (OU1) (1999 ROD). EPA stated in the 1999 ROD that it would address the potential site impacts to surface water, sediment, and wetland areas in the future.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has divided the Welsbach Site into four separate cleanup phases, or operable units (OUs). In the July 23, 1999 ROD, EPA, with support from the NJDEP selected a remedy for the radiologically contaminated soils at the Welsbach Site. The remedy for OU1 included demolition of the former GGM building, excavation of the radiologically contaminated soil and debris at the residential, commercial, and industrial properties at the Welsbach Site, and disposal of this material at a licensed off-site facility. The third Operable Unit (OU3) includes the surface water, sediment and wetland areas in the Welsbach Site study area. Additional operable units will address potential remedies for the former Welsbach-era building known as the Armstrong Building (Operable Unit 2), and the groundwater (Operable Unit 4). 

In April 2001, EPA started the surface water, sediment, and wetland investigation called for in the 1999 ROD.  In January 2005, EPA used sediment data from the surface water, sediment, and wetland investigation to evaluate the baseline human health risk from radionuclides and chemicals of potential concern. 

As part of the desig n investigations for OU1, EPA has investigated nearly 1,000 properties in the Camden and Gloucester City area. Based on information from this investigation, EPA has identified approximately 100 residential, commercial, and industrial properties with elevated radionuclide levels. EPA has completed cleanup activities on over 15 residential properties, a portion of the Gloucester City Swim Club, and the Popcorn Factory property in Study Area 6. At present, EPA is continuing its cleanup efforts on other residential properties in the Gloucester City and Camden area. 

In September 1997, Holt Hauling and Warehousing, Inc. (Holt), which owned the former Welsbach property at that time, entered into an Administrative Order on Consent (AOC) with EPA. Under the terms of the AOC, Holt agreed to perform an RI/FS on the Armstrong Building (the one remaining original Welsbach building). In January 2000, Holt submitted the RI/FS Report for EPA review and approval. Holt's RI/FS identified sporadic radiological contamination on the structural surfaces inside the building. In July 2000, EPA approved Holt's RI/FS Report, and will select a remedy for the Armstrong Building in the future based on information obtained from Holt's RI/FS. 

OU2 addresses, radioactive contamination in the Armstrong Building, the last remaining building from the Welsbach operations.

A Record of Decision addressing OU 02 at the Welsbach/General Gas Mantle Contamination Superfund Site was completed in September 2011.

A Record of Decision (ROD) addressing OU 3 was completed in September 2005.

The Zschiegner Refining Company (ZRC) site is located at 1442 Maxim Southard Road, Howell Township, Monmouth County, New Jersey. The ZRC site is a 6.1-acre former metals refining facility located in a rural residential area. The Haystack Brook and its associated wetlands run north-south on the eastern portion of the property and a small pond is on adjacent property immediately southeast of the site. An Ocean County Utilities Authority easement bounds the property to the north. Maxim-Southard Road and the Candlewood residential development are located west of the property. A residence located on private property is about 100 feet southwest of the ZRC site. The area surrounding the site is predominantly rural, but several densely populated developments are in the vicinity. A public drinking water well serving approximately 48,000 people is located 6.5 miles from the site; private wells serve the property and its three closest neighbors.

The primary structure on the site is a dilapidated single-story structure located about 140 feet east of Maxim-Southard Road. The building is composed of concrete blocks with a corrugated metal roof, and measures approximately 230 feet by 30 feet, with a partial basement under the western portion of the building. A cinder block and concrete loading dock runs along most of the north side of the building. The edge of the loading dock has been seriously eroded in places, probably due to acid spills. A small, aluminum yard shed is located in the southeast corner of the property near the adjacent pond. A variety of debris, such as an abandoned car, old tires, tin cans, and plastic bottles are scattered across the site, with additional debris within the building. The area immediately surrounding the building is fenced.

The Zschiegner Refining Company operated from 1964 to 1992 as a precious metals recovery facility. Operations included the chemical stripping of precious metals from watch bands, photographic film, and electrical compone nts. In October 1992, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency raided the facility based on suspicions of illegal drug manufacturing. At the time of the raid, approximately 3,000 different chemicals including peroxides, cyanides, caustics, and acids were found improperly stored at the facility.

On November 2, 1992, a removal action was initiated by EPA. Materials were segregated and transferred to acceptable containers, potentially explosive/reactive items were detonated, hazardous materials were removed off-site for disposal, liquids in vats and drums were sampled, and on-site soil and sediment samples were taken. Approximately 2,000 gallons of acidic solutions, 1,600 gallons of basic solutions, and 1,400 small containers of hazardous substances were gathered. Phase II of the removal action was initiated in March 1993 and involved the disposal of hazardous waste secured during Phase I. Further sampling was conducted in 1995; analysis of these samples revealed the presence of inorganic contaminants in the on-site soil and downstream surface water and sediment.

A Hazard Ranking System (HRS) report was prepared for the site in December 1997, and the site was placed on the National Priorities List (NPL) in March 1998. EPA is the lead agency, and the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) is the support agency.

Mr. and Mrs. Herbert and Frances Zschiegner are the owners of the site, and Mr. Zschiegner was the sole operator of the site. As such, they are potentially responsible parties (PRPs) for the site, and they were sent notice of their liability on April 28, 1998. In 1995, Mr. Zschiegner was criminally convicted on three counts of violating the Clean Water Act. He was ordered to serve a 16-month prison term and to pay restitution to EPA in the amount of $650,000. He is currently paying this restitution on a monthly basis. A thorough review of Mr. and Mrs. Zschiegner's finances has been conducted. They do not appear to be viable PRPs at this time,  nor is it likely that they will eventually be able to significantly contribute to the costs of investigating and cleaning up the site. However, their financial situation will continue to be monitored.

Information request letters were sent to 12 companies on July 15, 1998 in order to determine if they sent hazardous substances to the site. The responses did not yield information to support a finding of potential liability under Section 107(a)(3) of CERCLA.

Therefore, no viable PRPs have been identified for this site. Mr. Zschiegner continues to pay the court ordered restitution, but further cost recovery appears to be unlikely.

In September 1998, a Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (RI/FS) was initiated at the ZRC site to determine the nature and extent of contamination. Initial field investigations, which began in August 2000, included topographic and geophysical surveys, and a subsurface soil and groundwater screening program that consisted of collecting and field analyzing samples. The screening program was conducted to assist with the placement of groundwater monitoring wells on and downgradient of the site. Other activities included water level measurement, the installation of six piezometers in the wetland area, and a downhole geophysical survey. Samples were collected from surface soil, subsurface soil, wetland sediment, ground water, wetland seeps, surface water and sediment from Haystack Brook and the pond, and building material. In general, samples were analyzed for volatile organic compounds (VOCs), semivolatile organic compounds (SVOCs), pesticides, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and metals. Initial investigation activities were completed by November 2001.

Data obtained during the initial investigation activities was reviewed, and additional sampling was determined necessary to both fill in data gaps from the initial effort and to complete a full Baseline Ecological Risk Assessment (BERA) at the site. A Screening Level Ecological Ris k Assessment was completed during the initial effort, and it found that a full BERA was necessary at this site. Therefore, in August 2003 another sampling effort was conducted, which included additional sediment samples from the brook, pond, and wetland to fill in data gaps, as well as macroinvertebrate characterization, an avian survey, threatened and endangered species surveys, habitat studies and surveys, sediment sampling, biota sampling, and toxicity testing to complete the BERA.

Currently, the ZRC site is unoccupied and surrounded by a fence. It is zoned Agricultural Rural Estate, which leaves open the possibility for either residential or industrial development, and the ground water below the site is designated as a potable water supply.

A large portion of the site consists of wetland area through which runs the Haystack Brook. Haystack Brook is classified by NJDEP as FW2-NT, which means it is a water body that may be used for maintenance, migration, and propagation of the natural and established biota; primary and secondary contact recreation; industrial and agricultural water supply; and as a public potable water supply after such treatment as required by law or regulation. The brook flows towards three recreational fisheries along a 15-mile surface water pathway. A drinking water intake is located on the Metedeconk River 6.5 miles downstream of the site, and the site is located in a drinking water supply watershed.

A Record of Decision (ROD) addressing operable unit (OU) 1 was completed in September 2004.

The former Kil-Tone Company site is located at 527 East Chestnut Avenue, in the city of Vineland, Cumberland County, New Jersey.  The property was used for industrial activity from the early 1900s until the 1980s and began its operations manufacturing arsenate of lead.  It continued manufacturing arsenic based pesticides until the 1930s.  Currently the site is owned by Urban Manufacturing LLC (aka Urban Sign and Crane); the property was purchased in 2008 for manufacturing of commercial signs; Arsenic is not use in current site operations.  Reported elevated levels of arsenic and lead in on-site soil and groundwater above NJDEP Groundwater Quality Criteria of 3 parts per billion (ppb) and exceeds both NJDEP residential Direct Contact Soil cleanup standard (RDCSCS) of 400 ppm.  NJDEP interviewed residents in the Vineland area who confirmed the presence of the former Kil-Tone and the environmental impact from the facility.  

Soil sampling conducted by the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) in August 2014 discovered high concentrations of arsenic and lead in the soils at the site property and at several neighboring residential properties. NJDEP referred the site for removal action consideration on November 14, 2014.

EPA approved an action memorandum on September 28, 2015 for a removal action at the site in order to address the threats posed by lead and arsenic contaminated soil on residential properties located close to or adjacent to the Site property. The removal action was completed by the end of 2016 and consisted of the installation of a soil barrier in order to reduce direct contact. The Site was proposed to the National Priorities List (NPL) on September 30, 2015 and was added to the NPL on April 5, 2016. EPA signed an Engineering Evaluation/Cost Analysis (EE/CA) Approval Memorandum for the residential properties surrounding the site in order to complete the delineation of contamination on October 22, 2015. EPA is currently addressing the Site in four phases or operable units (OUs). 

OU1 addresses the residential properties identified in the EE/CA. EPA selected a remedy for OU1 and the OU1 Record of Decision (ROD) was signed on September 12, 2016. The OU1 remedy includes excavation of an estimated 21,000 cubic yards of soil contaminated primarily with arsenic and lead from approximately 57 residential properties; off-site disposal of contaminated soil; backfilling of excavated areas with clean fill; and restoration of the affected properties. Remedial Action for the cleanup of impacted OU1 residential properties was initiated in 2017.  As of April 2020, 32 impacted OU1 residential properties have been cleaned up. Clean up of the remainder of the impacted OU1 residential properties is expected to begin in 2022. 

Further investigation of the nature and extent of soil contamination at the former Kil-Tone Co. facility and other industrial and commercial properties will be addressed under OU2. OU3 includes delineation of the groundwater contamination, while OU4 will include the surface water and sediments of the Tarkiln and Parvin Branches, and if sampling indicates that contamination has migrated, possibly the Maurice River and Union Lake, although this will be coordinated with efforts at the Vineland Chemical Company Superfund site.

EPA selected a remedy for OU2 and the OU2 ROD was signed on September 30, 2019. The OU2 remedy includes excavation of an estimated 57,800 cubic yards of soil primarily contaminated with arsenic and lead from the former Kil-Tone facility and other impacted commercial or non-residential properties in the vicinity; off-site disposal of contaminated soil that exceeds the appropriate property-specific soil remediation standard, not to exceed the depth of the groundwater table; backfilling of excavated areas with clean fill; and restoration of the affected properties. Remedial Design for the OU2 is expected to be ready by end of 2022, and the Remedial Action is expected to be completed by 2028.

The Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study for OU3 was initiated in 2017 and is currently in progress.

The Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study for OU4 was  initiated in 2020 and is currently in progress.

The Crown Vantage Landfill Site (Site), EPA CERCLIS ID number NJN000204492, is located at Block 17.01 Lot 1 of the Alexandria Township Tax Map, at 500 Milford-Frenchtown Road in Alexandria Township, New Jersey. The Site is an inactive former landfill. The Site is roughly elliptical in shape and occupies an area of approximately ten acres with approximately 1,500 feet of frontage on the eastern bank of the Delaware River. To the west of the landfill, across the Delaware River, lies Bucks County, Pennsylvania. The Delaware and Raritan Canal foot path and a farm field bound the Site to the east. Historically, railroad tracks bounded the Site to the east. The landfill property is bounded to the south by the Delaware Raritan Canal State Park and to the north by the former Curtis Papers mill property. A mix of young and mature hardwood trees, shrubs and grasses currently covers the Site. Access to the landfill area is restricted by locked chain-link fencing. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is the lead agency for the Remedial Investigation and Feasibility Study (RI/FS) activities, with the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) functioning in a support role.

The landfill was reportedly utilized by the nearby former Curtis Specialty Papers mill, as well as by other nearby Riegel Paper Company facilities, for the disposal of waste beginning in the late 1930s through the early 1970s. The landfill may also have accepted flood-damaged items from the local community following record flooding of the Delaware River in 1955. Types of wastes disposed of at the landfill include fly ash, cinders, and bottom ash; paper mill and coating-related wastes, including foil-backed paper, off-specification paper, 55-gallon drums containing press room wastes, and paper fiber sludge from wastewater treatment plant operations; steel and fiber barrels and pallets; and construction and demolition debris. A review of historical aerial photos indicated that shallow  trenches in the surface of the landfill may have been used for the burial of drummed wastes in the early 1970s.

The Site has been characterized through numerous investigations that started in 1991 and continued to the recent Remedial Investigation (RI), which was conducted in 2008 and 2009. A Preliminary Site Investigation (PSI), including an aerial photograph analysis, geophysical survey of the landfill area, soil gas sampling, ground water sampling and a wetlands assessment, was conducted in 1991. The PSI was followed by the removal of drums (empty, full, and partially full) and paper products from the surface of the landfill. In 1994, monitoring wells were installed and the ground water quality was characterized. From 2001 through 2003, the NJDEP fenced the Site, removed additional surface debris, including drums, and collected surface soil samples. The EPA conducted additional sampling of surface water, sediment, surface soil and fly ash, and ground water in 2003 and 2004. Additional wastes were removed from the surface and riprap was placed in flood-impacted areas.

The Site was placed on the National Priorities List in 2005. In May 2005, Fort James Operating Company, a subsidiary of Georgia-Pacific, entered into an Administrative Order on Consent (AOC) with EPA for a Removal Action. Under the 2005 AOC, additional surficial drums were removed, additional fencing was provided, and an engineered slope stabilization wall was constructed to stabilize the landfill's western face. In total, over 700 surficial drums, drum remnants and drum carcasses were removed from the surface of the Site during investigations conducted between 1991 and 2007.

Recent investigations and removal actions at the Site have been performed by Georgia-Pacific Consumer Products, LP (GPCP) under an Administrative Agreement and Order on Consent signed in September 2007 and by International Paper Company (IP) under a Unilateral Administrative Order signed in December 2007. During the RI , more than 1,750 drums, drum carcasses and drum remnants were removed from the Site. The RI Report was completed in 2010.

A Record of Decision (ROD) addressing OU 01 of the Crown Vantage Landfill was signed in September 2011.

The Site is located within the city limits of Roswell, Chaves County, New Mexico. The Site is situated in the southeast portion of the City and spans approximately 500 acres in Sections 9, 10, 15, and 16 of Township 11 South, Range 24 East. The Site lies within a commercial and residential area where several dry cleaning businesses formerly operated. This area encompasses the former dry cleaning facilities located at 1107 and 1133 South Main Street, and an active dry cleaner at 1139 South Main Street.

The National Superfund Database Identification Number for the Site is NMD0000605386. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is the lead agency for conducting the remedial investigation/ feasibility study (RI/FS) and preparation of the record of decision (ROD). The New Mexico Environment Department (NMED) is the support agency for the RI/FS and the ROD. There are no current enforcement actions or potentially responsible parties (PRPs) identified for the Site; therefore, the expected source of cleanup monies is the Superfund trust fund.

Undocumented releases from dry cleaning facilities located within the 1100 block of South Main Street resulted in the formation of a ground water contaminant plume containing perchloroethylene (PCE) and its breakdown products trichloroethylene (TCE), cis 1,2-dichloroethylene (cis 1,2-DCE), trans 1,2-dichloroethylene (trans 1,2-DCE) and vinyl chloride. Current information from monitoring wells installed by NMED and EPA indicates that the ground water plume originates within the 1100 block of South Main Street and extends approximately 7,500 feet southeast toward the intersection of Poe Street and Atkinson Avenue.

The plume was discovered in November 1994 while NMED was overseeing the investigation of an underground storage tank (UST) gasoline release from the former Consolidated Bottlers Plant located at 108 West Reed Street. Very little is known about the cleaning chemicals, volume, or disposal methods used by the former  dry cleaning facilities that operated from the mid-1950s up to 1976. However, pre-RI investigations conducted by NMED concluded that hazardous substance releases from the dry cleaning facility formerly located at 1107 South Main Street were the primary source of the PCE detected in the ground water samples collected at the Site.

The Site (Source Area and Ground Water Plume Area or RI study area) is zoned and currently supports mixed commercial and residential land uses. There are several commercial buildings and two residential homes present within the Source Area. Within the larger Ground Water Plume Area, there are additional residential neighborhoods, an elementary school and numerous small businesses. Future zoning and land use are expected to remain consistent with current uses.

Based on surveys performed between 1995 and 2002, alluvial aquifer ground water is not being used within the RI study area as a drinking water source. However, alluvial aquifer ground water is being used for irrigation and livestock watering purposes within the southeast portion of the Ground Water Plume Area primarily in the vicinity of Atkinson Avenue and Poe Street, and the county fairgrounds.

There is currently limited information on the extent of alluvial aquifer ground water use outside of the RI study area. Artesian aquifer ground water within the RI study area is also being used for irrigation and livestock watering purposes. Based on current and future anticipated use patterns and knowledge of Site conditions acquired from the RI, it is expected that the alluvial aquifer would be designated as EPA Class II ground water (currently and potentially a source for drinking water). 

This section of the ROD provides the history of the Site and a brief summary of NMED's discovery and initial investigation work prior to EPA's involvement. The "Proposed Rule" proposing the Site to the National Priorities List (NPL) was published in the Federal Register (Fed. Reg.) on September  13, 2001 at 66 Fed. Reg. 47612. The "Final Rule" adding the Site to the NPL was published in the Federal Register on September 5, 2002, at 67 Fed. Reg. 56757. The effective date of the Final Rule was October 7, 2002. There have been no removal or enforcement actions at the Site.

PCE has been used as a dry cleaning fluid throughout the United States. PCE, a chlorinated volatile organic compound (VOC) considered to be a hazardous substance and a probable human carcinogen, was detected at the Site in November 1994 while the NMED was overseeing a gasoline-contaminated soils and ground water leaking UST investigation at a former bottling plant located at 108 West Reed Street. Laboratory analyses of ground water samples collected during the 1994 UST investigation revealed PCE concentrations between 18 parts per billion (ppb) and 23,000 ppb. However, significant VOC concentrations were not detected in soil headspace screening samples except at one location, where a reading of 43 parts per million (ppm) was recorded for a sample collected at a depth of 29 feet. The highest observed PCE concentration of 23,000 ppb was detected in a ground water sample taken from the alley adjacent to the northeast corner of the building at 1123 South Main Street. Subsequent investigations determined that historical dry cleaning facilities that formerly operated from the mid-1950s to 1976 in the vicinity of the 1100 block of South Main Street were the most likely source of this PCE contamination.

The NMED Ground Water Bureau initiated further investigations in November 1994 following the discovery of PCE in the 1100 block of South Main Street. NMED investigation work included a survey to identify domestic wells in the area, sampling of the domestic wells, installation and sampling of 14 new monitoring wells, a shallow soil vapor survey, and a soil vapor extraction (SVE) pilot test.

Approximately 22 private domestic and irrigation wells were identified, southeast of the suspected PCE  source area, through a search of well logs maintained by the New Mexico Office of the State Engineer (OSE) and in response to NMED press releases. Between 1994 and July 1995, ground water samples were collected from 15 of these wells with PCE concentrations ranging from less than 1 ppb to 260 ppb detected. Three of the residences using wells were subsequently connected to the City of Roswell water supply. The domestic wells were sampled again in April and October 2000 and PCE concentrations ranging from less than 1 ppb to 193 ppb reported.

A shallow soil gas study was performed in late 1995, which consisted of measuring/ screening soil vapors with a portable field analyzer [photoionization detector (PID)] at an array of shallow boreholes excavated to a depth of 2 to 3 feet. Elevated concentrations of total volatiles were detected in borehole headspace vapor tested at locations immediately south of the building at 1107 South Main Street.

An SVE pilot test was conducted by NMED in March 1996 to determine the potential effectiveness of SVE as a remedial technology. The SVE testing revealed that SVE had an estimated radius of influence of 5 feet, at a flow rate of 26 cubic feet per minute and initial PCE mass recovery rate of 26 pounds per day (lb/day). The small radius of influence observed from this testing indicates limited SVE effectiveness.

Thirteen monitoring wells were installed by NMED between September and November 1995 within an alluvial aquifer underlying the 1100 block of South Main Street (the Source Area). A 14th well was also installed approximately 0.6-mile southeast near the intersection of Jackson and Buena Vista streets. All monitoring wells, including those present at the neighboring UST site, were sampled between 1994 and 2001 and PCE concentrations ranging from less than 1 ppb to 27,000 ppb reported.

NMED prepared a comprehensive summary of its investigation findings, along with recommendations for remediation in July 2001. The report  concluded:
-Only a limited number of receptors have been affected. No persons who have a domestic well where PCE has been detected are consuming the water. All residents are connected to the City of Roswell water supply. However, there is potential risk associated with dermal and inhalation exposure where ground water is being used for irrigation purposes.
-PCE has been detected in four of the City of Roswell's public water supply wells at concentrations between 0.3 and 3.8 ppb. However, the levels present do not exceed EPA's National Primary Drinking Water maximum contaminant limit (MCL) of 5 ppb, and there is no evidence that PCE detected in the municipal wells is associated with the Site.
-Further investigation and remediation of the Source Area (1100 block of South Main Street) and ground water plume must be performed to prevent further plume migration and impacts to the public water supply.
-Remediation of vadose zone soil should be performed using ISCO, and remediation of Source Area ground water performed using accelerated bioremediation. 

NMED did not provide a recommendation for remediation of the larger ground water plume because of insufficient information, but did recommend installation of additional monitoring wells and evaluation of the Site for inclusion on the EPA's NPL. The Site was listed on the NPL effective October 7, 2002.

A ROD addressing operable unit 00 (OU00) was prepared in September 2008.

The Griggs and Walnut Ground Water Plume Superfund Site is located in the City of Las Cruces (CLC), Dona Ana County (County), New Mexico. The County is located in the south central part of the state and borders Mexico and Texas at its southern boundary. The Site is a ground water contaminant plume approximately 1.8 miles by one-half miles in size. The Site is defined by soil vapor samples and ground water samples found to be contaminated with primarily perchloroethylene (PCE, also known as tetrachloroethene or tetrachloroethylene). The PCE contamination detected in ground water begins at about 190 feet (ft) below ground surface (bgs) and affects the local municipal water supply to depths of about 650 feet bgs. There are four CLC municipal supply wells (Well Nos. 18, 19, 21, and 27) that have been affected by the PCE contamination at concentrations exceeding the Maximum Concentration Limit (MCL) for PCE established by the Federal Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA). The Site contamination is located in the subsurface generally between East Griggs Avenue and East Hadley Avenue, extending east to beyond Interstate 25 (I-25), and west to beyond North Solano Avenue. The property uses in this area are predominately recreational, light industrial/commercial, and residential land uses.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is the lead agency for the Remedial Action at the Site. The New Mexico Environment Department (NMED) is the support agency. The Potentially Responsible Parties (PRPs) for the Site are the CLC and the County. The CLC and the County entered into a Settlement Agreement with EPA on April 20, 2005, and financed EPA's Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (RI/FS) for the Site. The CLC and County entered into a memorandum of agreement with one another, and formed a local consortium called the Joint Superfund Project (JSP) prior to settling with EPA and assisting with the RI/FS. The JSP also assisted by performing a fate and transport ground water model anal ysis for the Site and assisted with the completion of the RI/FS. The fate and transport model was instrumental in the development of the alternatives for the Site.

The PCE-affected ground water occurs within the Mesilla Bolson Aquifer, an aquifer used by the CLC for public drinking water supply and irrigation. This aquifer extends below the entire length of the Mesilla Valley. Ground water occurs 100 ft or more bgs within the Site boundaries. A limited number of private wells also tap into this aquifer along with the municipal water supply wells. Among the private wells that remain in use, the property owners primarily use the wells for home landscape irrigation. Five of the private wells are located within one-half mile of the known boundary of PCE-affected ground water (i.e., plume boundary). There are no private wells known to exist within or immediately down-gradient of the plume boundary.

The CLC Well No. 18 is located northwest of the intersection of East Griggs Avenue and North Walnut Street, between East Griggs and Hadley Avenue (on the north side of the Dona Ana County Transportation Department [DACTD] maintenance facility). The CLC Well No. 19 is located on the west side of I-25 at the east end of East Griggs Avenue. The CLC Well No. 21 is located along the west side of I-25 at the east end of Craig Avenue. The CLC Well No. 27 is located near the southeast corner of the East Griggs Avenue and North Walnut Street intersection.

In 1993, the SDWA formally added PCE to the list of contaminants to be monitored in drinking water supplies during compliance monitoring. That same year, NMED detected PCE contamination in CLC Wells Nos. 21 and 27. In 2000, PCE was first detected in CLC Well No. 24 at slightly less than 1 micrograms per liter (ug/L). CLC Well No. 24 is located about one mile south of CLC Well Nos. 18, 19, 21, and 27. Three unaffected municipal supply wells (CLC Well Nos. 20, 26, and 61) are located between CLC Well No. 24 and CLC Well Nos. 18 , 19, 21, and 27.

The Site was added to EPA's National Priorities List (NPL) of Superfund sites on June 14, 2001 (66 Federal Register 32235 [June 14, 2001]). At the time of listing, four CLC municipal drinking water supply wells (CLC Well Nos. 18, 19, 21, and 27) were known to be affected by PCE contamination at concentrations above the MCL of 5 ug/L. The highest and most variable concentrations of PCE were found in CLC Well No. 18, ranging from slightly above (or below) 5 ug/L to over 45 ug/L. The concentrations of PCE in the other affected supply wells have increased over time, but have stayed near (slightly above or below) the MCL.

PCE has also been detected in the past at concentrations below the MCL in one private well (LRG-3191, located southwest and outside of the plume) and in one public school irrigation well (LRG-1457, located south and outside of the plume, near CLC Well No. 24). At the private residential well, the property owner reports that well LRG-3191 is used primarily for residential landscape watering. Recent samples at this well show no detections of PCE. Lynn Middle School used well LRG-1457 in the past to provide landscape irrigation at the school, but this well is no longer in service because of mechanical problems.

Of the four affected supply wells, only CLC Well No. 21 remains in service. PCE concentrations at this well have been detected at slightly above, or slightly below the MCL of 5 ug/L. The CLC manages Well No. 21's usage under a blending program approved by the NMED Drinking Water Bureau (DWB) on September 24, 2002. The CLC designed the Well No. 21 blending program to mix affected water with unaffected water in the Upper Griggs Reservoir in order to reduce PCE concentrations to levels below the MCL before the water reaches the distribution system. The CLC monitors the concentration of PCE in the Upper Griggs Reservoir to ensure that concentrations of PCE remain below the MCL. Periodic sampling performed in 2005 (from January  2005 through December 2005) revealed PCE concentrations at the Upper Griggs Reservoir ranged from not detected to 3.2 ug/L (with an average concentration of about 1.7 ug/L).

The NMED provided the first regulatory response at the Site. After PCE was detected at the CLC municipal supply wells by the NMED DWB, the NMED Superfund program performed a preliminary site assessment and site inspection activities in consultation with EPA. The NMED analyzed ground water and soil samples collected at new and existing monitoring well locations and tested soil vapor at the DACTD maintenance facility. The results confirmed the presence of PCE in ground water, soil vapor, and in soil. PCE was detected in only one soil sample, at a concentration of 241 micrograms per kilogram (ug/kg). This sample was collected at 135 ft bgs at MW-5. PCE was detected in the shallow soil vapor at the DACTD maintenance facility at concentrations up to 12 parts per billion by volume (ppbv).

EPA's Hazard Ranking System (HRS) documentation describes the results of these collective investigations as the basis for EPA adding the Site to the NPL. The data collected by NMED were helpful in establishing preliminary data trends and the NMED information was used to help characterize the nature and extent of contamination.

The EPA summarized the results and conclusions from this first mobilization in the report entitled "Identification of PCE Release Areas Report (IDRA Report)." The IDRA Report identified three source areas where PCE was released into the environment and helped support the issuance of the Special Notice Letters to the PRPs. These three PCE source areas are located as follows:
1. Near the intersection of East Hadley Avenue and North Walnut Street (along the former Crawford Municipal Airport runway and along the former arroyo that runs parallel to, and south of the former airport runway).
2. At the Dona Ana County Transportation Department (DACTD) maintenance facility on East Griggs Ave nue.
3. At the property where the former New Mexico Army National Guard facility was located on East Hadley Avenue.

On April 20, 2005, EPA signed a Settlement Agreement with the CLC and the County. This agreement addressed completion of the RI/FS at the Site. The CLC and the County formed the JSP to facilitate their participation in the remedial process. The EPA then formed a Technical Work Group with NMED and JSP to provide a forum for stakeholders to participate in the completion of the RI/FS and to provide input related to stakeholder needs. In addition to supporting and assisting field data collection data efforts, the JSP modeled flow and transport of PCE in the ground water to refine the conceptual site model (CSM) and to support the evaluation of remedial alternatives in the FS.

Working under the Settlement Agreement EPA, JSP and NMED finalized the RI/FS in November 2006. Prior to the Settlement Agreement, EPA had been conducting the early stages of the RI to determine the nature and extent of the ground water and soil vapor contamination throughout the Site. The JSP provided funds to complete the RI/FS through the Settlement Agreement and helped provide technical assistance as well as financial support towards the RI/FS. Ground water and soil vapor samples were collected and analyzed to complete the nature and extent characterization of the PCE contamination and to perform a baseline human health risk assessment (BHHRA). The BHHRA included modeling of indoor vapor intrusion, using soil vapor samples collected near residential properties and near recreational buildings. These data helped evaluate whether PCE vapor from shallow soil directly underlying the residential properties or recreational facilities presented an unacceptable risk to human health.

The Site is characterized by a broad mix of commercial, public recreational, light industrial and residential land uses. Just north of CLC Well No. 18 and extending between North Solano Drive and North  Walnut Street, a large portion of this area is served by various recreational facilities such as soccer fields, baseball and basketball facilities, and skate boarding designated areas. Residential neighborhoods are present west of North Solano Drive, east of North Walnut Street, north of East Hadley Avenue, and south of East Griggs Avenue. The rest of the area along East Hadley Avenue and East Griggs Avenue between North Solano Drive and just east of North Walnut Street, light industrial/commercial, activities are visible, along with the DACTD maintenance facility located on Griggs Avenue and the CLC fleet facility located on Hadley Avenue. Other commercial and light industrial properties can be found along the major roadways in the vicinity of the Site, including East Lohman Avenue, North Solano Drive, and East Spruce Avenue.

Development in the area of the Site has resulted in changes in land uses since the 1950s. The current land use activities and associated zoning are not expected to change in the near future. The community however, within the city limits continues to grow, and the demands on the ground water resource are expected to continue increasing. Ground water is the primary source of potable water for the area, and most, if not all municipal, industrial, and private wells are screened in the Lower Hydrologic Zone (LHZ).

A Record of Decision addressing Operable Unit 1 was completed in June 2007.

The Grants Chlorinated Solvents Plume (GCSP) Site is located in the City of Grants, Cibola County, New Mexico. The site is bounded by Second Street to the west; Adams Avenue and Jefferson Avenue to the North; Anderman Street, Washington Avenue, and Mesa View Elementary School property to the east; and Stephens Avenue and the Rio San Jose to the south. The GCSP Site is located in a mixed commercial and residential area.

The approximate area of ground water contamination at the GCSP Site is 20 acres. The approximate elevation of the Site is 6,420 ft above mean sea level (msl). The National Superfund Database Identification Number for the Site is NM007271768. The GCSP Site is a fund-lead site, with the EPA being the lead agency for the remedial activities, and the New Mexico Environment Department (NMED) the support agency. The Potential Responsible Party (PRP) for the site did not participate in the Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (RI/FS).

Dry cleaning operations have been historically performed at multiple facilities within the GCSP Site, although only a single dry cleaning facility, Holiday Cleaners at 715 First Street, is currently active. Dry cleaning has historically been performed at the R&L Laundry (reportedly prior to approximately 1987), at an abandoned facility at 605 First Street just north of Washington Avenue, and at a former Holiday Cleaners location at 313 First Street north of Stephens Avenue. The active Holiday Cleaners has operated at its current location since approximately 1969, and under the current ownership since approximately 1975.

Chlorinated solvents were first identified in ground water at the GCSP Site in 1993, during a NMED - Petroleum Storage Tank Bureau (NMED-PSTB) investigation of leaking underground storage tank (UST) sites in the vicinity. Several possible sources for the release of chlorinated solvents to the ground water were identified during the subsequent NMED Preliminary Assessment (PA), the NMED Site Investiga tion (SI), and the RI. The PA considered all of the UST sites in the vicinity of the ground water plume as potential sources for chlorinated solvents.

However, there was no record of the use or storage of chlorinated solvents at any of these sites. Several other sites were identified that are presently using or may have used chlorinated solvents in the past. These include the following locations:

-Holiday Cleaners (715 First Street)
-Former Holiday Cleaners (313 First Street) (currently Audio/Video Hill)
-R&L Laundry (604 First Street)
-Abandoned Dry Cleaning Facility (605 First Street)
-Former Wash 'n Clean World (located in Baties Shopping Center on north side of
Stephens Avenue between First Street and Anderman Street)
-Former Mountain States Telephone and Telegraph Company (MST&T) (621 Geis Street) maintenance yard, which is now a private residence and automotive hobby shop
-A work shed located behind a private residence at 700 First Street

Based on interviews conducted by the NMED-Superfund Oversight Section (NMED-SOS), the current and past owners of Holiday Cleaners on 715 First Street have used tetrachloroethene (PCE) for a number of years. During interviews, the current owner of Holiday Cleaners reported that historically PCE leaked from cleaning equipment onto the building floor, as well as from a storage container maintained in the rear portion of the building. When the container was full, PCE occasionally overflowed onto the ground surface in response to thermal expansion of the PCE fluid. This equipment has been removed from service and upgraded and the PCE storage tank is no longer in use at the Holiday Cleaners. The RI conducted by EPA identified the Abandoned Dry Cleaners property on First Street as a secondary source of ground water contamination. The remaining suspected locations identified above were not determined to be sources for ground water contamination based on available information.

Land use at the site currently includes  mixed residential homes and commercial businesses. Small businesses are mainly located along First Street and properties to the east are mostly residential. A daycare facility is located at the corner of Monroe Avenue and Peek Street and is just outside of the plume area. Other notable nonresidential structures within the plume boundary are the Knights of Columbus building on Geis and Jefferson Avenue and a bowling alley at the corner of Jefferson Avenue and Peek Street. To the east of the plume boundary is an elementary school. Based on the history of the area the future land use is unlikely to change from the current uses.

The shallow ground water at the GCSP Site is currently not used by residents in the area. However, owners are not legally prohibited from using the local ground water. The drinking water source for the City of Grants is from two upgradient wells approximately 2 miles west (upgradient) of the Site. The City of Grants is planning to install an additional supply well within 0.75 miles west of the Site. The interaction between the shallow aquifer and the deeper aquifer is not well known at this time and will be the subject of investigation prior to the design of the remedial alternatives for the GCSP Site. The future ground water use at the Site is as a potential drinking water source for the City of Grants.

A Record of Decision (ROD) addressing Site-wide Operable Unit (OU) 00 was completed in June 2006.
