Fort Eustis is located in southeastern Virginia, and borders the city of Newport New, Virginia.  Fort Eustis is an 8,228-acre military training facility that hosts a number of specialized US Army schools, plus garrisoned troops and support activities to manage the installation.  The installation is not a Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) permitted facility.  Fort Eustis is owned and operated by the U.S. Department of the Army and is located on the western side of a low-lying peninsula formed by the York River and the James River estuaries.  This peninsula is approximately 30 miles upstream of the confluence of the James River and the Chesapeake Bay.  The James River is a major commercial fishing and recreational resource.  It is the third largest tidal tributary of the Chesapeake Bay and the most productive estuary in Virginia.  Approximately 17,500 military personnel, their dependents, and civilians live or work at the installation.

The site began operations in 1918 as a training center known as Camp Abraham Eustis.  In 1923, it became a permanent military installation renamed Fort Eustis.  From 1931 to the early1940s, Fort Eustis was operated by several nonmilitary Federal agencies for various uses.  During World War II, it resumed military operations and was used for intensive antiaircraft training.  In 1946, Fort Eustis became the Transportation Corps Training Center, providing operations training in rail, marine, amphibious, and other modes of transportation.  In 1988, the U.S. Army Toxic and Hazardous Materials Agency identified 34 potential waste sources at Fort Eustis. The sources include unlined landfills, pesticide storage areas, firefighting training areas, maintenance shops, and range and impact areas resulting from antiaircraft training activities.  A landfill that received hazardous wastes is located at the headwaters of Bailey's Creek, a 160-acre wetland area adjacent to the site.  The Central Heating Fuel Spill Area, where waste oils w ere stored, is on a bluff overlooking Bailey's Creek.

EPA initially evaluated seven sources based on documented releases of hazardous substances to surface water.  Two of the sources are adjacent to Bailey's Creek, a 160-acre, low-lying wetland area.  Sampling conducted in 1987 and 1990 indicated contamination of sediments from Bailey's Creek.  The contamination included PCBs, chlordane, dichlorodiphenyldichloroethane (DDD), dichlorodiphenyldichloroethylene (DDE), DDT, and lead.  Fish collected from Bailey's Creek contained PCBs.  Sampling conducted at Bailey Creek during the summer of 1999 indicated PCB concentrations exceeding 2,200 parts per million (ppm) in sediment samples.  An Interim Removal Action addressing contamination at Bailey Creek has been completed at the site to address PCB contamination.  Long Term Monitoring and an FS are planned at the site.  In addition, a phased approach Removal Action to address lead contamination at the Former Skeet Range is ongoing.

Brown's Lake once was used as a drainage lagoon for the adjacent Helicopter Maintenance Area (HMA) and the upgradient Locomotive Area.  The lake was used for recreation but was closed to water sports and fishing in the late 1970s by the Fort Eustis Preventive Medicine Group.  A 1990 survey of Brown's Lake indicated that fish had lesions, ectoparasites, and skeletal deformities.  Contaminants detected in the lake in 1987 included PCBs, pesticides, and polyaromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs).  Sediment sampling in 1990 revealed contamination by PCBs and heavy metals in the lake and a tributary to the lake below the Locomotive Area.  An Interim Removal Action was initiated in the winter/spring of 1999 to address the contamination at Brown's Lake. The Removal Action was completed in the summer of 1999.  Long-term monitoring is currently being conducted at the site, and an FS is being evaluated.  Surface drainage from Brown's Lake flows south through a sanitary landfill adjacent to the HMA and enters w etlands along the Warwick River and Milstead Island Creek drainage way.

Sampling in Milstead Island Creek found sediments contaminated with PAHs and pesticides.  Wetland areas surround the site and are used for recreational and fishing purposes.  Groundwater monitoring wells at the landfills are sampled semi-annually (April - October).  Additional sampling and a Feasibility Study will be conducted at the site during 2004.
A Feasibility Study (FS) is currently being conducted at the Fire Training Area and includes additional sediment sampling in wetland areas surrounding the Fire Training Area, and deep well groundwater sampling. A Treatability Study is being discussed to identify the extent of a plume at the site.

An oil recovery system was installed at the Helicopter maintenance area in December 1995. This system is still in operation and is operating under the auspices of an approved corrective action plan that was submitted to the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality.

Fort Eustis initiated a field sampling program at Eustis Lake in October 1996 and it was completed in December 1996. The Army has submitted to EPA a draft RI for Eustis Lake and EPA has responded to the draft. Eustis Lake has a catch and release fishing restriction currently imposed at the site. Results from the Eustis Lake site RI indicated unacceptable levels of PCBs in fish tissue samples, as well as PCB's, pesticides and metals found in sediment. A Feasibility Study to address the remedial alternatives for Eustis Lake has been initiated, and should be completed in 2004.

Fort Eustis was proposed to the National Priorities List (NPL) in January 1984 and finalized on the NPL in December 1994.  A Federal Facility Agreement (FFA) for the site is being negotiated.

Operable Unit 1

The Site known as Bailey Creek, FTEUST-36 and Operable Unit #1 (OU-1), is located inside the boundary of the United States (U.S.) Army installation designated as Fort Eustis, Virginia. Under the Bas e Realignment and Closure Commission Report (2005), Fort Eustis realigned with Langley Air Force Base. On October 1, 2010, Fort Eustis became Joint Base Langley-Eustis and the Garrison functions changed to the 733d Mission Support Group. The Directorate of Public Works changed to 733 Civil Engineer Division and the Environmental and Natural Resource Department became the Environmental Element.

Bailey Creek is located inside the boundary of Fort Eustis, Virginia in the northwest corner of the facility. The Creek flows northwest into Skiffes Creek and to the James River. It is tidal throughout its entire length (approximately 1.5 miles) with less than 3 feet (ft) variation in depth between high tide and low tide. Depths measured in the upper and middle reaches during a reconnaissance survey in July 2007 at high tide ranged from 1.5 ft to 3.5 ft. The Creek's width varies from 3 feet at its upper end to more than 500 feet where it empties into Skiffes Creek.

The Creek collects drainage from an area of approximately 1.06 square miles, including areas of Fort Eustis along its northwestern boundary and the area immediately to the northeast. Bailey Creek is situated in a topographically low wetlands area. Drainage ways empty into the Creek on both the northern and southern banks. The upland edge of the Creek consists of a series of fingers that project into the wetland. These upland fingers are wooded and steep-sided, often rising 10 to 30 feet above the wetland.

Tidal input is the dominant source of water in the Creek. There is very little sustained freshwater input from the watershed, including groundwater. Groundwater elevations suggest that the small groundwater discharge to the Creek likely originates from upland areas both north and south of the Creek. The hydraulic gradients north and south of the Site mimic surface topography.

Fort Eustis was placed on the National Priorities List (NPL) on December 16, 1994. Important Fort Eustis historical events and re levant dates in the Site chronology are listed below. The identified events are illustrative, not comprehensive.

The PCBs detected in Bailey Creek are primarily the result of historical inputs, and continued resuspension of the in-creek sediments. The likely historical source of PCBs to Bailey Creek was a transformer fire in the Enlisted Barrack's area in the 1970s. This event would have allowed the oil containing PCBs to enter Storm Drain System 17, which discharges from Outfall 018. PCB-containing sediments along the Outfall 018 drainage served as a continuing source of PCBs to sediments in Bailey Creek following the release in the 1970s.

In the 1990s, following a preliminary assessment/site inspection, three phases of remedial investigation (RI) and an RI report were completed.  A monitoring program was implemented to assess the concentration, distribution, fate and transport of PCBs and lead in Bailey Creek sediment and surface water. The program was comprised of six semi-annual (Fall 1995 through Spring 1998) monitoring events to evaluate the temporal and spatial distribution of contaminants. Based on the RI report recommendations and subsequent monitoring results, an interim remedial action (IRA) consisting of hot-spot excavation of contaminated sediments was planned for the Outfall No. 18 tributary to Bailey Creek (drainage swale) and the surrounding wooded area and downstream marsh.  The IRA was completed in June 2000 to address PCB hot spot contamination in the Outfall No. 18 tributary (drainage swale) and to prevent further downstream migration of PCB-contaminated sediment into Bailey Creek. The top two feet of PCB-contaminated sediment were excavated from the drainage swale as well as soils from the surrounding wooded area and the marsh area downstream of Outfall No. 18. Excavated soil was disposed off-site. The excavated areas were backfilled to original elevations with clean fill and re-vegetated. Additional sampling and analyses were conducted to  characterize post-IRA contamination remaining in Creek sediments and re-assess the risks associated with the Site. The post-IRA characterization of PCBs in sediments at the Bailey Creek Site and the subsequent human health and ecological risk assessments were addressed in the focused feasibility study for the Site.

A Record of Decision for Operable Unit 01 of Fort Eustis was completed in September 2011.

Operable Unit 2 (Brown's Lake)
Brown's Lake is a man-made freshwater lake in the southern portion of the Fort Eustis Main Post Area. The Lake was formed in the 1950s by constructing an earthen dam across a small stream flowing south towards the Warwick River. The Lake is roughly triangular in shape, with the earthen dam forming the base of the triangle at the Lake's southern end. Brown's Lake has an approximate length of 650 feet, a maximum width of about 300 feet, and an approximate total surface area of 121,000 square feet. The Lake is very shallow at the northern end, and becomes progressively deeper as it approaches the dam. The maximum water depth in the Lake is approximately 10 feet.

The Lake's source is generally storm water runoff from various land use areas including vehicle maintenance facilities, a locomotive maintenance shop, and residential areas. The Lake is primarily fed by a stream emptying into the northern end of the Lake, the Upper Ditch, and discharges into a stream at the southern end of the Lake, to the Lower Ditch. The discharge stream flows into a tidal wetland and then into the Warwick River, which is located approximately 1,800 feet south of the Lake. At present, impacts to sediment in the Upper Ditch and Brown's Lake are lingering results of historical operations associated with the activities described above.

During a 1982 water quality study, the US Army Environmental Health Agency (USAEHA) observed fish with lesions in Brown's Lake and recommended that the Lake be off-limits to fishing; however, no sources of contamination  were identified for the Lake at the time. As a result, Brown's Lake has remained off-limits to fishing since that time. Signs posted along the shoreline of Brown's Lake prohibit fishing and swimming.

During site investigations of Brown's Lake conducted since 1982, sediment, water, and fish tissue samples have been collected, and monitoring of the benthic community has been conducted. Pesticides, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), metals, and petroleum hydrocarbons have been detected in the sediment of the Lake and drainage ditches.

Subsequent investigations through the 1980's and 1990's found that sediment in Brown's Lake and Upper Ditch was impacted by polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and Polynuclear Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs), pesticides, base-neutral acid extractable compounds (BNAs), total fuel hydrocarbons (TFH), heavy (TFH-H) and light (TFH-L) fractions, and metals. The investigations also found that the benthic population of Brown's Lake and the drainage ditches consisted of few individuals divided into only two species. This is an indicator that the biota of Brown's Lake was stressed by contamination, as the two species present were identified as resilient to contamination. The investigations led to an Interim Removal Action (IRA) in late 1999, which involved the removal of sediment from the Upper Ditch, draining the Lake, capping the Lake bottom, and removal of excess sediment from the southeastern corner of the Lake. The Lake was refilled and a monitoring program was conducted from 2000 to 2004.

Post-IRA monitoring analyzed sediment and surface water for PCBs, PAHs, pesticides, and metals in the Lake, Upper Ditch, and Lower Ditch. In 2004, fish tissue was also collected and analyzed for the above listed constituents. Additionally, the monitoring program contained a biotic indicator element via the collection and identification of benthic organisms.

After completion of five years of post-IRA monitoring , the 2004 Monitoring Report concluded that surface water quality in the Lake and the drainage ditches had generally been stable since the IRA. The post-IRA monitoring, however, found that a number of constituents continued to exceed US EPA Biological Technical Assistance Group (BTAG) screening values. The 2004 Monitoring Report concluded that though pesticide levels in the Lake sediment have not changed significantly for the five years after the IRA, the pesticide levels in Upper Ditch sediment have demonstrated a notable increase in concentration. In addition, semi-volatile organic compounds (SVOCs), which include PAHs, have been increasing primarily in the Upper Ditch, but to a lesser extent in the Lake, for the previous five years. Metals, including cadmium, chromium, copper, lead, and mercury, have also been detected above BTAG screening values in the Upper Ditch and Lake.

As an additional part of the post-IRA monitoring program, surveys of fish and benthic organisms have been performed. Benthic surveys of the Lake and drainage ditches have found that the number of organisms and species diversity has increased during the post-IRA monitoring from 2000 to 2004. Fish tissue collection and analysis was performed in 2004, five years after the restocking of Brown's Lake, which occurred immediately following the IRA. The samples of fish tissue collected in 2004 had 12 pesticide compounds and a single PCB compound detected. Most of these constituents detected in the fish tissue were detected at levels above USEPA Region III Risk-Based Concentration (RBC) values. In addition, ten metals were detected in the fish tissues samples at concentrations exceeding RBCs. The presence of these constituents in fish tissue at concentrations exceeding their RBCs contributes to an increased risk to human health for trespassing recreational fishermen. This increased risk is demonstrated in a supplemental Human Health Risk Assessment that evaluates this potential exposure pathway.

 
Overall, the post-IRA monitoring indicated the Lake had improved with respect to pre-IRA conditions. Increasing levels of a number of constituents, however, indicate the potential for ongoing impacts, degradation, and increased risk to human receptors. These increasing levels of constituents of potential concern have been attributed to impacted sediment in the lower half of the Upper Ditch. While this sediment was capped in place during the IRA, it is now believed to be migrating from beneath the cap.


Approximately 10,067 military and 6,269 Department of Defense (DOD) and contractor civilians are assigned or working at Fort Eustis. Also, approximately 3,545 military personnel and their dependents reside on Fort Eustis. While no residences are situated immediately adjacent to the Brown's Lake site, some are within a short walk. The best description of current land use would be green-space (i.e., the area around the pond) and undeveloped (area around the drainage ditches).

At present, no residences surround (i.e., are immediately adjacent to) the Lake or drainage ditches, and the land is not used for commercial or industrial uses. While the Lake does have a potential for limited recreational uses (e.g., swimming, wading, and fishing), warning signs have been posted prohibiting these activities. In addition, the drainage ditches offer little recreational opportunity due to topography, but could be susceptible to trespasser traffic. Thus, there are no receptors to the sediment in the Lake at this time; however, trespassers are potential receptors of sediments in the drainage ditch.

Fort Eustis worker personnel or residential population exposures to the surface water through water consumption would not be expected, as the Lake, due to its small size, would not be a reliable supply of water. It would be expected that Newport News Waterworks would continue to supply drinking water to Fort Eustis. In addition, swimming, wading and fishing in the Lake are prohibi ted, and signage is posted. 

Based on master planning issues for Fort Eustis, the facility is expected to remain government property. The potential for future development of the Lake and drainage ditches is minimal due to extremes in topography, as well as poor soils for building (i.e., Lake sediments would be unsuitable for any form of construction for habitation). Therefore, it can reasonably be expected that the land use of the pond and drainage ditches would remain similar to current use. Thus, future land use and potential receptors mimic current conditions, with the following exception: 

If homes are built closer to the drainage ditches, it could be reasonably expected that there is a greater opportunity for trespasser activities. As the area is not intended for recreational activities, adults and children that enter the area would be considered trespassers.

A ROD addressing OU 2 was completed in September 2007.

Operable Unit 03:

This ROD determines that no remedial action is necessary for sediment and surface water at Milstead Island Creek (FTEUST-27) at Fort Eustis, Virginia. United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has designated this Site as Operable Unit 03 (OU-03). The source of funds for Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act (CERCLA) activities at Milstead Island Creek will be those authorized and appropriated annually by Congress under the Environmental Restoration, Army (ER,A) appropriation in the Department of Defense Appropriations Act.

No federal or state enforcement activities have been undertaken at Milstead Island Creek.

Milstead Island Creek is a tidal waterway that links the James and Warwick Rivers. The creek is located in the southern portion of the Fort Eustis Main Post Area. Milstead Island Creek was initially a natural waterway until a drainage canal was constructed as a link between the James and Warwick Rivers during the Civil War. The resulting water way consists of three d istinct sections that comprise the extent of OU-03: the original extent of Milstead Island Creek, the dredged link in the center, and Butler's Gut (hence forth, unless specified otherwise, references to Milstead Island Creek include the complete extent of OU-03). The entire water way is tidal and flows in both directions, alternating between flowing into the Warwick and James Rivers in time with the tides. The drainage way is approximately 8,700 feet long and ranges from 40 to 100 feet across and 2 to 6 feet deep. The Site contains wetlands at both the James River and Warwick River intersections. The creek intersects the James River, along Harrison Road near the intersection of Taylor Road, and the Warwick River, adjacent to and south of Landfill 7.

Milstead Island Creek is a tidal waterway that extends in an east-west alignment from the Warwick River at the eastern boundary of Fort Eustis to the James River, which forms the western border of the Installation.

During investigations of Milstead Island Creek conducted since 1989, sediment and water samples have been collected and the biota of the creek have been examined. Pesticides, metals, and fuel-related polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) have been detected in the sediments and surface water of the creek.

Currently, approximately 4,510 military personnel and 4,944 Department of Defense (DoD) civilian and contractors are assigned to or working at Fort Eustis. As of 2006, there were 7,277 Permanent Party Active Duty Soldiers (including students) and 4,905 civilians on post, with 5,128 military personnel residing on post. While no residences are situated immediately adjacent to the Milstead Island Creek Site, some are within a short walk. Furthermore, the best description of current land use would be green-space or undeveloped. There are no current or planned restrictions on site use or access.

At present, no residences surround (i.e., are immediately adjacent to) the creek, and the land is not used  for commercial or industrial uses. The creek has a very limited potential for recreational uses (e.g., wading and fishing). In addition, the Creek could be susceptible to trespasser traffic, which by the nature of the site would be similar to recreational uses.

Fort Eustis worker personnel or residential population exposures to the surface water through water consumption would not be expected, as the creek, due to its small size and brackish nature, would not be a reliable supply of water. The Newport News Waterworks supplies drinking water to Fort Eustis. However, incidental ingestion of surface water during recreational or maintenance activities is possible.

Based on the master plan for Fort Eustis, the facility is expected to remain government property for the foreseeable future. The potential for future development of the creek is minimal due to local topography and the need for drainage in the area. Therefore, it is likely that the land use of the creek will remain similar to current use.

A ROD addressing OU-03 was completed in October 2008. 

Operable Unit 4:

Eustis Lake is a 45-acre reservoir located in the western portion of the main post. The lake was constructed between 1953 and 1956 by placing an earthen dam supporting a roadway and concrete spillway in a low-lying drainage area near the mouth of a tidal tributary to the James River. The lake receives stormwater from a large portion of the installation. The lake, which has an average depth of 4 feet and a maximum depth of 8 feet, is used for recreational purposes primarily by installation personnel seeking fishing and recreational boating activities. Elevated levels of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and pesticides were detected in fish and sediment collected from the lake for several studies. There have been no documented cases of spills or dumping of PCB contaminated materials (e.g. transformer oils) into the lake; however, transformer oil spills have been noted in the Enlisted Barracks a rea located north of the lake.

Previous Investigations
Montgomery Watson 1995 Background Site Sampling
Montgomery Watson conducted a remedial investigation (RI) at five sites at Fort Eustis. Eustis
Lake was identified as a background site for comparison of fish tissue data for one RI site, Brown's Lake. Numerous PCB congeners were detected in the liver analysis for catfish and muscle analysis for both catfish and shad at concentrations ranging from 331 to 1,605 micrograms per kilogram (ug/kg) (wet weight) for the shad and from 30 to 310 ug/kg for the catfish.

USACHPPM 1995 Human Health Risk Assessment
The U.S. Army Center for Health Promotion and Preventive Medicine (USACHPPM) conducted an interim human health risk assessment (HHRA) on the existing and newly collected fish data for a more detailed evaluation of potential health threats associated with consuming fish taken from Eustis Lake. Upon initial evaluation of the fish data, a preliminary evaluation was sent to Fort Eustis encouraging the issuance of a fish advisory and implementation of a "catch and release" program. Fort Eustis subsequently issued new policy concerning the lake in which a "catch and release" program was instituted.

Malcolm Pirnie 1997 RI
Malcolm Pirnie conducted a RI at Eustis Lake in 1997 to assess the nature and extent of contamination and to conduct a baseline HHRA and ecological risk assessment (ERA). The\ sampling program included the collection of numerous surface water, sediment, soil, and fish tissue samples with analysis for the target compound and target analyte lists. 

Malcolm Pirnie 2003/2004 Sampling Event
In 2003 and 2004, Malcolm Pirnie conducted a sampling and analysis program at Eustis Lake that included the collection and analysis of sediment and fish tissue samples. The purpose of this sampling program was to assess trends in the PCB data primarily in the Cove No. 2 and 8 areas since the last sampling event, which occurred in 1997. PCB concentrations in t he Cove No. 8 sediments increased between 1996 and 2004 while PCB concentrations in sediments in the Cove No. 2 area have changed little between 1996 and 2004. There was little change in PCB concentrations in the largemouth bass based on the 1996 and 2003 samples, which is somewhat consistent with the sediment data.

Current and Potential Future Land and Resource Uses
This section describes the current and future Site uses and identifies the potentially exposed populations at or near the Site under current and potential future conditions.

Current Situation
Approximately 4,510 military personnel and 3,390 DoD civilians and contractors are assigned to or are working at Fort Eustis. There are approximately 6,855 military dependents in addition to assigned military personnel. While no residences are situated immediately adjacent to the Eustis Lake Site, some are within a short walk. Furthermore, the best description of current land use would be recreational as primarily installation personnel seeking fishing and recreational boating activities use the site for recreational purposes.

Recreational users may come into contact with lake sediments by wading into the lake. In addition, the lake could be susceptible to trespasser traffic, which by the nature of the site would be similar to recreational uses.

Surface Water
Fort Eustis worker personnel or residential population exposures to the surface water through water consumption would not be expected, as the lake would not be a reliable supply of water. The Newport News Waterworks supplies drinking water to Fort Eustis. However, incidental ingestion of surface water during recreational activities is possible.

Based on the master plan for Fort Eustis, the facility is expected to remain government property for the foreseeable future. Therefore, it is likely that the future land use of the lake will remain similar to current use.

A Record of Decision addressing Operable Unit 4 of the Fort Eustis Site was completed in September, 2009.

OU 5: DOL Storage Yard Site, Building 1607
The DOL Storage Yard Site, Building 1607, is located on the installation at the intersection of Wilson Avenue and Patch Road in the post's northern developed area.  The yard itself is approximately 310 feet by 110 feet.  Three storage sheds are located along the northern edge of the yard.  Currently, the storage yard area within the fence-line is asphalt paved and is used for storage of government vehicles as well as contract vehicles, equipment, and communications-related supplies (such as cable).

Electrical transformers, equipment, and containers of various pesticide products were stored in the fenced-in, gravel DOL Storage Yard from 1980 to 1991.  At some time in the past, lightning apparently struck an oil switch transformer and its contents were spilled onto the ground.  The specific types and quantities of chemicals stored in the yard could not be established due to the uncertain historical use of the yard and numerous governmental activities using the site.  In July 1987, the Storage Yard was paved with four inches of gravel and 2 inches of asphalt.  It was then returned to service as a storage yard.

Polynuclear Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs), phthalates, and metals were detected in numerous surface (0- to 6-inch depth) and subsurface soil samples upgradient and downgradient of the site as well as at the site itself.  DDE and DDT were detected in the majority of soil samples collected at the site, in the drainage ditch along Patch Road, and downgradient of the site.  The highest concentrations of these compounds were detected in surface soils in the southern and central portions of the site.  The drainage ditch located along Patch Road also had high concentrations of the compou nds due to surface runoff from the fenced yard.  DDE and DDT concentrations greatly decrease with increasing depth in the soil borings at the site, in the drainage ditch along Patch Road, and downgradient of the site.

PAHs and phthalates were detected in sediment samples in the upper portions of the drainage ditch adjacent to the site, in the ditch in the wooded area near the site, and in samples collected from the wetland area near where the ditch discharges to the wetland.  Pesticides were detected in all sediment samples collected at the site, with DDD, DDE and DDT being the dominant compounds detected.  The highest concentrations of these compounds were detected in the ditch in the southeast corner of the site and in the wooded area at approximately the mid-point of the southern fence.  Pesticide concentrations greatly decrease from the surface to the 2- to 3-foot depth.  Numerous metals were detected in the ditch along the western boundary of the fenced yard.

Results of the risk assessment conducted as part of the Remedial Investigation (RI) indicated potential risks for the following populations due to the concentrations of pesticides and PAHs in site soils: Fort Eustis DOL Storage Yard Site workers exposed to surface soils within the fenced yard;  potential future residential populations exposed to surface soils within the fenced yard and sediment in the drainage ditch (this scenario presupposes that housing would be developed in the future); and various ecological risks including exposure of herbivorous mammals to surface soil in the fenced yard, exposure of small carnivorous mammals to surface soil and sediment in the wooded area, and exposure of semi-aquatic mall and avian species to surficial sediment in the tidal wetland area.

Thus, consideration of both human health and ecological potential exposures at the site indicate that remediation of site soils and sediment in the storage yard and surrounding areas is warranted.

A Record of Decision ( ROD) for OU 5 was signed in September 2001.

The Naval Surface Warfare Center-Dahlgren (NSWC) covers 4,300 acres in Dahlgren in King George County, Virginia, 40 miles south of Washington, DC, on the west bank of the Potomac River. The area is primarily residential and agricultural. Established in 1918, NSWC serves as the principal Navy research, development, testing, and evaluation facility for surface ship weaponry, naval mines, strategic systems, and warfare analysis. NSWC encompasses two areas: the Main Site, which occupies 2,678 acres, and the Explosive Experimental Area (EEA), an isolated testing range on a 1,614-acre island separated from the Main Site by Upper Machodoc Creek. Located on the Main Site are areas used for air operations, a security area where a variety of ordnance are tested, laboratories, computer facilities, administrative offices, and residential areas. The on-base population includes 3,200 civilians, 100 military personnel, and 154 housing units.

Two aquifers underlie NSWC: the shallow Nanjemoy Aquifer, which supplies drinking water to a small number of private homes; and the deeper Potomac Group Aquifer, which provides municipal water supplies and drinking water for NSWC. Municipal and private wells within 4 miles of NSWC supply drinking water to an estimated 6,900 people.

The Navy has identified several sources of contamination at NSWC-Dahlgren. The Fenced Ordnance Burial Area (Site 2) was used for burial for excess munitions and has metals detected in the surface soils, in addition to several nearby trenches filled with wastes. The Disposal/Burn Area (Site 9), a 2 to 3 acre landfill, is contaminated with polyaromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and the soils and sediment contain phenols, metals, pesticides waste. Site 9 is a threat to the groundwater as well as to the wetlands that surround the landfill. Hideaway Pond (Site 10) contains sediment and fish which are contaminated with mercury. The Chemical Burn Area (Site 12), was used for decontamination of testing materials and has 1,1 ,1-trichloroethane (TCA) in the alluvial aquifer below the site. The 1400 Area Landfill (Site 17), 5 to 10 acres in size, received municipal waste for three years in the 1970s and canisters of mercury may have been disposed of in this area. Low levels of mercury were detected in groundwater underlying Site 17 and in stream sediments nearby. The Transformer Draining Area (Site 19), where electrical transformer oil containing polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) was drained, has PCB contamination to a depth of 4 feet. The Former Electroplating Waste Underground Storage Tank (Site 20) has minor solvent contamination in the groundwater. The Pesticide Rinse Area (Site 25), where pesticide containers were rinsed, is contaminated with pesticides. The Lead Contamination Area (Site 37) contains used sand from firing ranges with residual heavy metals as contaminants. Landfill A: Stump Dump Road (Site 46), used in the 1940's and 1950's for general disposal, has PAH, PCB, and heavy metal contamination. The Fill Areas Northeast EEA (Site 50) is a small burial dump that has PAH and heavy metal contamination. The Gambo Creek Ash Dump (Site 61), where residual ash was deposited, may contain heavy metals, especially mercury, and is in contact with sediments in Gambo Creek. There are also six sites that are related to the former use of munitions, including depleted uranium, and explosives.

The response actions undertaken by the Navy have greatly reduced the potential threats and risk from several sites. Low levels of mercury were detected in ground water underlying Site 17 and stream sediments in the vicinity of the landfill. Sediments and the fish of Hideaway Pond (site 10), located downstream from the landfill, also are contaminated with mercury. A landfill cap has been constructed at Site 17 and the risks related to Site 10 will be reduced by implementing institutional controls. 1,1,1-trichloroethane (TCA) has been detected in the alluvial aquifer below Site 12. A response action w as started at this site in 1998 and recent monitoring of the groundwater indicates TCA levels are below the site-specific action levels. Site 9 was a threat to the groundwater below its location as well as to the wetlands that surround the landfill. The completed cap has eliminated the exposure threat from this site. Selected metals were detected in the surface soils in addition to several trenches filled with wastes near Site 2. The completed cap at Site 2 has also eliminated the exposure threat from this site. PCBs were discovered in the soil of the Transformer Area (Site 19) to a depth of 4 feet. A removal action has reduced the potential threat at this site, and a NFA Record of Decision was signed in September 1999. Soils at Site 25 were contaminated with several pesticides and a remedial action at this site was mostly completed by October 2001. Removal Actions at the two depleted uranium sites reduced residual risks and a NFA ROD was signed in September 2001 for these sites. A removal action was undertaken during the summer of 2002 at Site 50 to manage a small amount of metal waste and to help restore wetlands. A ROD for Site 46 was signed in September 2001 to excavate waste material from the old landfill and marsh area. The excavation at Site 46 was completed in October 2002. A ROD for Site 6 was signed in September 2002 to excavate waste material from the marsh area and excavation was started in April 2003.

NSWC was proposed for inclusion on the National Priorities List (NPL) in February 1992. The listing was finalized in October 1992.  A Federal Facility Agreement (FFA) between EPA Region 3, the Commonwealth of Virginia, and the U.S. Department of the Navy was finalized on September 30, 1994.

Operable Unit 1 (OU1):

Site 12, the Chemical Burn Area, is one of several Installation Restoration (IR) sites located at the NSWCDL facility.  Site 12 is situated on the Mainside of the base and is bounded on its western side by Gambo Creek.  Groundwater produc tion wells supplying potable water to NSWCDL are over 600 feet deep and located over 4,000 feet south of Site 12.  These wells are unaffected by contaminants related to Site 12.  The closest residences, on-base Navy housing consisting of over 150 homes, are within 6,000 feet southwest of Site 12.

Activity in the vicinity of Site 12 first began about 1952 when a 600 by 600-foot area was cleared of vegetation.  Later, around 1964, two pits were observed in the cleared area.  It was reported that fuel had been used to burn laboratory materials and metallic hardware and equipment at the pit.  The last burn was conducted in the fall of 1982.  By 1986, the pit and fence at Site 12 were no longer visible due to the amount of vegetation present in the area.  By late 1986, the fence was removed and the pit was filled in by regrading the area.  Known or potential wastes disposed of at Site 12 include fuel oils, spent solvents, metals, caustics, hypochlorite, polymers, glues, and decontaminated chemical warfare agent solution.

Site 12 was identified as a potential area of contamination in the initial investigation performed in the early 1980s.  Confirmation of contamination at Site 12 occurred between 1983 and 1984.  Results of sampling at the site were reported in 1986.  One of the two Records of Decision (RODs) issued in September 1997 address Site 12.

Site 37 is the area near Building 200 where gun butt sand was deposited. The remainder of the peninsula is considered part of the active Machine Gun Range.

Site 37 is located within the Machine Gun Range on the west side of a peninsula that extends into Upper Machodoc Creek. Site 37 is a small site where large quantities of sand containing residues from ammunition fired in nearby indoor ranges were historically disposed. Information taken from historical aerial photography, the Remedial Action Plan developed for cleanup of existing indoor machine gun firing bays, and interviews with personnel indicate that the Mach ine Gun Range was constructed in the early 1940s and has been expanded in at least two phases. The Machine Gun Range is currently active. Ammunition is fired at several indoor bays impacting sand "traps" located behind targets. One firing bay originates indoors but fires outdoors and is considered to be an open range. Several of the indoor bays were used solely for storage. The entire peninsula, including the outdoor area in the vicinity of the range building (Building 200) and the indoor firing bays, makes up the Machine Gun Range. Another range firing line is located north of the old Depleted Uranium (DU) Gun Butt area (Site 49). The DU Gun Butt area has been remediated according to human health and ecological risk goals and requires no further action. In 2001, a no further action Record of Decision (ROD) was signed for Site 49.

The ammunition historically fired at the range was reported to include 0.50- and 0.566-caliber, 7.62-millimeter (mm), 20-mm, and 40-mm anti-personnel munitions. Remnants of some of these rounds have been noted outside the range building in the surrounding area. The indoor bays are designed so that projectiles are fired into sand traps. The impact from projectiles crushes the sand and a portion of the projectile into a fine dust. The combination of projectile remnants and sand is referred to as gun butt sand. Over time, the accumulation of projectiles in the sand creates a ricochet hazard. Up to half of the sand in each trap has been replaced periodically. 

During times of heavy use, the sand may have been changed each month. The Machine Gun Range has not been used heavily since the mid-1970s. Until 1980, the sands were removed from the indoor bays through ceiling openings and placed in the proximity of Building 200. Sands removed from the range were not sifted to remove any spent rounds. The locations where these sands were placed near Building 200 comprise the area targeted for potential remedial action, which is Site 37. Since 1980 , sands have been removed and disposed offsite by a disposal contractor.

Between 1937 and 1943, dredged materials from the channel of Upper Machodoc Creek were placed both on the Machine Gun Range shoreline and across Upper Machodoc Creek on the Explosive Experimental Area (EEA) shoreline. No information was available regarding the chemical composition of the gun butt sands disposed of at Site 37 between 1937 and 1943 or of the dredged materials. The potential presence of Munitions and Explosives of Concern (MEC) at Site 37 is very high. Forty-mm anti-personnel munitions from range activities are a likely hazard, particularly offshore along the eastern perimeter of the peninsula. The offshore area has been designated as a "heavy grenades" area because of the bombardments that have historically taken place there and that could continue in the future.

Aerial photography indicates that the peninsula shoreline has changed over time in the vicinity of the Machine Gun Range. The eastern and southeastern edges of the Site 37 area of investigation are actively eroding from waves and currents in the Potomac River and Upper Machodoc Creek. These areas are not associated with gun butt sand disposal. Accretion appears to be occurring in the area where the northwest arm meets the western part of the site.

A site visit conducted during the Remedial Investigation (RI) indicated the presence of munitions-related materials at the soil surface only near the point where the northwest arm meets the western part of the peninsula near Building 200. Soils in this area were also noted to be of a different color and texture than those found elsewhere on the peninsula and were thought to represent gun butt sand.

Currently, Site 37 is located on an active range. Land use adjacent to Site 37 consists of range facilities including open land northeast of the site and a boat dock with support facilities to the west. Current operations at the active machine gun range are expected to co ntinue, future residential use is not anticipated. The potential sediment contaminants are most likely attributed to current and former machine gun operations and not past gun butt sand disposal activities at Site 37. The Machine Gun Range is an active range. Any subsequent closure of the range will be conducted in accordance with applicable laws and regulations protective of human health and the environment. Groundwater and surface water uses will not change. Groundwater as a potential potable source is limited due to naturally occurring iron and manganese. Direct contact with surface water and sediment at the site is not anticipated, since access to the site is controlled, due to unexploded ordnance related to range activities.

In September 2004, the Navy and USEPA Region III signed a ROD which selected Alternative 3 as the remedy for Site 37. The 2004 ROD selected the remedy of complete excavation with offsite disposal. The major components of the 2004 selected remedy were: 1) removal of surface soils contaminated by gun butt sand disposal, 2) offsite disposal of soils, 3) site restoration via backfilling and vegetative seeding, and 4) shoreline restoration to mitigate coastal erosion.

Based on the recent excavations and removal actions at Dahlgren (Sites 4, 6, 15 and 47) the Navy has realized that explosive safety concerns and restrictions could significantly extend construction schedules, resulting in excessive cost growth. The potential presence of MEC at Site 37 is very high. During pre-design, munitions larger than identified during the development of the Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (FS) were identified. Therefore, excavation would require a more extensive explosive-safety-arc setback of 1,000 feet or more impacting the nearby administrative offices, housing, critical research and development operations, and navigable waterways for extended periods of time.

On the basis of recent Naval Support Facility Dahlgren (NSFD) activities, the es timated time to implement Alternative 2 was increased from 3 months to 6 months and for Alternative 3 from 4 months to a range of 6 to 12 months. Because of the explosive safety risks involved with excavation, Alternative 2 will not only be more cost effective than Alternative 3, but will also require less time to construct then Alternative 3. Therefore, Alternative 2, as presented in the FS, is the selected remedy.

A ROD Amendment addressing Site 37 (OU 10) was completed in August 2006.

Between 2002 and 2005, the Navy implemented an enhanced bioremediation technology to further reduce groundwater volatile organic contaminant concentrations via cometabolism. The process involved injection of propane and nutrients via air sparging wells. This system, in the down gradient area, reduced contaminant concentrations; however, groundwater concentrations were not reduced sufficiently in the source area to allow for unlimited use and the system did not affect soil contaminant levels.

In 2006, the Navy further investigated geochemical and biological conditions in the shallow aquifer at Site 12. The results of this investigation indicated that some groundwater concentrations were increasing in the source area. The results of the investigation and the evaluation of alternatives were documented in the Technical Memorandum 2006 Sampling Results and Remedy Evaluation Site 12 Chemical Burn Area. The recommendations of this document included the excavation of the former burn pit and the continued monitoring of Site 12 groundwater following excavation.

An Explanation of Significant Differences addressing Operable Unit 1 was completed in September 2007.

The closest residences, on-base Navy housing consisting of over 150 homes, are within 6,000 feet southwest of Site 2.

In the early 1970s, a fenced landfill area was excavated and reportedly used for the disposal of metal ordnance materials that may have contained explosive residue. OU3:

The Disposal/Burn Area (Site 9) is an inactive landfill, approximately 5 acres in size, located off Caskey Road in the central portion of the Mainside, adjacent to the southwestern shore of Gambo Creek and associated marsh area.  Gambo Creek and its associated marsh area border approximately two-thirds of the site to the east and north.  The majority of the remaining area surrounding Site 9 is wooded.  Historic information indicates that the facility used this area as a sanitary landfill from the early 1940s until 1971.  However, dumping and occasional burial of construction debris and tree stumps continued until 1984.  Site 58, also called the Building 1350 Landfill, is an extension of Site 9 to the southwest and is approximately 0.7 acre in size.  This landfill was in use during a later period than Site 9.  A ROD addressing contaminated soil, groundwater, and sediments associated with Site 9 and Site 58 was completed in September 1998.


OU5:

The 1400 Area Landfill (Site 17) is an inactive landfill lo cated in the northwest corner of the NSWCDL.  Two unnamed drainage tributaries form the western and eastern boundaries of the site.  A small pond is located in the western portion of the site with a marsh on the eastern portion.  The site was used as a landfill, where municipal solid waste and construction debris were deposited, compacted, and covered on a periodic basis during the early 1970s and possibly until 1978.  The landfill is fully vegetated with tall grass.  Soil cover exists over the majority of the landfill.  The area bordering the site to the north and west is undeveloped and heavily wooded.  A ROD addressing contaminated soil and groundwater at Site 17 was completed in September 1998.

Site 6, Terminal Range Airplane Park, is located on the western bank of Gambo Creek, in the southeastern portion of the Mainside. Land within a 0.5-mile radius includes an industrial area to the south and southwest, magazines for ordnance storage to the north and west, a primarily undeveloped area to the northeast, and the Terminal Range to the east. The nearest Research, Development, Test and Evaluation (RDT&E) areas and operations areas are located approximately 0.35 mile south and east of Site 6. The nearest residential housing is located approximately 1 mile southwest of the site.

The site covers approximately 3 acres and is vegetated primarily with grass. A gravel and dirt access road loops through the main part of the site. A locked gate and the surrounding woods limit vehicular access to the area.

No current or future recreational use of the marsh is anticipated, due to its shallow depth and limited accessibility. The mission of the base is currently expanding, and potential for future base closure and conversion to residential land use is considered minimal.

Shallow groundwater at Nava Surface Warfare Center Dahlgren (NSWCDL) is known to discharge to adjacent shallow water bodies such as the marsh adjacent to Site 6, rather than to migrate vertically t hrough confining units. This is based on U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) studies that show the ratio of median horizontal hydraulic conductivity of the water table aquifer to median vertical hydraulic conductivity of the upper confining unit to be 2,600:l. According to the USGS study, the water table aquifer at NSWCDL is of generally poor quality because of naturally occurring high concentrations of some metals, especially iron and manganese Poor water quality, coupled with the thin saturated thickness and locally high percentages of fine grained sediment, diminishes the potential use of the water table aquifer as an industrial or potable water source.

The primary productive aquifer in the vicinity of NSWCDL is the Potomac Formation. NSWCDL and Dahlgren municipal wells collect water from the Potomac Formation, approximately 600 to 800 feet below . ground surface (bgs). The water supply in this aquifer originates from an area several miles upgradient of Dahlgren, where the Cretaceous sands and gravels are exposed at the surface along the Fall Line. Minimal or no recharge to the Cretaceous aquifers occurs from the surface directly downward at NSWCDL because of the 300-foot thick low-permeability Tertiary sediments that act as confining beds.

Since the 1940s, Site 6 has been used to store scrap metal, empty drums, inactive airplanes, gun mounts, steel shelters for personnel and camera equipment, items awaiting testing, and telephone poles. A study of aerial photographs by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) shows evidence of filling activity at Site 6 beginning in the early 1950s. Aerial photographs show an access road leading north to a fill area (which extended into the wetland) near Gambo Creek and a ground scar located within the forested area southeast of the fill area. Filling operations continued through 1953, and the fill area south of the wetland appears to have been graded. In the 1960 images, mounded material located on the eastern side of the  clearing is apparent, as is evidence of a liquid discharge flowing westward from the material. In the 1962 aerial photographs, the surface of the fill area appears to have been graded again. The 1990 images show many objects including boats, scrap metal, barrels, missile bodies, and other equipment in the clearing and along the access road leading into the site.

In the fall of 1992, drums of the gun barrel preservative Cosmoline that had been stored on wooden pallets in the center portion of the site were removed and stored in a proper drum storage area prior to disposal. The drums were not sampled and no soil/sediment samples were collected in the vicinity of the drums.

The only structure on the site at the time of the remedial investigation (RI) was a sheet metal shed on the northwestern side of the loop road. The shed was in disrepair and contained three pallets of 100-pound sacks (many of which were ripped) labeled 'Virginia Materials Corporation, Norfolk, Virginia, Black Blast," a sandblasting agent.

A wide variety of other items were in storage at Site 6 at the time of the RI, including several steel personnel and camera shelters, several crated 1950s vintage jets, various gun mounts, large blocks of steel and concrete, ship anchors, a jet airframe, aircraft wing tanks, a large quantity of steel plating and metal stock, several telephone poles, and portions of cut-up large caliber gun barrels. These items were stored in the center and around the edges of the access road. In addition, the site has several piles of partially buried railroad ties in multiple locations along the fringe of the marshy area. These ties did not appear to be on-site for storage, but as part of past filling or disposal activities.
An area west of Site 6, the Gun Barrel Decoppering Area (known as EPA SWMU52) previously contained equipment used for the washing of gun barrels to remove the build-up of residues from repeated use. The barrels were washed in a sulfuric and chromic  acid bath. Due to a corroded valve on the acid bath, the contents and stormwater from the site were directed to the marshy area southwest of Site 6 (i.e., marsh cove). The decoppering operation area was remediated in July and October 1997, but its previous use and residual contamination in the drain line have been identified as the source of elevated chromium and arsenic levels detected in the marsh cove adjacent to and just west of Site 6.

A Site Screening Process (SSP) investigation was performed at Naval Surface Warfare Center Dahlgren Site (NSWCDL) in 1994 and 1995 to provide information to support a decision to either investigate further, implement a removal action, or conduct no further action at ten Priority 1 sites, of which Site 6 is one. The specific objectives of the SSP investigation were to: identify the type, location, and concentration of contamination at the study site; identify the site-specific physical characteristics that may influence contaminant distribution; and determine the potential for contaminant migration.

Field activities for the SSP consisted of two phases. Phase I field activities were conducted in June 1994 and involved a surface geophysical survey at several sites, including Site 6. The surface geophysical investigation consisted of both magnetic and electromagnetic (EM) terrain conductivity surveys. Phase 1 results, discussed in detail in a Technical Memorandum (TM), were used to guide Phase II activities by focusing the investigation on specific anomalies identified by these surveys.

Phase II field activities, conducted between December 15, 1994, and March 30, 1995, included: drilling soil borings; installing monitoring wells; collecting and analyzing groundwater, surface water, sediment, and surface and subsurface soil samples; surveying monitoring wells; and collecting groundwater level measurements. The SSP at Site 6 involved the installation of monitoring wells and the sampling of groundwater, surface water, soil, and  sediment. A total of 36 environmental samples were collected at Site 6. The analytical data generally indicated that polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and inorganics were the chemicals most often found at Site 6 in concentrations exceeding their respective screening guidelines or criteria. The SSP concluded that a Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (RI/FS) was needed at Site 6.

RI field activities were conducted during the winter of 1996 and 1997 in accordance with work plans approved by the U.S. Navy, EPA, and the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (VDEQ). The RI field activities consisted primarily of collecting environmental samples to investigate data gaps and provide sufficient data for completion of quantitative site-specific risk assessments. Based on the RI, contaminants identified at levels of concern included certain pesticides, PAHs, and metals. These compounds were distributed randomly in surface soils at the site. In the adjacent marsh sediment, certain pesticides, PAHs, volatiles, and metals were identified at ecological levels of concern. The compounds detected in the marsh may have resulted from transport through site erosion and/or surface water runoff, and/or direct waste deposition. A few PAH and phthalate compounds and some metals were also detected at levels of environmental concern in surface water samples collected from the site.

Additional FS field work was conducted in 2000 and 2001 to fill data gaps identified during the Site 6 RI and to provide the necessary data to evaluate remedial alternatives in accordance with the Focused Feasibility Studies (FFSs) Priority 1 Sites Project Plans. This work included re-sampling of groundwater, surface soils, subsurface soils, sediments, and surface water. A trenching effort was also conducted to determine the location, nature, and volume of buried wastes present in subsurface soils. Groundwater samples were collected from permanent monitoring wells and used to re-evaluate  potential human health risks under the residential use scenario. Results from the FS samples were compared with the RI sample results to estimate a more accurate concentration of chemicals in groundwater. The FS used a new groundwater sampling methodology that more accurately measures the true contamination levels in groundwater. The RI samples were collected using an older method that may have introduced soil particles into the sample, resulting in less accurate data. Surface water samples were collected using a methodology designed to minimize the presence of suspended solids and thus provide more representative metal concentrations in the surface water than those collected during previous RI sampling.

An ecological assessment of Gambo Creek within the Mainside of NSWCDL was conducted from September 25 through October 13, 1995. The objectives of this assessment were to: (1) analyze contaminant concentrations in surface water and sediments at selected locations throughout Gambo Creek to determine the nature and extent of contamination; (2) evaluate the health of the animals (such as worms and clams) that live in the sediment and the toxicity of sediment-bound contaminants; and (3) determine whether contaminants present in Gambo Creek were capable of accumulating in plants and animals. Sampling points were located along Gambo Creek and also placed downstream of Sites 2, 9, 12, 6, 45, and 46 to further assess the potential impact of these sites on the ecology of Gambo Creek. Surface water, sediment, small animals within the sediment, and fish tissue samples were collected. The results of this assessment indicated that contaminant concentrations high enough to impact plants and animals were generally restricted to localized areas in Gambo Creek near Sites 2, 9, and 12. No evidence was found for widespread contamination that would pose a significant risk to plants and animals in the creek. Phase I1 of the Gambo Creek Ecological Risk Assessment was initiated in Octob er 2000 to further characterize contaminant concentrations in sediment and fish tissue, and to evaluate risks to marsh vegetation and wildlife feeding on the aquatic biota. Contaminants were identified in sediment near Site 6 that indicate unacceptable risks to ecological receptors.

A Record of Decision was completed for NSWCDL Site 6 September 23, 2002.
